Unit 1: Getting Started

1. Setting Up the Development Environment

To start programming in Java, you need two fundamental tools: a Java Development Kit (JDK) to compile and run your code, and an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) or code editor to write it efficiently.

1. Installing the JDK (Java Development Kit)

We recommend installing Oracle OpenJDK or Eclipse Temurin (Adoptium) (LTS version, such as Java 17 or Java 21).

  • Download: Visit adoptium.net or Oracle's official Java portal.
  • Installer: Run the installer for Windows, macOS, or Linux and ensure the option "Add to PATH" and "Set JAVA_HOME" is checked.

2. Verifying Installation in Terminal

Terminal / Command Prompt 
# Check Java runtime version
java -version

# Check Java compiler version
javac -version

If installed correctly, you will see output displaying the version number (e.g., openjdk version "21.0.2").

3. Choosing an IDE

IntelliJ IDEA (Recommended)

The industry standard for professional Java developers. The free Community Edition provides intelligent code completion, refactoring tools, and built-in debugging.

Visual Studio Code

Lightweight and fast editor. Install the official "Extension Pack for Java" by Microsoft for IntelliSense, Maven/Gradle support, and test runners.

Unit 1: Getting Started

2. Anatomy of a Java Program

Every Java program consists of building blocks structured hierarchically: Packages → Classes → Methods → Statements.

Main.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}
Keyword / Component Role & Technical Explanation
public Access modifier allowing JVM and external code full visibility to the class or method.
class Main Blueprint container. In Java, all executable logic strictly resides inside a class definition.
static Allows JVM to invoke the main method without first instantiating an instance of the class.
void Return type indicating that this method returns no value to its caller.
main(String[] args) The canonical program entry point accepting command-line string arguments.
System.out.println() Prints text to standard console followed by a newline separator.
Unit 1: Getting Started

3. Your First Java Program

Follow these 3 quick steps to create, compile, and execute your very first Java console application:

  1. Create File: Open your editor and save a new file as Main.java. The filename must match the public class name exactly.
  2. Write Code: Type the standard entry point method and console output statement.
  3. Compile & Run: Execute via command line or click the "Run" button in your IDE.
Console Execution 
# Step 1: Compile source code into bytecode
javac Main.java

# Step 2: Execute bytecode via JVM
java Main

# Output:
Hello, World!
⚠️ Case Sensitivity Notice: Java is strictly case-sensitive. main is not equal to Main, and system.out.println will fail to compile because System must be capitalized.
Unit 1: Getting Started

4. How Java Code Gets Executed

Unlike languages that compile directly to native machine code (C/C++) or interpreted languages (JavaScript/Python), Java uses a hybrid two-phase execution model: Compilation to Bytecode followed by JVM JIT Execution.

1. Java Source Main.java (Human readable)
➔
2. javac Compiler Compiles to Bytecode
➔
3. Bytecode Main.class (Portable binary)
➔
4. JVM Execution JIT Compiler / Interpreter
➔
5. Hardware CPU Native Machine Code

JDK vs JRE vs JVM Triad

Component Full Form Core Function
JDK Java Development Kit Developer toolset containing compiler (javac), debugger, docs, and the runtime.
JRE Java Runtime Environment Runtime libraries and JVM needed to run compiled Java applications on client machines.
JVM Java Virtual Machine Execution engine that loads, verifies bytecode, and translates it into machine instructions.
Unit 1: Getting Started

5. 5 Interesting Facts about Java

1. Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA):

Java bytecode runs without modification on Windows, macOS, Linux, and embedded hardware provided a compatible JVM is installed.

2. Originally Named "Oak":

Created in 1991 by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems and originally named Oak after an oak tree outside Gosling's office, before being rebranded to Java in 1995.

3. Over 3 Billion Devices:

Powers millions of enterprise cloud backends, 90% of Fortune 500 server infrastructures, ATM networks, SIM cards, and Android smartphones worldwide.

4. Automatic Garbage Collection:

Java eliminates manual memory deallocation pointers (as in C/C++). An intelligent background Garbage Collector frees unreachable memory automatically.

5. Statically & Strongly Typed:

Variable types must be declared explicitly and checked at compile time, eliminating an entire category of runtime type crashes before code reaches production.

Unit 2: Types

10. Introduction to Types in Java

In Java, every piece of data is categorized by its Type. Because Java is a statically typed language, the type of every variable must be declared before it can be used, dictating both the value operations permitted and the exact memory layout allocated by the JVM.

1. Primitive Types (8 Types)

Store simple, raw numeric, character, or boolean values directly in fast Stack Memory (e.g., byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean).

2. Reference Types (Objects)

Store addresses (pointers) in the Stack that reference complex objects and data structures allocated on the dynamic Heap Memory (e.g., String, Arrays, Date, custom classes).

Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Variables in Java: Types, Scope, Memory & Naming Rules

1. What is a Variable in Java?

A variable is a reserved, named memory location used to store data in a program during execution. The stored value can be accessed and, when permitted, updated as the program runs.

In Java (which is statically typed), every variable has an explicitly defined data type that determines the kind of value it can hold and the exact amount of memory allocated to it.

Real-Life Student Record Example:

VariableDeclarationExample.java 
String name = "Abhinav";   // Stores textual data
int age = 21;              // Stores whole integer numbers
double percentage = 85.5;  // Stores fractional/decimal numbers

2. Formal Syntax of a Variable

Java Syntax Structure 
dataType variableName = value;

// Example:
int age = 21;
Syntax Component Example Role & Description
dataType int Declares the type of data (specifies memory size and allowed values).
variableName age Unique identifier used to reference the memory location.
value 21 The actual data literal assigned to the variable.

3. Types of Variables in Java (Scope & Lifetime)

Java classifies variables into three primary categories based on where they are declared and their lifecycle in memory:

A. Local Variable

Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Its scope is strictly confined to that method or block.

LocalVariableDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 21; // Local variable (allocated on call stack)
        System.out.println(age);
    }
}
⚠️ Critical Rule for Local Variables: Local variables do NOT receive default values from the JVM. You must explicitly initialize a local variable before reading its value, otherwise the compiler throws an error (variable might not have been initialized).

B. Instance Variable (Non-Static Field)

Declared inside a class but outside methods, constructors, or blocks. Created when an object is instantiated (on the Heap), and destroyed when the object is garbage-collected. Every object has its own distinct copy.

Student.java 
class Student {
    String name; // Instance variable
    int age;     // Instance variable
}

// In main method:
Student s1 = new Student();
s1.name = "Abhinav";
s1.age = 21;

C. Static Variable (Class Variable)

Declared using the static keyword within a class. Only one shared copy exists per class, stored in Metaspace/Method Area regardless of how many instances are created.

StaticVariableDemo.java 
class Student {
    static String college = "Ambalika"; // Shared across all Student objects
}

// Access directly using ClassName:
System.out.println(Student.college); // Output: Ambalika

4. Common Data Types Used in Variables

Data Type Code Example Category & Description
int int age = 21; Standard whole integers (32-bit).
long long population = 8000000L; Large whole numbers (64-bit; suffix with L).
float float price = 10.5f; Single-precision floating-point (suffix with f).
double double marks = 85.75; Double-precision floating-point (default decimal type).
char char grade = 'A'; Single 16-bit Unicode character enclosed in single quotes.
boolean boolean passed = true; Logical truth values (true or false).
String String name = "Java"; Textual sequence (a reference class, not a primitive).
💡 Primitive vs Reference Note: Java has exactly 8 primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean. String is an immutable reference class, not a primitive!

5. Declaration, Initialization, and Reassignment

These represent the three core lifecycle steps of a variable:

VariableLifecycle.java 
int number;      // 1. Declaration: Allocates name and type
number = 10;     // 2. Initialization: Assigns initial value
number = 20;     // 3. Reassignment: Updates the existing value

System.out.println(number); // Output: 20

// Combined declaration & initialization in a single line:
int count = 10;

6. Rules and Best Practices for Naming Variables

  • Legal Characters: May contain letters (A-Z, a-z), digits (0-9), underscores (_), and dollar signs ($).
  • Cannot Start with a Digit: 2age is illegal; age2 is valid.
  • No Whitespace or Hyphens: Spaces (student age) and hyphens (my-age) are syntax errors.
  • Keywords are Forbidden: Reserved words such as class, int, static cannot be used as identifiers.
  • Case-Sensitive: age, Age, and AGE are three distinct variables.
  • Naming Convention: Use meaningful, self-explanatory names adhering to standard camelCase.
Valid Identifiers Invalid Identifiers & Error Reason
int age = 21; int 2age; (Starts with a digit)
String studentName; String student name; (Contains space)
double totalMarks; double class; (Reserved Java keyword)
int _count; int my-age; (Hyphen parsed as minus operator)

7. Complete Working Java Program

Main.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String name = "Abhinav";
        int age = 21;
        double marks = 85.5;
        boolean passed = true;

        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
        System.out.println("Marks: " + marks);
        System.out.println("Passed: " + passed);
    }
}

Program Output:

Name: Abhinav
Age: 21
Marks: 85.5
Passed: true
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Primitive Data Types: Memory Sizes, Ranges & Default Values

1. What Are Primitive Data Types in Java?

Primitive data types are the foundational built-in data types predefined by the Java programming language. They store raw data values directly in memory (typically on the call stack) rather than references to memory locations.

Java provides exactly 8 primitive data types, categorized into four core groups:

  • Integer Types (Whole Numbers): byte, short, int, long
  • Floating-Point Types (Fractional/Decimals): float, double
  • Character Type (Single Character Unit): char
  • Boolean Type (Logical Truth Values): boolean

2. Master Comparison of the 8 Primitive Types

Data Type Size (Bits / Bytes) Value Range / Legal Literal Representation Default Field Value
byte 8 bits (1 byte) -128 to 127 (-2⁷ to 2⁷ - 1) 0
short 16 bits (2 bytes) -32,768 to 32,767 (-2¹⁵ to 2¹⁵ - 1) 0
int 32 bits (4 bytes) -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (-2³¹ to 2³¹ - 1) 0
long 64 bits (8 bytes) -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 (-2⁶³ to 2⁶³ - 1) 0L
float 32 bits (4 bytes) ~6 to 7 significant decimal digits of precision (suffix with f/F) 0.0f
double 64 bits (8 bytes) ~15 to 16 significant decimal digits of precision (default decimal type) 0.0d
char 16 bits (2 bytes) '\u0000' (0) to '\uFFFF' (65,535) (single UTF-16 code unit) '\u0000' (null char)
boolean JVM-dependent true or false false
⚠️ JVM Implementation Note: Java strictly specifies the exact bit sizes and 2's complement ranges for all numeric primitive types across every operating system. However, the exact physical memory size of a boolean is JVM-dependent (typically represented as a byte in arrays or 32-bit integer in stack operands).

3. Detailed Breakdown of Integer Types

A. byte (8 bits)

Ideal for saving memory in large arrays or processing low-level binary data streams.

ByteExample.java 
byte age = 21;
byte temperature = -10;

System.out.println(age);         // 21
System.out.println(temperature); // -10

B. short (16 bits)

Twice the size of byte, useful when memory conservation is required but numbers exceed 127.

ShortExample.java 
short marks = 25000;
System.out.println(marks); // 25000

C. int (32 bits)

The standard, most commonly used data type for whole numbers, loops, counting, and array indexing.

IntExample.java 
int salary = 50000;
int numberOfStudents = 300;

System.out.println(salary);           // 50000
System.out.println(numberOfStudents); // 300

D. long (64 bits)

Used when values exceed the 2-billion limit of int. Suffix integer literals with an L (or l, uppercase L preferred to avoid confusion with the number 1).

LongExample.java 
long population = 8000000000L; // Suffix 'L' required for literals exceeding int
System.out.println(population); // 8000000000

4. Floating-Point Data Types (float vs. double)

FloatingPointDemo.java 
float price = 99.5f;       // Single precision (suffix 'f' is required)
double percentage = 89.75; // Double precision (default decimal literal type)

System.out.println(price);      // 99.5
System.out.println(percentage); // 89.75
Feature float double
Memory Size 32 bits (4 bytes) 64 bits (8 bytes)
Precision ~6 to 7 decimal digits ~15 to 16 decimal digits (high precision)
Literal Suffix 10.5f or 10.5F (Mandatory) 10.5 (Optional d/D)
Typical Use-Case Memory-sensitive graphics or sensor feeds Standard mathematical & scientific calculations
💡 Financial Arithmetic Warning: Due to binary floating-point rounding errors (IEEE 754), never use float or double for currency and exact financial transactions. Always use java.math.BigDecimal for financial engineering.

5. Character Type — char

Stores a single 16-bit Unicode character enclosed in single quotes (' ').

CharExample.java 
char grade = 'A';
char symbol = '#';

System.out.println(grade);  // A
System.out.println(symbol); // #
⚠️ Unicode Surrogate Note: A Java char represents a single 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. Certain supplementary Unicode characters (such as certain emojis and historical scripts) require two char values, known as a surrogate pair.

6. Boolean Type — boolean

Represents truth values with only two possible states: true or false. Widely used for conditional branching and flow control.

BooleanExample.java 
boolean isPassed = true;
boolean isLoggedIn = false;

// Boolean expression evaluation:
int marks = 75;
boolean hasCleared = marks >= 40;

System.out.println(hasCleared); // Output: true

7. Complete Java Program: All 8 Primitive Types in Action

Main.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Integer types
        byte a = 100;
        short b = 20000;
        int c = 500000;
        long d = 8000000000L;

        // Floating-point types
        float e = 10.5f;
        double f = 99.99;

        // Character and boolean types
        char g = 'A';
        boolean h = true;

        System.out.println("byte: " + a);
        System.out.println("short: " + b);
        System.out.println("int: " + c);
        System.out.println("long: " + d);
        System.out.println("float: " + e);
        System.out.println("double: " + f);
        System.out.println("char: " + g);
        System.out.println("boolean: " + h);
    }
}

8. Primitive Types vs. Reference Types

Dimension Primitive Types Reference (Non-Primitive) Types
What is Stored Holds the actual raw value directly. Holds a memory address (reference) pointing to an object/array on the heap.
Predefined Scope Fixed to exactly 8 built-in types in Java. Created by programmer or library (Classes, Interfaces, Arrays).
Nullability Cannot hold null (compiler error). Can store null (leads to NullPointerException if accessed).
Method Invocations No methods can be called directly (e.g. a.toString() is illegal). Can invoke methods defined on the class.
Examples int, char, boolean, double String, Student, int[], Scanner
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Reference Types: Objects, Memory References & == vs .equals()

1. What Are Reference Types in Java?

A reference type is any non-primitive data type in Java where the variable does not hold raw data directly. Instead, it stores a memory reference (address) pointing to an object, array, or complex data structure allocated in the JVM Heap.

ReferenceTypeBasics.java 
String name = "Abhinav";       // Refers to a String object in the String Pool
int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30};  // Refers to an array object on the heap

Unlike primitive variables (such as int or boolean) which always store a concrete value, any reference variable can also hold null, indicating that it currently points to no object.

2. The Four Primary Categories of Reference Types

Reference Type Core Description Prominent Examples
1. Class Types Blueprints defining state (fields) and behavior (methods). String, Scanner, custom classes (Student)
2. Array Types Indexed collections of a fixed number of homogeneous elements. int[], String[], Object[]
3. Interface Types Abstract contracts specifying methods that implementing classes must fulfill. List, Map, Runnable, Comparable
4. Enum Types Specialized class types defining a fixed set of named constants. enum Day { MONDAY, TUESDAY }

3. Creating Objects & Accessing Fields

A class serves as a blueprint, while an object is a concrete runtime instance allocated on the Heap using the new keyword.

StudentObjectDemo.java 
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 's1' is a reference variable stored on the Stack;
        // 'new Student()' creates the actual object on the Heap:
        Student s1 = new Student();

        // Accessing object fields via the dot (.) operator:
        s1.name = "Abhinav";
        s1.age = 21;

        System.out.println(s1.name); // Abhinav
        System.out.println(s1.age);  // 21
    }
}

4. Understanding Reference Variable Semantics

When you assign one reference variable to another, no new object is created. Both variables now hold the exact same memory address, pointing to the identical object in the heap.

SharedReferenceDemo.java 
Student s1 = new Student();
Student s2 = s1; // Both s1 and s2 now point to the EXACT same Student object

s1.name = "Abhinav";
s2.name = "Rahul"; // Mutating via s2 changes the underlying object!

System.out.println(s1.name); // Output: Rahul
💡 Pointer Visualization: s1 ──┐
     ├──➔ [ Heap Object: name="Rahul", age=0 ]
s2 ──┘
Modifications made through s2 are immediately visible through s1 because only one object exists in memory.

5. The null Reference & NullPointerException

A reference variable initialized to null does not point to any allocated memory block.

NullPointerDemo.java 
String name = null;
System.out.println(name); // Prints: null

// Attempting to invoke an instance method on a null reference:
System.out.println(name.length()); 
// ❌ Throws: java.lang.NullPointerException (NPE) at runtime!
⚠️ Golden Rule: Always verify that an object reference is non-null (e.g. if (obj != null) or Objects.requireNonNull(obj)) before dereferencing methods or accessing fields to prevent runtime NullPointerException.

6. Comprehensive Comparison: Primitive Types vs. Reference Types

Feature Primitive Types Reference Types
Underlying Storage Direct raw value (stored on execution stack) Memory address pointer to heap object
Memory Allocation Fixed bit size determined by Java spec Dynamically allocated on the Heap via new
Can Hold null? No (compiler error) Yes (indicates unassigned reference)
Supports Methods? No methods (raw value only) Yes (can invoke any accessible member methods)
Default Field Value Numeric 0, boolean false, char '\u0000' Always null
Code Example int age = 21; String name = "Abhinav";

7. 🎯 Core Interview Concept: == vs. .equals()

One of the most frequently asked questions in Java technical interviews is the crucial difference between the identity operator == and the .equals() method:

Comparison Type What It Actually Evaluates Behavior on Objects
== Operator Reference Identity: Checks if both variables point to the exact same memory address. Returns true only if both references point to the identical heap location.
.equals() Method Logical Content Equality: Checks if two distinct objects contain equivalent data. Returns true if the internal content/characters are identical (when overridden by class).
EqualityComparisonInterview.java 
// Creating two distinct String objects explicitly on the Heap:
String a = new String("Java");
String b = new String("Java");

// 1. Reference comparison (different memory addresses):
System.out.println(a == b); // Output: false

// 2. Value/content comparison:
System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // Output: true
💡 Key Takeaway: For primitive types, always use ==. For reference types (especially String, collections, and custom domain models), always use .equals() when comparing contents!
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Primitive Types vs. Reference Types: Memory Models, Copy Semantics & Decision Guide

1. Introduction to the Dual Type System

In Java, all data types belong to one of two fundamental categories:

  • Primitive Types: Directly store concrete, standalone values (numbers, single characters, truth states) on the execution stack.
  • Reference Types: Store memory pointers (addresses) pointing to dynamically allocated objects, arrays, and complex structures on the JVM Heap.

Mastering this distinction is foundational for understanding memory management, method parameter passing (pass-by-value of references), object mutation, and technical interview questions.

2. Master Differences Matrix

Dimension / Feature Primitive Types Reference Types
Primary Purpose Represent simple, unboxed atomic values. Reference and coordinate complex objects or collections.
Prominent Examples int, double, char, boolean (8 types) String, Student, int[], List
Variable Contents Actual primitive value directly. A 64-bit/32-bit reference address (or null).
Can Store null? No (Compiler error). Yes (Indicates no active referenced object).
Method Invocations No methods available directly. Objects can provide methods (e.g. name.length()).
Default Values (Fields) Numeric 0 / 0.0, boolean false, char '\u0000' Always null
Equality with == Compares primitive raw values. Compares reference identity (memory addresses).
Object Creation Never created using new (direct literals). Created using new, factory methods, or literals.
⚠️ Critical Scope Rule for Defaults: Default field values apply exclusively to instance fields and static fields. Local variables declared inside methods do not receive default values and must be explicitly assigned before being read!

3. The Memory Difference Explained Through Code

Understanding how assignment (=) works differently for primitives versus reference types is essential to avoid accidental data mutation bugs:

ValueCopyVsReferenceCopy.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // 1. Primitive Assignment (Copies the actual Value)
        int a = 10;
        int b = a;  // 'b' receives a completely independent copy of 10
        b = 20;     // Modifying 'b' has ZERO impact on 'a'

        System.out.println("Primitive a: " + a); // Output: 10
        System.out.println("Primitive b: " + b); // Output: 20

        // 2. Reference Assignment (Copies the Memory Address)
        int[] x = {10, 20};
        int[] y = x;  // 'y' receives the SAME memory address pointing to the array
        y[0] = 99;    // Mutating index 0 via 'y' modifies the shared array!

        System.out.println("Array x[0]: " + x[0]); // Output: 99
        System.out.println("Array y[0]: " + y[0]); // Output: 99
    }
}
Primitive Assignment a = 10, b = 20 (Independent boxes)
vs
Reference Assignment x & y ➔ [ Shared Array: 99, 20 ]
💡 Memory Anatomy: Changing b does not change a because the primitive value is copied bit-by-bit during assignment. Conversely, changing an array element through y also changes what is observed through x because both reference variables point to the same array object on the heap.

4. 🎯 Key Interview Concept: == vs. .equals()

Because reference variables store memory addresses, the behavior of == differs radically between primitives and objects:

EqualityDemo.java 
String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = new String("Java");

// '==' compares whether both reference variables refer to the EXACT SAME object in memory:
System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // Output: false (two distinct heap objects)

// '.equals()' compares logical equality (actual textual characters):
System.out.println(s1.equals(s2));  // Output: true (same text content)

5. Practical Decision Guide: When to Use Each

  • Use Primitive Types: For high-throughput mathematical calculations, counting loops, simple flags, status codes, and array indexing where maximum execution speed and zero heap overhead are required.
  • Use Reference Types: When building domain models, working with collections (such as List, Set, Map), representing nullable values (e.g. database foreign keys or optional API payload fields), and leveraging object-oriented polymorphism.
  • Standard Types: Default to int for ordinary integer math and double for standard decimals. Use String for textual information and dedicated classes (e.g. Student) to encapsulate structured entities.

Strings in Java: Core String API, Built-in Methods & StringBuilder

💡 Two-Part String Architecture Guide: This section (Part 1) focuses on practical String manipulation: the core String API (length(), substring(), indexOf(), etc.), == vs .equals() semantics, string concatenation performance, and mutable StringBuilder. For the internal JVM memory architecture, String Constant Pool (SCP) Heap mechanics, and intern(), see Section 7: String Pool & Memory Deep Dive →.

1. What Is a String in Java?

A String is an indexed, immutable sequence of characters used to represent textual data in Java. It is a reference type provided in the core java.lang package, which means it is globally available without any import statement.

StringDeclaration.java 
String name = "Abhinav";
String language = "Java";
String message = "Welcome to Java Programming";

2. How to Create a String: Literal vs. new Keyword

Java provides two distinct mechanisms for instantiating strings with different memory locations:

Creation Mechanism Syntax Example Memory & String Pool Behavior
A. String Literal
(Recommended)		 String s1 = "Java"; Stored in the String Constant Pool (SCP) within the Heap. If "Java" already exists, Java reuses the existing pooled instance without allocating new memory.
B. Using new Keyword String s2 = new String("Java"); Guarantees the creation of a brand new object in the general Heap memory, even if an identical literal already resides in the String Pool.
CreationComparisonDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s1 = "Java";                  // Pooled reference
        String s2 = new String("Java");      // Distinct heap object

        System.out.println(s1); // Output: Java
        System.out.println(s2); // Output: Java
    }
}

3. Critical Property: Strings Are Immutable

Immutability means that once a String object is constructed on the heap, its internal character array cannot be altered. Any method that appears to modify a string actually creates and returns a new String object.

ImmutabilityProof.java 
String s = "Hello";
s.concat(" World"); // The returned new string is discarded!

System.out.println(s); // Output: Hello (Original object remains unchanged!)

// Correct pattern: Reassign the reference to point to the new string object:
s = s.concat(" World");
System.out.println(s); // Output: Hello World
💡 Why are Strings Immutable in Java?
  • String Pool Caching: Multiple references can point to the same literal safely without fear of one modifying it for others.
  • Security: Strings are used for database URLs, network connections, and passwords. Immutability prevents tampering.
  • Thread Safety: Automatically safe for concurrent access across multiple threads without synchronization.
  • Hashcode Caching: The hashcode is computed once and cached, making Strings ultra-fast keys in HashMap and HashSet.

4. Common Built-in String Methods

Method Signature Purpose & Return Value Concrete Example & Output
length() Total number of UTF-16 code units "Java".length() ➔ 4
charAt(int index) Character at the specified index (0-based) "Java".charAt(1) ➔ 'a'
substring(int begin) Extracts substring from beginIndex to end "Programming".substring(3) ➔ "gramming"
toUpperCase() Converts all characters to uppercase "java".toUpperCase() ➔ "JAVA"
toLowerCase() Converts all characters to lowercase "JAVA".toLowerCase() ➔ "java"
equals(Object obj) Compares textual content case-sensitively "Java".equals("Java") ➔ true
equalsIgnoreCase(String str) Compares textual content ignoring case "Java".equalsIgnoreCase("JAVA") ➔ true
contains(CharSequence s) Checks if character sequence exists within string "Hello Java".contains("Java") ➔ true
indexOf(int ch / String s) Index of first occurrence (-1 if not found) "Java".indexOf('v') ➔ 2
trim() Strips leading and trailing whitespace " Java ".trim() ➔ "Java"
replace(char old, char new) Replaces matching characters "Java".replace('a', 'o') ➔ "Jovo"
StringMethodsDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String name = "Abhinav Nagvanshi";

        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Length: " + name.length());
        System.out.println("Uppercase: " + name.toUpperCase());
        System.out.println("Lowercase: " + name.toLowerCase());
        System.out.println("Contains Java: " + name.contains("Java"));
        System.out.println("First character: " + name.charAt(0));
    }
}

5. 🎯 Master Interview Comparison: == vs. .equals() with String Pool

StringPoolEqualityDemo.java 
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";
String s3 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // Output: true  (Both point to identical pooled literal in SCP)
System.out.println(s1 == s3);      // Output: false (s3 points to a separate object in Heap)
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3)); // Output: true  (Content equality: both contain "Java")
💡 Golden Interview Rule: Always use .equals() (or equalsIgnoreCase()) when comparing String text contents in application code! Use == only when strictly verifying reference identity.

6. String Concatenation & Loop Performance

ConcatenationDemo.java 
// 1. Using '+' operator:
String firstName = "Abhinav";
String lastName = "Nagvanshi";
String fullName = firstName + " " + lastName;
System.out.println(fullName); // Output: Abhinav Nagvanshi

// 2. Using concat() method:
String a = "Hello";
String b = " Java";
System.out.println(a.concat(b)); // Output: Hello Java

7. Architectural Face-off: String vs. StringBuilder vs. StringBuffer

Dimension String StringBuilder StringBuffer
Mutability Immutable (constant content) Mutable (can append/modify) Mutable (can append/modify)
Thread Safety Safe (inherently thread-safe) Not thread-safe Thread-safe (synchronized methods)
Performance / Speed Slow for frequent modifications Fastest (no synchronization lock) Moderate (synchronization overhead)
Memory Storage String Pool + Heap Heap memory Heap memory
Best Practice Use Fixed text, keys, constants Building strings inside loops / single-thread Legacy code with multithreaded sharing
StringBuilderDemo.java 
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello");
sb.append(" Java"); // Modifies existing buffer without creating new objects

System.out.println(sb); // Output: Hello Java

8. High-Yield Interview Questions Checklist

  • 1. What is a String in Java? Reference type in java.lang representing an immutable character sequence.
  • 2. Why is String immutable? Caching security, thread safety, String Pool integrity, and hashcode caching.
  • 3. What is the String Pool? A special memory zone in the Heap that caches unique string literals to minimize memory allocations.
  • 4. Difference between == and .equals()? == compares heap memory addresses; .equals() compares character-by-character content.
  • 5. Difference between String, StringBuilder, StringBuffer? Immutability vs. mutability; thread safety and speed differences.
  • 6. Difference between length() and charAt()? length() returns total character count; charAt(i) retrieves the character at index i.
  • 7. Why is String preferred as a HashMap key? Because of immutability and pre-calculated hashcode caching, preventing key corruption after insertion.
Strings Series: Part 2 of 2

String Architecture Deep Dive: String Constant Pool (SCP), Memory Allocation & intern()

📌 Two-Part String Architecture Guide: This section (Part 2) focuses exclusively on the internal JVM memory architecture of Strings: why String was designed immutable, Heap vs SCP memory allocation, mutation lifecycles, and manual pool caching via intern(). For practical String methods, operations, and StringBuilder, see ← Section 6: Strings in Java (Core API).

1. Introduction: The Twin Pillars of Java String Architecture

In Java, String Pool and String Immutability work hand-in-hand to deliver memory efficiency, security, and predictability.

  • String Pool: A designated caching zone in the Java Heap where the JVM reuses existing string instances rather than allocating duplicate memory.
  • String Immutability: The architectural rule that once constructed, the internal char/byte payload of a String object cannot be modified.

2. What Is the String Constant Pool (SCP)?

Also referred to as the String Intern Pool, the String Pool is a specialized hashtable within the JVM Heap. When a string literal is created, the JVM checks the pool first:

  • If an equal string is already in the pool, the existing reference is returned.
  • If not, a new string object is created in the pool and returned.
StringLiteralPoolDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s1 = "Java";
        String s2 = "Java";

        System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // Output: true (Same pooled memory address)
        System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // Output: true (Same text contents)
    }
}
Reference s1 Stack Variable
➔
[ String Pool: "Java" ] One Shared Object in Heap
⬅
Reference s2 Stack Variable

3. Creating Strings Using the new Keyword

When you instantiate a string using new String("Java"), Java bypasses automatic pool reuse and explicitly creates a distinct object in the non-pool Heap.

NewKeywordDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s1 = "Java";             // Resides in String Pool
        String s2 = new String("Java"); // Resides in regular Heap outside the Pool

        System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // Output: false (Different memory addresses!)
        System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // Output: true  (Equal text contents)
    }
}
⭐ Industry Best Practice: Always prefer string literals (String s = "text";) for ordinary code. Use new String() only when there is an explicit requirement to maintain an isolated, unshared object in memory.

4. Mechanics of String Immutability

Any method on String that seems to modify content (such as concat(), replace(), or toUpperCase()) always allocates and returns a brand new String object. The original object is completely unaffected.

ImmutabilityCheck.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = "Hello";
        s.concat(" World"); // Return value is unassigned and lost!

        System.out.println(s); // Output: Hello

        // Reassigning captures the newly constructed object:
        s = s.concat(" World");
        System.out.println(s); // Output: Hello World
    }
}

5. Step-by-Step Memory Mutation Lifecycle

Observe how memory references shift when two variables point to the same string and one is concatenated:

ReassignmentLifecycle.java 
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = s1; // Both s1 and s2 point to "Java"

s1 = s1 + " Programming"; // A new String "Java Programming" is created

System.out.println(s1); // Output: Java Programming (s1 points to the new string)
System.out.println(s2); // Output: Java (s2 STILL points to the original "Java")
Step 1: Initial Assignment s1 & s2 ➔ [ "Java" ]
➔
Step 2: Concatenation & Reassignment s1 ➔ [ "Java Programming" ] (New Object)
s2 ➔ [ "Java" ] (Original Unchanged)

6. Why Is String Immutable in Java? (Architectural Rationale)

Pillar Architectural Benefit & Rationale
1. Security Strings store sensitive data: file system paths, network sockets, database connection URLs, and security credentials. If strings were mutable, an untrusted thread could alter a verified URL after permission checks.
2. String Pool Optimization If strings were mutable, changing the value via one reference (e.g. s1) would silently corrupt the data for every other variable sharing that pooled instance. Immutability makes pooling safe.
3. Thread Safety Read-only objects are inherently thread-safe. Multiple threads can access string instances concurrently without synchronization locks or race conditions.
4. Hash Code Caching Because the characters cannot change, Java computes hashCode() on the first call and caches the 32-bit integer in a private field. This makes Strings the most performant keys in HashMap and HashSet.

7. What Is the intern() Method?

The intern() method allows you to programmatically add or fetch a string from the String Constant Pool.

  • If an equal string already exists in the pool, intern() returns that canonical pooled reference.
  • If not, it places the string into the pool and returns its reference.
InternMethodDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s1 = new String("Java"); // Non-pool Heap object
        String s2 = s1.intern();        // Retrieves canonical String Pool reference
        String s3 = "Java";             // String Pool reference

        System.out.println(s1 == s2); // Output: false (s1 is heap; s2 is pool)
        System.out.println(s2 == s3); // Output: true  (Both point to the same pool instance!)
    }
}

8. Master Comparison: String Pool vs. String Immutability

Feature String Pool (SCP) String Immutability
What It Is A physical caching memory region in the Heap. An architectural design property of the String class.
Primary Goal Reduce redundant duplicate objects and conserve memory. Preserve data integrity, enable thread safety, and allow safe sharing.
Key Enabling Mechanism intern() method and String Literals. final char[] / byte[] internal array without setters.
Code Illustration String a = "Java"; String b = "Java"; (a == b) a.concat(" Code"); does not modify a.
Symbiotic Relationship The String Pool could not exist without immutability. Immutability enables the String Pool to operate safely.
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Escape Sequences in Java: Syntax, Special Characters & Best Practices

1. What Is an Escape Sequence in Java?

An escape sequence is a special character combination beginning with a backslash (\) called an escape character. It instructs the Java compiler to treat the character following the backslash differently, enabling developers to represent characters that are either impossible to type directly or hold special syntactical meaning in Java strings or character literals.

Escape sequences are essential for formatting console output, creating multi-line strings, escaping quote delimiters, and navigating system paths.

BasicEscapeDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello\nJava");
    }
}
Console Output:
Hello
Java
(Here, \n instructs the JVM to break the line and resume printing on the next row.)

2. Master Reference: Common Escape Sequences in Java

Escape Sequence Character Name Description & Behavior Example Expression
\n New Line Advances the cursor to the beginning of the next line. "Hello\nJava"
\t Horizontal Tab Inserts a horizontal tab space (standard alignment gap). "Name\tAge"
\" Double Quote Embeds a literal double quote inside a string without terminating it. "Say \"Hello\""
\' Single Quote Embeds a literal single quote inside a character literal without closing it. char ch = '\'';
\\ Backslash Embeds a single literal backslash in strings or paths. "C:\\Java\\bin"
\s Space Character Explicitly represents a single whitespace (standardized in Java 15+). "Hello\sJava"
\b Backspace Pushes cursor back one position (console-dependent behavior). "ABC\bD"
\r Carriage Return Returns cursor to start of line without advancing down. "Hello\rJava"
\f Form Feed Page break for printer feeds (rarely used in modern consoles). "Hello\fJava"
⚠️ Console Note on \b, \r, and \f: These legacy control characters depend heavily on terminal/console rendering engines. For instance, in some modern IDE consoles, \b or \r may print raw control symbols instead of physically deleting or overwriting previous text.

3. Detailed Examples & Practical Use Cases

A. New Line (\n)

Splits text across lines without requiring multiple System.out.println() statements.

NewLineDemo.java 
System.out.println("Hello\nWorld");

// Output:
// Hello
// World

B. Horizontal Tab (\t)

Aligns tabular text output into neat columns.

TabDemo.java 
System.out.println("Name\tAge");
System.out.println("Abhinav\t21");

// Output:
// Name    Age
// Abhinav 21

C. Double Quote (\")

Because double quotes delimit string literals in Java, escaping with \" is mandatory to print quotes.

QuoteDemo.java 
System.out.println("He said, \"Java is easy!\"");

// Output:
// He said, "Java is easy!"

D. Single Quote (\')

Used primarily inside char literals where an unescaped single quote would prematurely close the character token.

SingleQuoteDemo.java 
char ch = '\'';
System.out.println(ch);

// Output:
// '

E. Literal Backslash (\\)

Because a single \ begins an escape sequence, a literal backslash must be doubled (\\). This is ubiquitous in Windows file system paths.

BackslashDemo.java 
System.out.println("C:\\Users\\Java");

// Output:
// C:\Users\Java

F. Space Character (\s) — Java 15+

Introduced formally in Java 15 to safeguard trailing whitespace in text blocks and maintain readable spacing.

SpaceEscapeDemo.java 
System.out.println("Hello\sJava");

// Output:
// Hello Java

4. Complete Executable Java Program

EscapeSequencesFullDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello\nWorld");
        System.out.println("Name:\tAbhinav");
        System.out.println("He said, \"Learn Java\"");
        System.out.println("Path: C:\\Java\\Projects");
        System.out.println("Language:\sJava");
    }
}
Expected Console Output: 
Hello
World
Name:   Abhinav
He said, "Learn Java"
Path: C:\Java\Projects
Language: Java

5. Conceptual Distinction: Escape Sequences vs. Ordinary Characters

String Expression Compiler Interpretation Printed Output
"A\nB" Escape sequence \n triggers a line break. A and B printed on 2 separate lines.
"A\\nB" First backslash escapes the second; \n is printed literally. A\nB on a single line.
"A\tB" Escape sequence \t triggers a tab gap. A B (tab-spaced).
"A\\B" Escape sequence \\ renders a single backslash. A\B
ComparisonDemo.java 
System.out.println("A\nB");
System.out.println("A\\nB");

// Output:
// A
// B
// A\nB

6. 🎯 Key Rules & Interview Takeaways

  • 1. Escape Prefix: Java escape sequences always start with an escape backslash (\).
  • 2. Valid Scope: Escape sequences are only interpreted inside string literals ("...") and character literals ('...').
  • 3. Double Backslash Rule: In regular string literals, every intended literal backslash requires double backslashes (\\), e.g., regex patterns and file paths.
  • 4. Java 15+ Feature: \s was standardized in modern Java (Java 15+) for clear space representation, notably useful in multi-line Text Blocks (""").
  • 5. Escape Sequences vs. Unicode Escapes: Standard escape sequences (like \n, \t) represent specific control characters. In contrast, Unicode Escapes (like \u0041 for uppercase A) are processed during Java's lexical translation phase before token parsing and can represent any UTF-16 code unit.
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Arrays in Java: Declaration, Memory Layout, Multi-Dimensional & Core Operations

1. What Is an Array in Java?

An array is a container object in Java that holds a fixed number of values of a single component data type. Each element in the array is stored in contiguous memory slots and is accessed via a numeric index.

Arrays are used when you have multiple related items of data (such as student test scores, daily temperatures, or product IDs) and need to handle them as a cohesive unit instead of declaring individual isolated variables.

ArrayIntroDemo.java 
// Storing marks of 5 students in a single array variable:
int[] marks = {85, 90, 78, 92, 88};

System.out.println("First student mark: " + marks[0]); // Output: 85
System.out.println("Total students: " + marks.length);   // Output: 5
Key Structural Facts:
  • int[] specifies the array reference data type.
  • marks is a reference variable pointing to the array object on the Heap.
  • The array has a length of 5, indexed from 0 through 4.

2. Why Do We Need Arrays?

Consider storing marks for 5 students without arrays versus using an array:

Scenario Code Implementation Drawbacks / Benefits
Without Arrays int mark1 = 85;
int mark2 = 90;
int mark3 = 78;
int mark4 = 92;
int mark5 = 88; 		Unscalable. Cannot easily iterate with loops, sort values, or calculate sums dynamically.
With an Array int[] marks = {85, 90, 78, 92, 88}; Clean and scalable. Elements are easily traversed in a single loop, searched, sorted, and aggregated.

3. Array Indexing & Memory Representation

Java arrays use zero-based indexing. The first item is at index 0, and the last item is at index array.length - 1.

Value: 10 Index [0]
➔
Value: 20 Index [1]
➔
Value: 30 Index [2]
➔
Value: 40 Index [3]
➔
Value: 50 Index [4]
IndexAccessDemo.java 
int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

System.out.println(numbers[0]); // Output: 10 (First element)
System.out.println(numbers[2]); // Output: 30 (Middle element)
System.out.println(numbers[4]); // Output: 50 (Last element: length - 1)

// Attempting to access an illegal index:
// System.out.println(numbers[5]); // 💥 Throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException!
⚠️ Critical Runtime Exception: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Occurs whenever code attempts to access an index < 0 or >= array.length. The JVM performs strict boundary checks on every array access.

4. Types of Arrays in Java

Array Structure Description Declaration & Initialization
1. One-Dimensional Array Linear sequence of elements of the same component type. int[] arr = {10, 20, 30};
2. Two-Dimensional Array Matrix structure organized as rows and columns (tables/grids). int[][] matrix = {
  {1, 2},
  {3, 4}
};
3. Jagged Array (Ragged) A 2D array where each row can have a completely different column length. int[][] jagged = {
  {1, 2},
  {3, 4, 5},
  {6}
};
💡 Architectural Insight: In Java, multi-dimensional arrays are physically arrays of array references! The outer array holds pointers to distinct sub-arrays in Heap memory. This is why Java natively supports Jagged Arrays with non-uniform row lengths.

5. How to Declare, Instantiate, and Initialize Arrays

Java supports several syntax patterns to create arrays:

ArrayCreationSyntaxes.java 
// Pattern A: Declaration Only (allocates reference on stack; no heap object yet)
int[] numbers;

// Pattern B: Memory Allocation via 'new' (initializes elements to default zeros)
numbers = new int[5];

// Pattern C: Declaration + Instantiation Together
int[] scores = new int[5];

// Pattern D: Direct Literal Initialization (Compiler determines size from elements)
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11};

// Pattern E: Anonymous Array (Useful when passing arrays directly into method calls)
printArray(new int[] {10, 20, 30});

6. Iterating Arrays & The .length Field

To traverse array elements by their index, use a standard for loop. Notice that length for arrays is an immutable public final field, not a method!

PrintArrayDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

        // Standard indexed for loop:
        for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
            System.out.println("Element at index " + i + " = " + numbers[i]);
        }
    }
}
Expected Output:
Element at index 0 = 10
Element at index 1 = 20
Element at index 2 = 30
Element at index 3 = 40
Element at index 4 = 50

⭐ Golden Rule: Always write arr.length for arrays, compared to str.length() for Strings and list.size() for Collections!

7. Enhanced For Loop (For-Each Loop)

Java 5 introduced the enhanced for loop (for-each) for concise sequential traversal without tracking index counters.

EnhancedForLoopDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

        for (int num : numbers) {
            System.out.println("Value: " + num);
        }
    }
}
Loop Technique When to Use Capabilities
Standard Indexed Loop
for (int i = 0; ...)		 When you need access to the index i, need to modify array elements in-place, or want reverse/step iteration. Full positional read/write access.
Enhanced For-Each Loop
for (int x : arr)		 When you only need forward, read-only sequential traversal of every element. Cleanest syntax, eliminates off-by-one boundary bugs.

8. Core Array Operations & Algorithms

A. Calculate the Sum & Average

ArraySumDemo.java 
int[] arr = {10, 20, 30, 40};
int sum = 0;

for (int num : arr) {
    sum += num;
}

double average = (double) sum / arr.length;
System.out.println("Sum = " + sum);        // Output: Sum = 100
System.out.println("Average = " + average); // Output: Average = 25.0

B. Find the Largest (Maximum) Element

ArrayMaxDemo.java 
int[] arr = {10, 50, 30, 90, 20};
int max = arr[0]; // Assume first element is max

for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] > max) {
        max = arr[i];
    }
}

System.out.println("Maximum = " + max); // Output: Maximum = 90

C. Linear Search for a Target Element

ArraySearchDemo.java 
int[] arr = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int target = 30;
int foundIndex = -1;

for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] == target) {
        foundIndex = i;
        break; // Stop immediately once target is found
    }
}

System.out.println("Target " + target + " found at index: " + foundIndex); // Output: Index = 2

9. Default Values of Array Elements

When an array is allocated using the new keyword without explicit values, the JVM automatically populates every slot with the type's standard default value:

Array Data Type Default Element Value Example Verification
byte[], short[], int[] 0 new int[3] ➔ [0, 0, 0]
long[] 0L new long[2] ➔ [0L, 0L]
float[] 0.0f new float[2] ➔ [0.0f, 0.0f]
double[] 0.0d new double[2] ➔ [0.0d, 0.0d]
char[] '\u0000' (null char) new char[2] ➔ ['\0', '\0']
boolean[] false new boolean[2] ➔ [false, false]
Reference types (e.g. String[], Object[]) null new String[2] ➔ [null, null]
DefaultValuesDemo.java 
int[] intArr = new int[3];
System.out.println(intArr[0]); // Output: 0

String[] strArr = new String[2];
System.out.println(strArr[0]); // Output: null

10. Important Properties & Interview Gotchas

  • Fixed Capacity: Once instantiated, an array's length cannot be grown or shrunk. If resizing is required, a new array must be created and elements copied (or use java.util.ArrayList).
  • Reference Type: Arrays are objects stored on the JVM Heap. The array variable is a reference holding the memory address.
  • Contiguous Memory: Primitive array elements are stored in contiguous blocks, making indexed access blistering fast with O(1) time complexity.
  • Null Elements in Object Arrays: In an array of objects (like Student[] students = new Student[5];), the slots contain null until explicitly instantiated with objects. Invoking methods on them before instantiation triggers a NullPointerException.
  • Array Cloning: Calling arr.clone() produces a shallow copy of the array.

11. Master Comparison: Individual Variables vs. Arrays

Criterion Individual Variables Java Arrays
Capacity Stores exactly 1 discrete value per variable. Stores multiple values of identical component type.
Identification Requires a unique variable identifier for each value. Single variable name; elements are indexed numerically.
Iteration & Processing Requires redundant, repetitive statements. Effortlessly processed with for and for-each loops.
Memory Storage Allocated as independent primitive values or references. Allocated as a single contiguous Heap object.
Example int a = 10, b = 20, c = 30; int[] arr = {10, 20, 30};
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Multidimensional & Jagged Arrays: Memory Architecture, 2D/3D Grids & Matrix Algorithms

1. What Is a Multidimensional Array in Java?

A multidimensional array in Java is essentially an array whose elements are themselves arrays. It enables programmers to organize structured, relational data into multiple dimensions such as rows and columns (tables, matrices, spreadsheets, pixel grids, or multi-floor floorplans).

Real-World Example: A classroom with 3 rows of desks where each row seats 4 students. You can represent all student scores in a single 2D array:

ClassroomGridDemo.java 
// 3 rows, 4 students in each row:
int[][] marks = {
    {80, 85, 90, 75}, // Row 0
    {70, 88, 92, 81}, // Row 1
    {95, 89, 84, 78}  // Row 2
};

System.out.println("Row 1, Student 2: " + marks[1][2]); // Output: 92
Key Structural Facts:
  • int[][] declares a reference to a two-dimensional integer array.
  • The array has 3 rows and 4 columns per row (12 total elements).
  • Individual elements are accessed with two coordinate brackets: marks[row][column].

2. Dimensional Hierarchy: 1D vs. 2D vs. 3D

Array Dimension Mental Model & Data Shape Declaration Syntax
1D Array A linear sequence of values (Single list). int[] arr = {10, 20, 30};
2D Array A grid structured as rows and columns (Table / Matrix). int[][] arr = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
3D Array A collection of 2D grids (Layers / Cubes / Time-series grids). int[][][] arr = new int[2][3][4];
💡 Architectural Truth (Array of Arrays): In Java, multidimensional arrays are not stored as single contiguous rectangular blocks in memory (unlike C/C++). Instead, an outer array stores reference pointers to completely independent 1D array objects in the JVM Heap. Because of this, rows are not required to have the same length!

3. Two-Dimensional Array (2D Array) & Grid Coordinates

A 3x3 matrix initialized with values:

MatrixInitDemo.java 
int[][] numbers = {
    {10, 20, 30}, // Row 0
    {40, 50, 60}, // Row 1
    {70, 80, 90}  // Row 2
};

Visual Matrix Grid Coordinates:

10
[0][0]
20
[0][1]
30
[0][2]
40
[1][0]
50
[1][1]
60
[1][2]
70
[2][0]
80
[2][1]
90
[2][2]
AccessCoordinatesDemo.java 
System.out.println(numbers[0][0]); // Output: 10 (Row 0, Col 0)
System.out.println(numbers[1][2]); // Output: 60 (Row 1, Col 2)
System.out.println(numbers[2][1]); // Output: 80 (Row 2, Col 1)

4. Creating a 2D Array Using new Keyword

When values are not immediately known, allocate memory specifying dimensions. The JVM populates all elements with default values (0 for numeric types):

NewKeyword2DDemo.java 
// Allocates 3 rows and 4 columns (12 integer slots, all initialized to 0):
int[][] arr = new int[3][4];

// Dynamically assign values to coordinates:
arr[0][0] = 10;
arr[1][2] = 50;

System.out.println("arr[0][0] = " + arr[0][0]); // Output: 10
System.out.println("arr[1][2] = " + arr[1][2]); // Output: 50
System.out.println("arr[2][3] = " + arr[2][3]); // Output: 0 (default value)

5. Traversing a 2D Array Using Nested Loops

To visit every cell, utilize a nested loop where the outer loop iterates through rows, and the inner loop traverses columns within each row.

NestedLoopTraversal.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] arr = {
            {1, 2, 3},
            {4, 5, 6},
            {7, 8, 9}
        };

        // Outer loop: traverses each row
        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
            // Inner loop: traverses columns in row i
            for (int j = 0; j < arr[i].length; j++) {
                System.out.print(arr[i][j] + " ");
            }
            System.out.println(); // Newline after finishing each row
        }
    }
}
Console Output: 
1 2 3
4 5 6
7 8 9

⭐ Pro Tip: Always use arr[i].length for the inner loop rather than a hardcoded number. This guarantees safe traversal across both standard matrices and uneven jagged arrays without throwing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

6. Jagged Arrays in Java (Ragged Arrays)

A jagged array is a multidimensional array where different rows have varying numbers of columns.

JaggedArrayDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Row 0 has 2 items; Row 1 has 3 items; Row 2 has 1 item:
        int[][] arr = {
            {1, 2},
            {3, 4, 5},
            {6}
        };

        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < arr[i].length; j++) {
                System.out.print(arr[i][j] + " ");
            }
            System.out.println();
        }
    }
}
Expected Console Output: 
1 2
3 4 5
6

7. Three-Dimensional Array (3D Array)

A 3D array is an array of 2D arrays, useful for representing 3D spatial volumes, RGB image color planes, or time slices. Coordinates follow the pattern: arr[layer][row][column].

ThreeDimensionalDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 2 layers, each containing a 2x2 matrix:
        int[][][] arr = {
            { // Layer 0
                {1, 2},
                {3, 4}
            },
            { // Layer 1
                {5, 6},
                {7, 8}
            }
        };

        // Access layer 0, row 0, col 0:
        System.out.println("First element (Layer 0): " + arr[0][0][0]); // Output: 1

        // Access layer 1, row 1, col 1:
        System.out.println("Last element (Layer 1):  " + arr[1][1][1]); // Output: 8
    }
}

8. Common Algorithms & Operations on 2D Arrays

A. Calculate the Sum of All Elements

MatrixSumDemo.java 
int[][] arr = {
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6}
};

int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < arr[i].length; j++) {
        sum += arr[i][j];
    }
}

System.out.println("Sum = " + sum); // Output: Sum = 21

B. Inspecting Grid Dimensions (Rows and Columns)

DimensionsCheck.java 
int[][] arr = {
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6}
};

System.out.println("Total Rows: " + arr.length);             // Output: 2
System.out.println("Columns in Row 0: " + arr[0].length);    // Output: 3

C. Print the Main Diagonal of a Square Matrix

The main diagonal elements are where the row index equals the column index (arr[i][i]):

MainDiagonalDemo.java 
int[][] arr = {
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6},
    {7, 8, 9}
};

System.out.println("Main Diagonal Elements:");
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    System.out.println("arr[" + i + "][" + i + "] = " + arr[i][i]);
}

// Output:
// arr[0][0] = 1
// arr[1][1] = 5
// arr[2][2] = 9

9. Master Comparison: 1D vs. 2D vs. 3D Arrays

Feature 1D Array 2D Array 3D Array
Logical Structure Linear Sequence Grid (Rows & Columns) Volume (Layers, Rows, Columns)
Number of Indexes 1 index: [i] 2 indexes: [i][j] 3 indexes: [i][j][k]
Declaration Type int[] int[][] int[][][]
Access Syntax arr[i] arr[row][col] arr[layer][row][col]
Loop Traversal Single loop Nested loop (2 deep) Triply nested loop (3 deep)
Common Real-World Uses Lists, scores, queues Matrices, chess boards, image bitmaps 3D space points, video frames, time cubes
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Constants in Java: The final Keyword, static final Architecture & Immutability Rules

1. What Is a Constant in Java?

A constant is a variable whose value is fixed and cannot be modified or reassigned once initialized during program execution. In Java, constants are declared using the final non-access modifier keyword.

Constants represent immutable domain values such as mathematical coefficients (like $\pi$), tax percentages, maximum connection limits, API base URLs, and application configuration thresholds.

BasicConstantDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final double PI = 3.14159;

        System.out.println("Value of PI: " + PI); // Output: 3.14159

        // Attempting to reassign triggers a compile-time failure:
        // PI = 3.14; // 💥 Compilation Error: cannot assign a value to final variable PI
    }
}
⚠️ Compiler Enforcement: The Java compiler strictly enforces immutability for final variables. Any reassignment attempt results in a compile-time error: cannot assign a value to final variable.

2. Why Do We Need Constants?

Consider calculating the area of a circle ($\text{Area} = \pi \times r^2$). Pi must remain constant throughout the lifecycle of the calculation:

Approach Code Pattern Safety & Robustness
Without final (Fragile) double pi = 3.14159;
// Later in code:
pi = 0.0; // Accidental bug! 		High risk. Any developer or loop could inadvertently reassign the value, producing silent calculation errors.
With final (Robust) final double PI = 3.14159;
double area = PI * r * r; 		Compile-time safe. Protects against accidental mutation and clearly documents developer intent.
CircleAreaDemo.java 
final double PI = 3.14159;
double radius = 5;
double area = PI * radius * radius;

System.out.println("Calculated Area: " + area); // Output: 78.53975

3. The Three Types of Constants in Java

A. Local Constants

Declared inside a method, constructor, or code block using final. It exists only within that method's execution stack.

LocalConstantsDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final int MAX_MARKS = 100;
        final double TAX_RATE = 0.18;

        System.out.println("Max Marks: " + MAX_MARKS); // Output: 100
        System.out.println("Tax Rate:  " + TAX_RATE);  // Output: 0.18
    }
}

B. Instance Constants (Blank Final Fields)

A final field that belongs to an object instance. It must be initialized either at declaration or inside every constructor before constructor completion. Each instance can have a different value, but once created, it cannot be modified.

InstanceConstantDemo.java 
class Student {
    final int rollNumber; // Blank final field

    // Initialized during object creation:
    Student(int rollNumber) {
        this.rollNumber = rollNumber;
    }
}

Student s1 = new Student(101);
Student s2 = new Student(102);
// s1.rollNumber = 200; // 💥 Error: cannot reassign final field

C. Static Constants (Class-Level Global Constants)

Declared using static final. It belongs to the class itself rather than any individual object. A single copy is loaded into the JVM Method/Metaspace area and shared across all instances.

StaticConstantsDemo.java 
class MathConstants {
    public static final double PI = 3.141592653589793;
    public static final double E = 2.718281828459045;
}

// Accessed globally via the Class Name without instantiating objects:
System.out.println("Pi constant: " + MathConstants.PI); // Output: 3.141592653589793

4. Master Comparison: final vs. static vs. static final

Keyword Combination Core Meaning Memory Allocation Standard Code Example
final Prevents variable reassignment. Per-instance (Heap) or per-method call (Stack). final int age = 21;
static Belongs to the class, shared among all instances. Mutable unless paired with final. Single copy in Metaspace/Method Area. static int userCount = 0;
static final True Constant: Single class-level reference that cannot be reassigned. Single immutable copy in Metaspace. public static final double PI = 3.14159;
🎯 Critical Interview Gotcha: final Reference vs. Object Immutability!

Declaring a reference variable as final locks the reference pointer to that object in memory. However, it does NOT make the underlying object immutable if the object itself is mutable! 

final int[] numbers = {10, 20, 30};

numbers[0] = 99;              // ✅ ALLOWED! The array's internal contents are modified.
// numbers = new int[]{1, 2}; // 💥 COMPILE ERROR! The reference pointer cannot be reassigned.

5. Industry Naming Conventions for Constants

  • Class-Level Constants (static final): By Java convention, use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (all uppercase letters separated by underscores):
    public static final int MAX_RETRY_COUNT = 3;
    public static final double DEFAULT_INTEREST_RATE = 7.5;
    public static final String APPLICATION_NAME = "EnterpriseApp";
  • Local Final Variables: Typically written in standard camelCase:
    final int maxMarks = 100;
    final double taxRate = 0.18;

6. Complete Executable Program

ConstantsCompleteDemo.java 
public class Main {
    // Class-level static constant:
    static final double PI = 3.14159;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Local constants:
        final int MAX_MARKS = 100;
        double radius = 5;

        double area = PI * radius * radius;

        System.out.println("Pi: " + PI);
        System.out.println("Maximum Marks: " + MAX_MARKS);
        System.out.println("Circle Area: " + area);
    }
}
Expected Console Output: 
Pi: 3.14159
Maximum Marks: 100
Circle Area: 78.53975
Operators Series: Part 1 of 2

Arithmetic Operators & Expressions: Calculation Rules, Type Promotion & Division Gotchas

💡 Operators & Calculations Series: This section focuses on arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %), increment/decrement operations (++, --), compound assignment, and numeric promotion traps. For the comprehensive 15-level Java Operator Precedence Hierarchy Table and Left-to-Right Associativity rules across all Java operators, see Section 13: Order of Operations & Precedence Master Table →.

1. What Is an Arithmetic Expression?

An arithmetic expression is an algebraic formula combining numeric literals, variables, and mathematical operators that the Java compiler evaluates to produce a single resulting numeric value.

In Java, arithmetic expressions power standard mathematical computations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and remainder extraction (modulus).

BasicArithmeticDemo.java 
int a = 10;
int b = 5;

// 'a + b' is an arithmetic expression producing 15:
int sum = a + b;

System.out.println("Computed Sum: " + sum); // Output: 15

2. Master Reference: Core Arithmetic Operators in Java

Operator Operation Name Sample Syntax Result Behavioral Rule
+ Addition 10 + 5 15 Calculates sum. Also acts as String concatenator if either operand is String.
- Subtraction 10 - 5 5 Subtracts right operand from left operand. Also serves as unary negation (-x).
* Multiplication 10 * 5 50 Multiplies both operands.
/ Division 10 / 5 2 Discards fraction if both operands are integers (truncates towards zero).
% Modulus (Remainder) 10 % 3 1 Computes the remainder left over after integer division.

3. Operator Behaviors & Practical Patterns

A. Integer Division vs. Floating-Point Division

Division behavior in Java is dictated entirely by operand data types:

DivisionDistinctionDemo.java 
// 1. Integer Division (both operands are ints -> fractional part is truncated):
System.out.println(10 / 3);   // Output: 3

// 2. Floating-point Division (at least one operand is double or float):
System.out.println(10.0 / 3); // Output: 3.3333333333333335
System.out.println(10 / 3.0); // Output: 3.3333333333333335

B. Modulus Operator (%) & Even/Odd Checking

The remainder operator is frequently employed in algorithms to test parity, cycle through arrays, or format clocks.

ModulusParityDemo.java 
int number = 7;

if (number % 2 == 0) {
    System.out.println(number + " is Even");
} else {
    System.out.println(number + " is Odd"); // Output: 7 is Odd
}

4. All Operators Evaluated in an Executable Program

ArithmeticOperationsDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 20;
        int b = 10;

        System.out.println("Addition:       " + (a + b)); // Output: 30
        System.out.println("Subtraction:    " + (a - b)); // Output: 10
        System.out.println("Multiplication: " + (a * b)); // Output: 200
        System.out.println("Division:       " + (a / b)); // Output: 2
        System.out.println("Remainder:      " + (a % b)); // Output: 0
    }
}

5. Operator Precedence & Associativity

Precedence determines the binding priority of operators in complex unparenthesized expressions.

Precedence Rank Operators Associativity Description
1 (Highest) () Left-to-Right Parentheses override all other rules.
2 ++, -- Right-to-Left (Unary) Increment and decrement.
3 *, /, % Left-to-Right Multiplicative operations.
4 (Lowest) +, - Left-to-Right Additive operations.
PrecedenceDemo.java 
// 1. Without parentheses (* executes before +):
int result1 = 10 + 5 * 2; // Evaluates to: 10 + 10 = 20
System.out.println("result1: " + result1); // Output: 20

// 2. With parentheses (() forces + to execute first):
int result2 = (10 + 5) * 2; // Evaluates to: 15 * 2 = 30
System.out.println("result2: " + result2); // Output: 30

6. Increment & Decrement Operators: Pre vs. Post

Java provides unary operators to increment or decrement an integer variable by 1:

Post-Increment: a++ 1. Uses current value in expression.
2. Increments variable in memory afterward.
Pre-Increment: ++a 1. Increments variable in memory first.
2. Delivers updated value to expression.
IncrementComparisonDemo.java 
// Case 1: Post-increment (a++)
int a = 5;
int b = a++; // b gets original 5, then a increments to 6
System.out.println("Post-increment -> a: " + a + ", b: " + b); // Output: a: 6, b: 5

// Case 2: Pre-increment (++x)
int x = 5;
int y = ++x; // x increments to 6 first, then y receives 6
System.out.println("Pre-increment  -> x: " + x + ", y: " + y); // Output: x: 6, y: 6

7. Compound Assignment Operators (Shorthand)

Compound assignment operators combine an arithmetic operation with assignment. They also include an implicit type cast in Java.

Compound Form Equivalent Expression Example Evaluation
a += b a = (type)(a + b) 10 += 5 ➔ 15
a -= b a = (type)(a - b) 15 -= 3 ➔ 12
a *= b a = (type)(a * b) 10 *= 2 ➔ 20
a /= b a = (type)(a / b) 20 /= 4 ➔ 5
a %= b a = (type)(a % b) 10 %= 3 ➔ 1

8. 🎯 The 4 Major Interview Gotchas & Common Pitfalls

1. Integer Truncation Bug

double result = 7 / 2; stores 3.0, NOT 3.5!
Reason: The integer division 7 / 2 executes first, yielding 3, which is then widened to 3.0. To preserve decimals, at least one operand must be a double: 7.0 / 2.

2. Division by Zero: Integer vs. Floating-Point

ZeroDivisionDemo.java 
// 1. Integer zero division throws an unchecked exception:
// System.out.println(10 / 0); // 💥 ArithmeticException: / by zero

// 2. Floating-point zero division conforms to IEEE 754 (no exception!):
System.out.println(10.0 / 0.0);  // Output: Infinity
System.out.println(-10.0 / 0.0); // Output: -Infinity
System.out.println(0.0 / 0.0);   // Output: NaN (Not a Number)

3. Integer Overflow (Wraparound)

Java integer arithmetic wraps around without throwing errors when exceeding maximum limits:

OverflowDemo.java 
int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE; // 2147483647
int overflowed = max + 1;
System.out.println(overflowed); // Output: -2147483648 (Wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE!)

4. String Concatenation Trap with +

Because the + operator evaluates left-to-right, preceding strings turn subsequent numbers into strings:

ConcatTrapDemo.java 
// Without parentheses: "Result: 10" + 20 -> "Result: 1020"
System.out.println("Result: " + 10 + 20);   // Output: Result: 1020

// With parentheses: (10 + 20) evaluates first to 30:
System.out.println("Result: " + (10 + 20)); // Output: Result: 30
Operators Series: Part 2 of 2

Order of Operations & Operator Precedence: Master Hierarchy Table, Associativity & Evaluation Flow

📌 Operators & Calculations Series: This section is the definitive reference for the full 15-level Java Operator Precedence Hierarchy Table and evaluation associativity rules. For individual arithmetic operators and division behaviors, see ← Section 12: Arithmetic Operators & Expressions.

1. What Is the Order of Operations?

The order of operations defines the exact sequential priority with which the Java compiler evaluates expressions containing multiple operators.

Without rigid precedence rules, mathematical expressions would be ambiguous. Java strictly enforces operator precedence, while allowing developers to explicitly override evaluation order using parentheses ().

PrecedenceIntroDemo.java 
int result = 10 + 5 * 2;
System.out.println("Result: " + result); // Output: 20 (NOT 30!)
Evaluation Breakdown:
Multiplication (*) holds higher precedence than addition (+):
1. First: 5 * 2 = 10
2. Second: 10 + 10 = 20

2. Master Reference: Complete Java Operator Precedence Table

Operators are listed from highest priority (evaluated first) to lowest priority (evaluated last):

Priority Operators Category / Description Associativity
1 (Highest) (), [], . Parentheses, array subscript, member access Left-to-Right
2 expr++, expr-- Postfix increment / decrement Left-to-Right
3 ++expr, --expr, +, -, !, ~, (type) Prefix unary, logical NOT, bitwise NOT, cast Right-to-Left
4 *, /, % Multiplicative (multiply, divide, modulus) Left-to-Right
5 +, - Additive (addition, subtraction) Left-to-Right
6 <<, >>, >>> Bitwise bit shifts (left, signed right, unsigned right) Left-to-Right
7 <, >, <=, >=, instanceof Relational comparison and type comparison Left-to-Right
8 ==, != Equality and inequality checks Left-to-Right
9 & Bitwise AND Left-to-Right
10 ^ Bitwise XOR (exclusive OR) Left-to-Right
11 | Bitwise OR (inclusive OR) Left-to-Right
12 && Logical AND (short-circuit) Left-to-Right
13 || Logical OR (short-circuit) Left-to-Right
14 ? : Ternary conditional operator Right-to-Left
15 =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %= Assignment and compound assignment Right-to-Left
16 (Lowest) -> Lambda expression operator Right-to-Left

3. Step-by-Step Practical Examples

Example 1: Multiplication Before Addition

MultBeforeAddDemo.java 
int result = 10 + 5 * 2;
System.out.println(result); // Output: 20

// Step 1: 5 * 2 = 10
// Step 2: 10 + 10 = 20

Example 2: Parentheses Override Precedence

ParenthesesOverrideDemo.java 
int result = (10 + 5) * 2;
System.out.println(result); // Output: 30

// Step 1: Parentheses evaluated first -> (10 + 5) = 15
// Step 2: 15 * 2 = 30

Example 3: Division & Multiplication (Left-to-Right Associativity)

When two operators share the exact same precedence tier, evaluation proceeds strictly left to right:

DivMultDemo.java 
int result = 20 / 5 * 2;
System.out.println(result); // Output: 8 (NOT 2!)

// Step 1: 20 / 5 = 4
// Step 2: 4 * 2 = 8

Example 4: Addition & Subtraction (Left-to-Right Associativity)

AddSubDemo.java 
int result = 20 - 5 + 3;
System.out.println(result); // Output: 18 (NOT 12!)

// Step 1: 20 - 5 = 15
// Step 2: 15 + 3 = 18

Example 5: Complex Multi-Operator Expression

ComplexExpressionDemo.java 
int result = 10 + 6 / 2 * 3 - 1;
System.out.println("Result: " + result); // Output: 18
Step 1: Division 6 / 2 ➔ 3
Expr: 10 + 3 * 3 - 1
➔
Step 2: Multiplication 3 * 3 ➔ 9
Expr: 10 + 9 - 1
➔
Step 3: Addition 10 + 9 ➔ 19
Expr: 19 - 1
➔
Step 4: Subtraction 19 - 1 ➔ 18
Final Result: 18

4. Understanding Operator Associativity

Associativity determines whether operators of identical precedence bind to their operands from the left or from the right:

Direction Applies To Demonstration
Left-to-Right Arithmetic, relational, bitwise, and logical operators 20 / 5 * 2 is grouped as (20 / 5) * 2 ➔ 8
Right-to-Left Unary operators, ternary ?:, and assignment operators (=, +=) a = b = c = 10; is grouped as a = (b = (c = 10));.
All 3 variables receive 10.

5. Essential Rule: Integer vs. Floating-Point Division in Expressions

Data Type Dictates Result:
System.out.println(7 / 2); // Output: 3 (Integer division drops decimal)
System.out.println(7.0 / 2); // Output: 3.5 (Double operand preserves precision)
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Type Casting in Java: Widening, Narrowing, Reference Conversions & Precision Traps

1. What Is Type Casting in Java?

Type casting is the mechanism of converting a value from its original data type into another compatible data type.

In Java, type casting is employed when assigning values between differing numeric types, passing arguments to overloaded methods, performing mixed-type arithmetic, or navigating object inheritance hierarchies.

BasicTypeCastDemo.java 
int a = 10;
double b = a; // Automatically converted from int (32-bit) to double (64-bit)

System.out.println("Integer a: " + a); // Output: 10
System.out.println("Double  b: " + b); // Output: 10.0

2. The Two Core Categories of Primitive Casting

Casting Category Direction Syntax Requirement Risk Level
1. Widening Casting (Implicit) Smaller range / precision ➔ Wider range Automatic by compiler (no cast operator required) Safe (minimal or zero data truncation)
2. Narrowing Casting (Explicit) Larger range / precision ➔ Narrower range Explicit cast operator required: (targetType) Lossy (fractional truncation or numeric overflow)

3. Widening Casting (Implicit / Automatic)

Java automatically performs widening casting for compatible numeric types because the destination type has sufficient bit-width to accommodate the source value.

byte 8-bit
➔
short / char 16-bit
➔
int 32-bit
➔
long 64-bit
➔
float 32-bit IEEE
➔
double 64-bit IEEE
WideningDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 50;
        double b = a; // Implicit widening

        System.out.println(a); // Output: 50
        System.out.println(b); // Output: 50.0
    }
}
⚠️ Subtlety on Widening Precision: While converting integer primitives to floating-point types (e.g., long ➔ float) is categorized as widening, it can result in loss of least-significant bits for very large magnitudes because a 32-bit float allocates only 24 bits for its mantissa!

4. Narrowing Casting (Explicit / Manual)

When squeezing a wider value into a narrower data type, explicit syntax is required: (targetType) value.

A. Fractional Part Discarded (Truncation)

NarrowingTruncationDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double a = 25.89;
        int b = (int) a; // Discards decimal digits entirely

        System.out.println("Original double: " + a); // Output: 25.89
        System.out.println("Narrowed int:    " + b); // Output: 25 (NOT rounded to 26!)
    }
}

B. Byte Overflow & Two's Complement Wraparound

ByteOverflowDemo.java 
int a = 130;
byte b = (byte) a; // byte range is -128 to 127

System.out.println("Original int: " + a); // Output: 130
System.out.println("Narrowed byte: " + b); // Output: -126
Why does 130 become -126 in byte?
