The binary representation of 32-bit 130 is ...0000 1000 0010. Narrowing to an 8-bit byte truncates all higher bits, keeping only the lowest 8 bits: 1000 0010. In two's complement notation, a leading 1 signifies a negative number, decoding exactly to -126.

5. Master Comparison: Widening vs. Narrowing

Feature Widening Casting (Implicit) Narrowing Casting (Explicit)
Direction Smaller to wider range Wider to narrower range
Cast Operator Not required (Automatic) Mandatory: (type)
Information Preservation Preserved (with potential precision caveats) Truncated (decimals dropped, bits truncated)
Syntax Example double x = 10; int x = (int) 10.5;

6. Type Casting Between char and Numeric Primitives

Because a Java char internally stores a 16-bit unsigned Unicode/UTF-16 code point (0 to 65535), it freely interconverts with integers:

CharCastDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // char to int (Implicit Widening):
        char ch = 'A';
        int asciiValue = ch;
        System.out.println("Character 'A' as int: " + asciiValue); // Output: 65

        // int to char (Explicit Narrowing):
        int number = 66;
        char letter = (char) number;
        System.out.println("Number 66 as char:    " + letter);     // Output: B
    }
}

7. Numeric Promotion in Arithmetic Expressions

When operators encounter operands of different types, Java executes automatic numeric type promotion before evaluating the operation:

  • If either operand is double, the other is promoted to double.
  • Otherwise, if either is float, the other is promoted to float.
  • Otherwise, if either is long, the other is promoted to long.
  • Otherwise, all byte, short, and char values are promoted to int.
PromotionDemo.java 
int a = 10;
double b = 3.0;

// 'a' is automatically promoted to double before division:
double result = a / b;
System.out.println("Result: " + result); // Output: 3.3333333333333335

8. Reference Type Casting (Upcasting vs. Downcasting)

Casting also applies to objects within an inheritance hierarchy:

ObjectCastingDemo.java 
class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Upcasting: Subclass object assigned to Superclass reference (Automatic & Safe)
        Animal animal = new Dog();

        // 2. Downcasting: Superclass reference converted back to Subclass (Requires Explicit Cast)
        Dog dog = (Dog) animal;
        dog.bark(); // Output: Dog barks
    }
}
⚠️ Critical Runtime Risk: ClassCastException
Downcasting blindly to an incompatible subtype (e.g., casting a Cat object to a Dog reference) throws an immediate runtime ClassCastException. Always verify with instanceof before downcasting!

9. 🎯 The 3 Most Frequent Casting Traps

Trap 1: Expecting Rounding on Float-to-Int

int b = (int) 9.99; // Results in 9, NOT 10!
Narrowing simply drops all fractional digits. If mathematical rounding is needed, invoke Math.round(9.99).

Trap 2: Large long to float Precision Erosion

PrecisionLossDemo.java 
long big = 16777217L;
float f = big; // Widening, but loses 1 unit of precision!
System.out.println((long) f); // Output: 16777216

Trap 3: Confusing Casting with String Parsing

int x = (int) "123"; // 💥 COMPILE ERROR! String cannot be cast to int.
In Java, converting string characters into numbers requires parsing, not casting:
int x = Integer.parseInt("123"); // Correct approach!
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

The Math Class in Java: Mathematical Methods, Rounding Engines & Exact Arithmetic

1. Introduction to the Java Math Class

The java.lang.Math class provides a comprehensive suite of static methods and fundamental mathematical constants for performing elementary numeric operations, exponentiation, logarithms, trigonometry, and rounding.

Property Specification & Architectural Role
Package java.lang (automatically imported by default into every Java compilation unit).
Class Modifiers public final class Math (cannot be extended or inherited).
Constructor private Math() (private constructor prevents instantiation; pure static utility class).
Access Pattern Static method invocation: Math.methodName(arguments) without creating objects.
BasicMathDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Math.sqrt(25));      // Output: 5.0 (returns double)
        System.out.println(Math.max(10, 20));   // Output: 20
    }
}

2. Core Algebraic & Comparison Methods

2.1 Math.max(a, b) & 2.2 Math.min(a, b)

Overloaded for int, long, float, and double to return the extremum value:

MinMaxDemo.java 
System.out.println(Math.max(10, 20));     // Output: 20
System.out.println(Math.max(45.5, 30.2)); // Output: 45.5

System.out.println(Math.min(10, 20));     // Output: 10
System.out.println(Math.min(5.5, 2.5));   // Output: 2.5

2.3 Math.abs(x) (Absolute Value)

Returns the non-negative magnitude of a number by dropping the negative sign:

AbsDemo.java 
System.out.println(Math.abs(-10));   // Output: 10
System.out.println(Math.abs(-15.5)); // Output: 15.5
System.out.println(Math.abs(8));     // Output: 8
🎯 Critical Edge Case: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)
Calling Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) (which is -2147483648) returns -2147483648!
Reason: Positive 2147483648 exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (2147483647) by 1, wrapping around in two's complement arithmetic without error.

2.4 Math.sqrt(x) & 2.5 Math.cbrt(x)

Calculate square roots and cube roots, returning double:

RootsDemo.java 
// Square root:
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(25)); // Output: 5.0
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(49)); // Output: 7.0
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(2));  // Output: 1.4142135623730951

// Cube root (supports negative inputs):
System.out.println(Math.cbrt(27)); // Output: 3.0
System.out.println(Math.cbrt(64)); // Output: 4.0
System.out.println(Math.cbrt(-8)); // Output: -2.0

2.6 Math.pow(base, exponent)

Computes $\text{base}^{\text{exponent}}$ and always returns a 64-bit double:

PowerDemo.java 
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 3));  // Output: 8.0 (2^3)
System.out.println(Math.pow(5, 2));  // Output: 25.0 (5^2)
System.out.println(Math.pow(10, 0)); // Output: 1.0 (Any number to power 0 is 1.0)

3. Master Comparison: The 4 Rounding Methods

Choosing the correct rounding function is essential for financial, geometric, and game development logic:

Method Return Type Rounding Rule / Direction Examples
Math.round(x) long for double
int for float		 Standard arithmetic rounding to nearest integer ($x + 0.5$ floored). 4.6 ➔ 5
4.3 ➔ 4
Math.ceil(x) double Ceiling: Smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$ (rounds toward $+\infty$). 4.2 ➔ 5.0
-4.2 ➔ -4.0
Math.floor(x) double Floor: Largest integer less than or equal to $x$ (rounds toward $-\infty$). 4.9 ➔ 4.0
-4.2 ➔ -5.0
Math.rint(x) double Round to Integer: Nearest double; uses Banker's ties-to-even rule for .5. 4.5 ➔ 4.0
5.5 ➔ 6.0
RoundingComparisonDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("round(4.6): " + Math.round(4.6)); // Output: 5
        System.out.println("ceil(4.2):  " + Math.ceil(4.2));  // Output: 5.0
        System.out.println("floor(4.9): " + Math.floor(4.9)); // Output: 4.0
        System.out.println("rint(4.5):  " + Math.rint(4.5));  // Output: 4.0 (even tie-break)
    }
}

4. Sign Inspection & Random Number Generation

4.1 Math.signum(x)

Extracts the mathematical sign: returns 1.0 for positive, -1.0 for negative, and 0.0 for zero.

SignumDemo.java 
System.out.println(Math.signum(25));  // Output: 1.0
System.out.println(Math.signum(-25)); // Output: -1.0
System.out.println(Math.signum(0));   // Output: 0.0

4.2 Math.random() & Integer Scaling Formula

Returns a pseudo-random double in the half-open interval $[0.0, 1.0)$ (includes 0.0, strictly excludes 1.0).

RandomFormulaDemo.java 
// Formula to generate random integer between MIN and MAX (inclusive):
// int randomNum = (int) (Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;

// Example: Random integer from 1 to 10:
int number = (int) (Math.random() * 10) + 1;
System.out.println("Random number (1-10): " + number);
Math.random() Generates [0.0, 1.0)
➔
* 10 Scales to [0.0, 10.0)
➔
(int) Truncates to [0, 9]
➔
+ 1 Offsets to [1, 10]

5. Mathematical Constants

The Math class provides high-precision mathematical constants declared as public static final double:

  • Math.PI: Ratio of circumference to diameter ($\approx 3.141592653589793$)
  • Math.E: Natural logarithm base Euler's constant ($\approx 2.718281828459045$)
CircleAreaMathDemo.java 
double radius = 5;
double area = Math.PI * Math.pow(radius, 2);

System.out.println("Circle Area = " + area); // Output: Area = 78.53981633974483

6. Trigonometric Functions & Radian Conversion

⚠️ Radians Required: All trigonometric methods (sin, cos, tan) accept angles measured in radians, NOT degrees!
TrigDemo.java 
// Convert degrees (90°) to radians:
double rad = Math.toRadians(90);
System.out.println("sin(90 deg): " + Math.sin(rad)); // Output: 1.0

// Convert radians (PI) back to degrees:
System.out.println("toDegrees(PI): " + Math.toDegrees(Math.PI)); // Output: 180.0

7. Logarithmic & Exponential Methods

LogExpDemo.java 
System.out.println(Math.log(Math.E));   // Output: 1.0 (Natural log ln(e))
System.out.println(Math.log10(100));    // Output: 2.0 (Base-10 log log10(100))
System.out.println(Math.exp(1));        // Output: 2.718281828459045 (e^1)
System.out.println(Math.expm1(0.001));  // e^x - 1 (accurate for tiny values)

8. Java 8+ Overflow-Checking Exact Arithmetic

Standard arithmetic overflows silently. The *Exact methods throw an ArithmeticException on overflow:

Method Purpose Behavior on Overflow
Math.hypot(x, y) Calculates $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ without intermediate overflow Safe Euclidean distance (e.g. Math.hypot(3, 4) ➔ 5.0)
Math.addExact(a, b) Adds two integers Throws ArithmeticException on integer overflow
Math.multiplyExact(a, b) Multiplies two integers Throws ArithmeticException on integer overflow
Math.toIntExact(longVal) Casts long to int safely Throws ArithmeticException if long doesn't fit in int

9. Complete Demonstration Program

MathComprehensiveDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = -15;
        int b = 25;

        System.out.println("Maximum:     " + Math.max(a, b));
        System.out.println("Minimum:     " + Math.min(a, b));
        System.out.println("Absolute:    " + Math.abs(a));
        System.out.println("Square Root: " + Math.sqrt(64));
        System.out.println("Power:       " + Math.pow(2, 4));
        System.out.println("Round:       " + Math.round(7.6));
        System.out.println("Ceiling:     " + Math.ceil(7.2));
        System.out.println("Floor:       " + Math.floor(7.8));
        System.out.println("PI:          " + Math.PI);
    }
}
Expected Console Output: 
Maximum:     25
Minimum:     -15
Absolute:    15
Square Root: 8.0
Power:       16.0
Round:       8
Ceiling:     8.0
Floor:       7.0
PI:          3.141592653589793

10. 🎯 Top 10 High-Yield Interview Takeaways

  • 1. Package: Belongs to java.lang; no import needed.
  • 2. Static Methods: Almost all methods are static, called via Math.method().
  • 3. Return Types: Methods like Math.sqrt() and Math.pow() always return double.
  • 4. Ceil vs. Floor: ceil() rounds toward $+\infty$; floor() rounds toward $-\infty$.
  • 5. Round Return: Math.round(double) returns long; Math.round(float) returns int.
  • 6. Random Interval: Math.random() outputs in half-open range $[0.0, 1.0)$.
  • 7. Trigonometry Unit: Requires angles in radians; use Math.toRadians().
  • 8. Constants: Math.PI and Math.E are public static final double.
  • 9. Final Class: Math is a final class with private constructor; cannot be subclassed or instantiated.
  • 10. Precision Guard: Performs standard IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic; use BigDecimal when exact monetary precision is mandatory.
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Formatting Numbers in Java: printf(), NumberFormat, DecimalFormat & Localization

1. Introduction to Number Formatting in Java

Number formatting is the process of converting raw numeric values into human-readable strings following grammatical, scientific, cultural, or financial presentation rules.

Consider raw numeric data 1234567.891 presented in various business formats:

Presentation Format Formatted Display Output Context / Use Case
Raw Unformatted 1234567.891 Machine processing / debug logs
Fixed 2 Decimals 1234567.89 General metrics / science measurements
US Standard Grouping 1,234,567.891 US / International financial reports
Indian Grouping Format 12,34,567.891 Lakhs & Crores financial accounting
Percentage Display 75.50% Progress indicators / discounts / tax rates
Java provides 4 primary mechanisms for formatting numbers:
  1. System.out.printf() — Quick formatted printing directly to the console.
  2. String.format() — Generates reusable formatted strings.
  3. java.text.NumberFormat — Locale-sensitive formatting for numbers, currencies, and percentages.
  4. java.text.DecimalFormat — Custom pattern-based numeric formatting.

2. Formatted Console Printing with printf()

The printf() method writes formatted strings directly to the output stream using format specifiers starting with %.

PrintfPrecisionDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double price = 123.456789;

        System.out.printf("%.2f%n", price); // 2 decimal digits (rounds up to .46)
        System.out.printf("%.3f%n", price); // 3 decimal digits
        System.out.printf("%.0f%n", price); // 0 decimal digits
    }
}
Expected Console Output:
123.46
123.457
123
Note: %n inserts a platform-independent newline (equivalent to \r\n on Windows and \n on Linux/macOS).

Master Format Specifiers Reference Table

Specifier Data Type & Purpose Code Example Formatted Result
%d Integral integers (byte, short, int, long) printf("%d", 100) 100
%f Floating-point numbers (default 6 decimals) printf("%f", 12.5) 12.500000
%.2f Floating-point fixed to 2 decimals printf("%.2f", 12.5) 12.50
%,d Integer with locale grouping commas printf("%,d", 1000000) 1,000,000
%e Scientific exponential notation printf("%e", 2500.5) 2.500500e+03
%g Compact scientific or decimal notation printf("%g", 12.5) 12.5
%% Literal percent character % printf("20%%") 20%
%n Platform-independent line separator printf("%n") Newline
PrintfSpecifiersDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int population = 1000000;
        double amount = 2500.5;

        System.out.printf("Population: %,d%n", population); // Output: Population: 1,000,000
        System.out.printf("Amount:     %.2f%n", amount);     // Output: Amount:     2500.50
        System.out.printf("Scientific: %e%n", amount);       // Output: Scientific: 2.500500e+03
        System.out.printf("Discount:   20%%%n");             // Output: Discount:   20%
    }
}

3. Reusable Formatting with String.format()

While printf() prints directly to standard output, String.format() constructs and returns a formatted String without printing, allowing you to store it, pass it to APIs, or render it in UI templates.

StringFormatDemo.java 
double price = 999.999;

// Formats and rounds to 2 decimal places:
String formattedPrice = String.format("%.2f", price);

System.out.println("Stored String: " + formattedPrice); // Output: 1000.00

4. Locale-Aware Formatting with NumberFormat

The java.text.NumberFormat abstract class provides locale-sensitive formatting factories that automatically adjust decimal points and grouping commas according to regional norms.

LocaleFormattingDemo.java 
import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.util.Locale;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double number = 1234567.89;

        // US Locale (Thousands grouping: 1,234,567.89):
        NumberFormat us = NumberFormat.getNumberInstance(Locale.US);
        System.out.println("US Format:    " + us.format(number));

        // Indian Locale (Lakhs & Crores grouping: 12,34,567.89):
        NumberFormat india = NumberFormat.getNumberInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("en-IN"));
        System.out.println("India Format: " + india.format(number));
    }
}

Essential NumberFormat Methods

Method Signature Purpose & Description
NumberFormat.getNumberInstance(locale) Creates a general-purpose numeric formatter for the specified locale.
NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale) Creates a currency formatter including regional currency symbols.
NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(locale) Creates a percentage formatter (multiplies by 100 and appends %).
setMinimumFractionDigits(int n) Forces a minimum number of decimal places (pads with trailing zeros).
setMaximumFractionDigits(int n) Caps the maximum decimal precision allowed.
setGroupingUsed(boolean used) Enables or disables thousand/lakh grouping separators.

5. Formatting Currencies with getCurrencyInstance()

Rather than hardcoding currency strings (like "$" + price), rely on getCurrencyInstance() to dynamically fetch the correct symbol, spacing, and placement.

CurrencyFormatDemo.java 
import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.util.Locale;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double price = 123456.789;

        // Indian Currency Format (₹):
        NumberFormat inr = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("en-IN"));
        System.out.println("INR: " + inr.format(price)); // Output: ₹1,23,456.79

        // US Currency Format ($):
        NumberFormat usd = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.US);
        System.out.println("USD: " + usd.format(price)); // Output: $123,456.79
    }
}
💰 Financial Best Practice: For core monetary calculations, always use java.math.BigDecimal with explicit rounding modes (e.g. RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) to eliminate IEEE floating-point precision drift before formatting!

6. Formatting Percentages with getPercentInstance()

A percentage formatter automatically scales fractional decimal numbers by multiplying by 100 and appending the percent sign:

PercentageFormatDemo.java 
import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.util.Locale;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double score = 0.755;

        NumberFormat percent = NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.US);
        percent.setMinimumFractionDigits(2);
        percent.setMaximumFractionDigits(2);

        System.out.println("Percent: " + percent.format(score)); // Output: 75.50%
    }
}

7. Custom Pattern Formatting with DecimalFormat

java.text.DecimalFormat is a concrete subclass of NumberFormat that lets you design bespoke pattern strings.

DecimalFormat Pattern Symbols

Symbol Behavior Example with 5 Example with 0
0 Required digit: prints digit, or zero if absent Pattern 00 ➔ 05 Pattern 0.00 ➔ 0.00
# Optional digit: prints digit, suppresses leading/trailing zeros Pattern ## ➔ 5 Pattern #.## ➔ . (blank)
. Decimal separator position — —
, Grouping separator position Pattern #,### —
% Multiplies by 100 and shows percent sign — —
DecimalFormatCustomPatterns.java 
import java.text.DecimalFormat;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Pattern 1: Force exact 2 decimal digits ("0.00")
        DecimalFormat df1 = new DecimalFormat("0.00");
        System.out.println("df1: " + df1.format(123.4567)); // Output: 123.46

        // Pattern 2: Grouping commas with 2 fixed decimals ("#,##0.00")
        DecimalFormat df2 = new DecimalFormat("#,##0.00");
        System.out.println("df2: " + df2.format(1234567.8)); // Output: 1,234,567.80

        // Pattern 3: Optional fractional digits ("#,##0.##")
        DecimalFormat df3 = new DecimalFormat("#,##0.##");
        System.out.println("df3 (single decimal):   " + df3.format(1234.5));   // Output: 1,234.5
        System.out.println("df3 (multiple decimals): " + df3.format(1234.567)); // Output: 1,234.57
    }
}

8. Master Comparison: All 4 Formatting Tools

Feature printf() String.format() NumberFormat DecimalFormat
Direct Console Print Yes No No No
Returns String No (prints to stream) Yes Yes Yes
Locale Automatic Default locale (overloadable) Default locale (overloadable) Full Locale engine built-in Locale symbol support
Currency Support Manual formatting Manual formatting Built-in factory: getCurrencyInstance() Custom currency patterns
Best Suited For Quick console diagnostics String interpolation / templates Internationalization (i18n) / localized apps Complex custom numeric masks

9. 🎯 Common Mistakes & Gotchas

  • 1. Formatting Is Non-Mutating: Formatting produces a rounded textual representation; it does not modify the original numeric variable stored in memory.
  • 2. Format Specifier Type Mismatch: Passing floating-point numbers to integer specifiers (e.g. printf("%d", 12.5)) triggers an immediate IllegalFormatConversionException.
  • 3. Locale Separator Assumption: Never assume commas separate thousands and periods separate decimals universally. In countries like Germany or France, 1.234,56 is standard (period for grouping, comma for decimals). Rely on locale-driven formatters.
Chapter 1: Java Fundamentals

Reading User Input in Java: Scanner, BufferedReader, Buffer Pitfalls & Defensive Parsing

1. Introduction to User Input in Java

Reading input is the mechanism of accepting interactive runtime data from users via standard input (the keyboard) or redirected streams, eliminating the need to hardcode static values into source code.

Java provides several input-reading constructs:

  • java.util.Scanner: The most versatile, beginner-friendly token parser with built-in primitive type conversion.
  • java.io.BufferedReader: A high-throughput, buffered character stream preferred for large I/O workloads and competitive programming.
  • java.io.Console: Dedicated console input provider featuring password masking without echoing characters.
  • System.in: The fundamental raw byte input stream connected to standard keyboard input.

2. Reading Input Using the Scanner Class

The Scanner class parses primitive types and strings using regular expressions. It breaks its input into tokens using a whitespace delimiter by default.

ScannerStringDemo.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Create a Scanner connected to standard input:
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter your full name: ");
        String name = sc.nextLine(); // Reads the complete line including spaces

        System.out.println("Hello, " + name);

        sc.close();
    }
}
Console Session:
Enter your full name: Abhinav Nagvanshi
Hello, Abhinav Nagvanshi
(Here, nextLine() scans through the entire string until it encounters the enter/newline key.)

3. Master Scanner Methods Reference Table

Scanner Method Data Type Returned Sample Valid Input Behavior / Delimiter
next() String "Abhinav" Reads a single whitespace-delimited token.
nextLine() String "Abhinav Nagvanshi" Reads until the end of the current line (consumes newline).
nextInt() int 25 Scans the next token as a 32-bit integer.
nextLong() long 9876543210L Scans the next token as a 64-bit integer.
nextFloat() float 12.5f Scans the next token as a 32-bit floating point.
nextDouble() double 99.99 Scans the next token as a 64-bit double precision float.
nextBoolean() boolean true / false Scans case-insensitively (e.g., "True").
nextShort() short 100 Scans a 16-bit short value.
nextByte() byte 10 Scans an 8-bit byte value.
MultipleInputTokensDemo.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter two numbers (space or newline separated): ");
        int a = sc.nextInt();
        int b = sc.nextInt();

        System.out.println("Sum = " + (a + b)); // Handles "10 20" or "10\n20" identically

        sc.close();
    }
}

4. Master Distinction: next() vs. nextLine()

Feature sc.next() sc.nextLine()
Scope Reads exactly 1 individual token (word) Reads the entire line up to the newline character
Whitespace Handling Stops immediately at any whitespace (space, tab, newline) Includes spaces and tabs within the captured string
Line Separator Leaves the trailing newline in the stream buffer Consumes and discards the newline character
NextVsNextLineDemo.java 
System.out.print("Enter full name: ");
String name = sc.nextLine(); // Input: "Abhinav Nagvanshi" -> name = "Abhinav Nagvanshi"

System.out.print("Enter city: ");
String city = sc.next();     // Input: "Lucknow UP" -> city = "Lucknow" (stops at space)

5. 🎯 The Infamous nextInt() ➔ nextLine() Skipping Trap

One of the most notorious bugs in Java beginner programming occurs when invoking nextLine() directly after a token reader like nextInt() or nextDouble().

User Types: 21\n Buffer has ['2','1','\n']
➔
sc.nextInt() Consumes 21, leaves \n in buffer
➔
sc.nextLine() Immediately eats \n ➔ returns empty ""!
BufferFlushingDemo.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter your age: ");
        int age = sc.nextInt();
        
        // 💡 THE CRITICAL FIX: Flush/consume the lingering newline character!
        sc.nextLine(); 

        System.out.print("Enter your full name: ");
        String name = sc.nextLine(); // Now successfully waits for user text input

        System.out.println("Age:  " + age);
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);

        sc.close();
    }
}

6. Reading Characters with Scanner

Because the Scanner class contains no built-in nextChar() method, character input is achieved by reading a string token and extracting the first character using charAt(0):

CharInputDemo.java 
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

System.out.print("Enter grade (A/B/C): ");
char grade = sc.next().charAt(0); // Reads token string and grabs character at index 0

System.out.println("Recorded Grade: " + grade);

7. High-Performance Input with BufferedReader

BufferedReader reads text from a character input stream, buffering characters to provide for efficient reading of characters, arrays, and lines.

BufferedReaderDemo.java 
import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.InputStreamReader;
import java.io.IOException;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        // Wrap InputStreamReader around standard input:
        BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));

        System.out.print("Enter name: ");
        String name = br.readLine();

        System.out.print("Enter age: ");
        int age = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); // Manual string-to-int parsing

        System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", Age: " + age);
    }
}

Architectural Comparison: Scanner vs. BufferedReader

Criterion java.util.Scanner java.io.BufferedReader
Internal Buffer Size Small (1 KB buffer) Large (8 KB default buffer)
Parsing Capability Built-in automatic tokenization via regex Only reads raw lines; requires manual parsing (e.g. Integer.parseInt)
Execution Speed Slower (overhead from regex token parsing) Blisteringly fast (direct stream buffering)
Thread Safety Not synchronized (not thread-safe) Synchronized (thread-safe reads)
Exception Handling Does not require checked exception handling Must handle checked IOException
Recommended Usage Everyday applications, console menus, parsing Competitive programming, bulk file I/O

8. Scanner Lifecycle & System.in Caution

⚠️ Critical Stream Warning on sc.close():
Invoking sc.close() does not just close the scanner object; it closes the underlying System.in input stream for the entire JVM process! Once closed, System.in cannot be reopened. In multi-module applications, do not close standard input unless the application is actively shutting down.

9. Defensive Input Validation with hasNextInt()

Preventing crash bugs caused by users entering non-numeric characters when integers are expected:

DefensiveValidationDemo.java 
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

System.out.print("Enter an integer: ");
if (sc.hasNextInt()) {
    int val = sc.nextInt();
    System.out.println("Valid integer: " + val);
} else {
    System.out.println("Invalid input! Input was not an integer.");
}

10. Complete Student Registration Program

StudentRegistrationApp.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter student name: ");
        String name = sc.nextLine();

        System.out.print("Enter roll number: ");
        int rollNumber = sc.nextInt();

        System.out.print("Enter marks: ");
        double marks = sc.nextDouble();

        System.out.println("\n==================================");
        System.out.println("        STUDENT ENROLLMENT        ");
        System.out.println("==================================");
        System.out.println("Name:        " + name);
        System.out.println("Roll Number: " + rollNumber);
        System.out.println("Marks:       " + marks);
        System.out.println("==================================");

        sc.close();
    }
}
Expected Console Output: 
Enter student name: Abhinav Nagvanshi
Enter roll number: 101
Enter marks: 87.5

==================================
        STUDENT ENROLLMENT        
==================================
Name:        Abhinav Nagvanshi
Roll Number: 101
Marks:       87.5

1. Project Overview & Applied Concepts

The Mortgage Calculator is an end-to-end practical Java console application that calculates the monthly amortized installment (EMI), total payout, and total accrued interest on a home loan based on the principal amount, annual interest rate, and repayment duration.

This capstone project synthesizes all foundational Java concepts learned across Chapter 1:

Java Concept Implementation Role in Mortgage Calculator
Variables & Data Types Stores loan principal (double), interest rate (double), and years (int).
Standard Input (Scanner) Captures dynamic keyboard input interactively from standard in (sc.nextDouble()).
Arithmetic Expressions Normalizes annual rate to monthly decimal rate and computes monthly counts.
The Math Class Leverages Math.pow(1 + r, n) to compute exponential compounding factors.
Conditional Logic (if-else) Validates non-negative inputs and handles 0% zero-interest edge cases ($M = P / n$).
Formatted Output (printf) Renders currency figures formatted to two decimal places (%.2f%n).

2. System Workflow & Processing Architecture

1. User Input Principal $P$, Annual Rate %, Term in Years
➔
2. Rate & Term Normalization $r = \text{Rate} / 1200$
$n = \text{Years} \times 12$
➔
3. Amortization Formula $M = P \frac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}$
➔
4. Formatted Summary Monthly EMI, Total Paid, Total Interest

3. Mathematical Loan Amortization Formula

The standard fixed monthly installment ($M$) for a fully amortizing loan is derived via the annuity formula:

M = P × [ r(1 + r)n / ((1 + r)n - 1) ]
Symbol Meaning Mathematical Transformation
M Monthly Installment (EMI) Computed monthly payment
P Principal Loan Amount Base borrowing balance
r Monthly Interest Rate (decimal) $\displaystyle r = \frac{\text{Annual Rate}}{12 \times 100} = \frac{6}{1200} = 0.005$
n Total Monthly Payment Cycles $n = \text{Years} \times 12 = 20 \times 12 = 240$
💡 Zero-Interest Edge Case: If the interest rate is 0%, the formula encounters a division by zero error ($0 / 0$). In Java, we handle this gracefully with a conditional branch: monthlyPayment = principal / months;.

4. Complete Executable Java Source Code (Solution)

MortgageCalculator.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class MortgageCalculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        // 1. Reading input from user
        System.out.print("Enter loan amount: ");
        double principal = sc.nextDouble();

        System.out.print("Enter annual interest rate (%): ");
        double annualRate = sc.nextDouble();

        System.out.print("Enter loan term (years): ");
        int years = sc.nextInt();

        // 2. Input validation
        if (principal <= 0 || annualRate < 0 || years <= 0) {
            System.out.println("Invalid input. Values must be positive numbers.");
            sc.close();
            return;
        }

        // 3. Normalizing time and interest rates
        int months = years * 12;
        double monthlyRate = annualRate / 100 / 12;
        double monthlyPayment;

        // 4. Calculating monthly payment
        if (monthlyRate == 0) {
            monthlyPayment = principal / months; // Zero interest edge case
        } else {
            double factor = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, months);
            monthlyPayment = principal * (monthlyRate * factor) / (factor - 1);
        }

        // 5. Total payments and interest
        double totalPayment = monthlyPayment * months;
        double totalInterest = totalPayment - principal;

        // 6. Formatted summary receipt
        System.out.println("\n=================================");
        System.out.println("        MORTGAGE SUMMARY         ");
        System.out.println("=================================");
        System.out.printf("Loan Amount:     %.2f%n", principal);
        System.out.printf("Monthly Payment: %.2f%n", monthlyPayment);
        System.out.printf("Total Payment:   %.2f%n", totalPayment);
        System.out.printf("Total Interest:  %.2f%n", totalInterest);
        System.out.println("=================================");

        sc.close();
    }
}

6. Detailed Architectural Breakdown of Key Logic

  • Input Normalization: int months = years * 12; converts calendar years into discrete monthly payment intervals.
  • Rate Conversion: double monthlyRate = annualRate / 100 / 12; transforms a nominal percentage (e.g. 6%) into a decimal monthly rate (0.005).
  • Compound Compounding Factor: double factor = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, months); evaluates $(1 + r)^n$ using high-performance IEEE 754 hardware operations.
  • Decimal Display Guard: System.out.printf("Monthly Payment: %.2f%n", monthlyPayment); rounds to 2 decimal places solely for clean visualization without mutating underlying floating-point precision.

Unit 2: Types

28. Summary of Types

Key takeaways and mental models from Unit 2:

Concept Key Rule / Behavior Quick Example
Primitive Types Stored directly by value in Stack memory. Fast, fixed size, no object overhead. int age = 30;
Reference Types Store reference address; object lives in Heap. Must be instantiated with new (except String literals). Point p = new Point(1, 2);
Strings Immutable reference type stored in JVM String Pool for memory optimization. String msg = "Hello";
Arrays Fixed length upon creation. Zero-indexed. Access out of bounds throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. int[] numbers = new int[5];
Constants Created with final keyword. Value cannot be reassigned once initialized. final float PI = 3.14F;
Type Casting Implicit widening (safe, e.g. int to double). Explicit narrowing (potential data loss, e.g. (int) 3.9). int x = (int) 4.5; // 4
Scanner Input Reads console input. Use scanner.next() for tokens and scanner.nextLine() for sentences. int n = sc.nextInt();
Unit 3: Control Flow

29. Introduction to Control Flow

By default, Java programs execute sequentially from top to bottom, line by line. Control Flow statements break this linear progression by directing program execution based on runtime conditions and repetition requirements.

1. Conditional Branching

Make decisions based on boolean logic: if, else if, else, switch, and the compact ternary operator ?:.

2. Iterative Loops

Execute code blocks repeatedly: for (known count), while (condition-driven), do..while (at least once), and enhanced for-each.

Chapter 2: Control Flow & Decision Making

Comparison Operators: Relational Logic, Floating-Point Precision & Object Equality

1. Introduction to Comparison (Relational) Operators

In Java, comparison operators (also known as relational operators) evaluate the relationship between two operands and always produce a strict boolean result: either true or false.

Unlike languages like C/C++ where comparisons can yield numeric integers (1 or 0), Java is strictly type-safe: all comparison expressions evaluate to the primitive boolean type.

Where Comparison Operators Are Used:
  • Decision-Making: Governing branching conditions in if, if-else, and ternary operator expressions.
  • Loop Terminators: Formulating guard conditions in while, do-while, and for loop constructs.
  • Input Sanitization: Guarding ranges (e.g. age >= 0 && age <= 120).
  • Sorting & Searching Algorithms: Comparing keys in Bubble Sort, QuickSort, and Binary Search.
ComparisonDemo.java 
public class ComparisonDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 20;

        System.out.println(a < b);  // true  (10 is strictly less than 20)
        System.out.println(a > b);  // false (10 is not greater than 20)
    }
}
Console Output: 
true
false

2. The Six Comparison Operators in Java

Java provides six standard binary relational operators capable of comparing primitive numeric and character types:

Operator Name Semantic Meaning Code Example Evaluated Result
== Equal to Returns true if both operands represent the exact same value. 10 == 10 true
!= Not equal to Returns true if the operands are mathematically distinct. 10 != 20 true
> Greater than Returns true if the left operand exceeds the right operand strictly. 20 > 10 true
< Less than Returns true if the left operand is strictly below the right operand. 10 < 20 true
>= Greater than or equal to Returns true if the left operand is greater than or identical to the right. 10 >= 10 true
<= Less than or equal to Returns true if the left operand is less than or identical to the right. 10 <= 5 false

3. Equal to Operator (==) vs. Assignment (=)

The equality operator compares two operands for equivalence. One of the most notorious bugs in programming is conflating single equals = with double equals ==:

⚠️ Critical Trap: = vs ==
  • = is the Assignment Operator: it assigns the evaluated value of the right side into the left variable.
  • == is the Relational Equality Operator: it checks equivalence and returns a boolean.
EqualityDemo.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 10;
        int c = 20;

        System.out.println(a == b); // true (10 equals 10)
        System.out.println(a == c); // false (10 does not equal 20)

        // Assignment vs Comparison:
        int x = 5;                  // Variable assignment
        System.out.println(x == 5); // Comparison evaluates to true
    }
}

4. Not Equal to Operator (!=)

The inequality operator != checks whether two operands are unequal. If the values differ, it returns true; otherwise, it returns false:

InequalityDemo.java 
int a = 10;
int b = 20;

System.out.println(a != b);  // true  (10 and 20 are different)
System.out.println(a != 10); // false (both sides evaluate to 10)

5. Strict Inequalities: Greater Than (>) and Less Than (<)

Strict inequalities exclude boundary equality. If the left and right values are identical, strict operators evaluate to false:

StrictComparisonDemo.java 
int age = 21;

System.out.println(age > 18); // true  (21 is strictly greater than 18)
System.out.println(age < 18); // false (21 is not less than 18)
System.out.println(age > 21); // false (21 is equal to 21, NOT strictly greater)

6. Inclusive Inequalities: >= and <=

Inclusive inequalities incorporate boundary parity. They return true if the value is either strictly greater/smaller OR equal:

InclusiveComparisonDemo.java 
int marks = 40;

System.out.println(marks >= 40); // true  (40 is equal to 40, condition satisfied)
System.out.println(marks <= 40); // true  (40 is equal to 40, condition satisfied)
System.out.println(marks > 40);  // false (strict inequality fails on equality)
Key Takeaway:
  • > and < strictly exclude boundary equality.
  • >= and <= safely include boundary equality.

7. Practical Usage with if-else Branching

Comparison expressions form the conditional predicate in control flow statements:

VotingEligibility.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 20;

        if (age >= 18) {
            System.out.println("Eligible to vote");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Not eligible to vote");
        }
    }
}
Execution Flow: The expression age >= 18 evaluates to true (since $20 \ge 18$). Hence, the JVM executes the primary if body and skips the else branch entirely.

8. Character Comparisons & Unicode Codepoints

In Java, char is a 16-bit unsigned numeric primitive that stores UTF-16 Unicode codepoints. When comparison operators are applied to characters, Java compares their underlying integer codes:

CharComparison.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        char a = 'A'; // Unicode value: 65
        char b = 'B'; // Unicode value: 66

        System.out.println(a < b);  // true  (65 < 66)
        System.out.println(a == b); // false (65 != 66)

        // Checking character classification via ranges:
        char ch = 'k';
        boolean isLowerCase = (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z'); // true (97 <= 107 <= 122)
        System.out.println("Is lowercase: " + isLowerCase);
    }
}

9. Floating-Point Precision Pitfall (float & double)

Floating-point primitives adhere to the IEEE 754 standard. Because fractional decimals like 0.1 and 0.2 have repeating fractions in binary, arithmetic operations accrue minor rounding imprecisions:

FloatPrecisionBug.java 
double a = 0.1 + 0.2; // Evaluates in binary to 0.30000000000000004
double b = 0.3;

System.out.println(a == b); // FALSE! Never use == directly on computed floating-point numbers
⚡ Safe Solution: Epsilon Tolerance Comparison
Compare whether the absolute difference between the numbers falls within a designated microscopic tolerance ($\epsilon$):
EpsilonComparison.java 
double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
double b = 0.3;

// Define an acceptable threshold (epsilon)
double epsilon = 0.000001; // 1e-6

boolean isEqual = Math.abs(a - b) < epsilon;
System.out.println("Safe comparison result: " + isEqual); // true
💡 Pro-Tip for Financial Systems: For monetary calculations requiring absolute accuracy, avoid double entirely and use java.math.BigDecimal with compareTo().

10. Primitive Equality (==) vs. Object Reference Equality (.equals())

A core tenet of Java memory mechanics is understanding what == evaluates when applied to objects versus primitives:

Mechanism When Used On Primitives When Used On Objects / Strings
== Compares raw literal values (e.g. 5 == 5 is true). Compares memory addresses (reference pointers in heap memory). Returns true only if both point to the identical object instance.
.equals() Not applicable (primitives have no methods). Compares logical contents/values encapsulated inside the objects.
StringEqualityPitfall.java 
String s1 = new String("Java"); // Created as a distinct object in Heap
String s2 = new String("Java"); // Created as another distinct object in Heap

System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // false (distinct memory references)
System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // true  (character sequences are identical)
Safe String Comparison: Always utilize str1.equals(str2) or null-safe java.util.Objects.equals(s1, s2) when validating string contents.

11. Common Mistakes & Best Practices Matrix

Common Beginner Mistake Why It Causes Bugs Correct Idiomatic Java Approach
Writing if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5) Causes compilation error (or accidental assignment if boolean). Use == for relational equality comparison.
Using str1 == str2 to check string match Compares heap memory references instead of text characters. Always invoke str1.equals(str2).
Assuming > includes boundary values Off-by-one errors in loops and decision filters. Use >= when boundary parity must be included.
Comparing calculated floats directly with == Binary floating-point precision imprecision triggers unexpected false. Use tolerance comparison: Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-6 or BigDecimal.
Assuming comparisons return numeric 1 or 0 Java does not permit treating booleans as numbers. Comparison expressions exclusively yield true or false.

Chapter 2: Control Flow & Decision Making

Logical Operators: Short-Circuit Evaluation, Bitwise Parallels (&, |), Truth Tables & Precedence

1. Introduction to Logical Operators

In Java, logical operators operate on one or more boolean operands to perform conditional logic, combine multiple relational tests, or invert truth values. Like comparison operators, logical operators always evaluate to a strict boolean result: true or false.

Everyday Practical Applications:
  • Branching Guard Conditions: Formulating multi-criteria predicates in if-else and ternary constructs.
  • Loop Invariants: Complex termination conditions in while and for loops.
  • Defensive Null-Guards: Verifying references exist prior to invoking member methods.
  • Access Control & Authentication: Enforcing composite role permissions (e.g. isAuthenticated && hasRole("ADMIN")).

Java defines three foundational logical operators:

&&
Logical AND
Returns true ONLY if both conditions evaluate to true.
||
Logical OR
Returns true if at least one condition evaluates to true.
!
Logical NOT (Unary)
Inverts/reverses a boolean: !true → false, !false → true.

2. Logical AND (&&)

The conditional-AND operator requires strict unanimity: every single sub-condition must evaluate to true for the compound expression to pass.

Operand A Operand B Evaluated (A && B) Logic Explanation
true true true Both criteria satisfied
true false false Operand B fails
false true false Operand A fails
false false false Both criteria fail
LogicalAndDemo.java 
public class LogicalAndDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 22;
        boolean hasLicense = true;

        // Both age >= 18 (true) AND hasLicense (true)
        System.out.println(age >= 18 && hasLicense); // true

        // Real-world candidate eligibility screening:
        int candidateAge = 20;
        int qualifyingMarks = 75;

        if (candidateAge >= 18 && qualifyingMarks >= 60) {
            System.out.println("Candidate Status: Eligible");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Candidate Status: Not Eligible");
        }
    }
}
Console Output: 
true
Candidate Status: Eligible

3. Logical OR (||)

The conditional-OR operator returns true if any operand is true. It yields false only when both operands evaluate to false.

Operand A Operand B Evaluated (A || B) Logic Explanation
true true true Both criteria satisfied
true false true Operand A satisfies condition
false true true Operand B satisfies condition
false false false No criteria satisfied
LogicalOrDemo.java 
public class LogicalOrDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        boolean isWeekend = false;
        boolean isHoliday = true;

        System.out.println(isWeekend || isHoliday); // true (isHoliday is true)

        // Real-world discount concession eligibility:
        int customerAge = 65;
        boolean isStudent = false;

        // Senior citizen OR student discount
        if (customerAge >= 60 || isStudent) {
            System.out.println("Pricing: Concession Discount Available");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Pricing: Standard Tariff (No Discount)");
        }
    }
}

4. Logical NOT (!)

The logical NOT operator is a unary operator that negates or flips the truth value of its boolean target operand.

Operand A Evaluated (!A) Effect
true false Truth inverted to false
false true False inverted to true
LogicalNotDemo.java 
public class LogicalNotDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        boolean isRaining = false;
        System.out.println(!isRaining); // true

        // User session guard:
        boolean isLoggedIn = false;

        if (!isLoggedIn) {
            System.out.println("Redirecting: Please log in to continue.");
        }
    }
}

5. Short-Circuit Evaluation: Performance & Safety Mechanics

Java's binary logical operators && and || execute using short-circuit evaluation: the JVM evaluates operands from left to right, and stops immediately as soon as the definitive boolean result is established.

A. Short-Circuit AND (&&)

If the left operand is false, the entire outcome must be false regardless of the right side. The right operand is never evaluated.

false && [SKIPPED] → false

B. Short-Circuit OR (||)

If the left operand is true, the entire outcome must be true regardless of the right side. The right operand is never evaluated.

true || [SKIPPED] → true
ShortCircuitSafety.java 
public class ShortCircuitSafety {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 0;

        // 1. Preventing ArithmeticException (Division by Zero):
        // Since (a < 5) is false, the expression (10 / b > 1) is NEVER computed!
        System.out.println(a < 5 && 10 / b > 1); // false (no crash)

        // Since (a > 5) is true, the division by zero (a / 0 > 1) is NEVER computed!
        System.out.println(a > 5 || a / 0 > 1);  // true (no crash)

        // 2. The Defensive Null-Pointer Guard Pattern:
        String name = null;

        // Safe: If name == null, name.length() is skipped. NullPointerException is avoided!
        if (name != null && name.length() > 0) {
            System.out.println("Valid non-empty name: " + name);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Defensive guard triggered: Invalid name reference");
        }
    }
}
🛡️ The Gold Standard Null Guard:
Always place the null check on the left side of &&: ref != null && ref.method(). Reversing the order (ref.method() && ref != null) will throw a fatal NullPointerException before the null check is ever reached.

6. Critical Difference: && vs. &

Both && and & compute logical AND when applied to boolean operands, but their operational semantics differ drastically:

Architectural Feature && (Conditional-AND) & (Logical / Bitwise AND)
Short-Circuiting Yes (skips right side if left is false) No (always evaluates both sides)
Side-Effect Safety Prevents side-effects on right side when left is false Executes side-effects on right side unconditionally
Null-Guard Suitability Safe for ref != null && ref.op() Dangerous: throws NullPointerException on right side
Bitwise Capabilities Boolean operands only Operates on booleans AND integral bitmasks (int, long)
SideEffectComparisonAnd.java 
// Scenario 1: Using Short-Circuit &&
int a = 10;
System.out.println(a < 5 && a++ > 0); // false
System.out.println("Value of a: " + a); // 10 (a++ was SKIPPED!)

// Scenario 2: Using Bitwise & on booleans
int b = 10;
System.out.println(b < 5 & b++ > 0);  // false
System.out.println("Value of b: " + b); // 11 (b++ was EXECUTED!)

7. Critical Difference: || vs. |

Similarly, || short-circuits as soon as a true condition is detected, whereas | forces both sides to compute:

Architectural Feature || (Conditional-OR) | (Logical / Bitwise OR)
Short-Circuiting Yes (skips right side if left is true) No (always evaluates both sides)
Side-Effect Execution Skips right side evaluation when left is true Executes right side regardless of left value
SideEffectComparisonOr.java 
// Scenario 1: Using Short-Circuit ||
int a = 10;
System.out.println(a > 5 || a++ > 0); // true
System.out.println("Value of a: " + a); // 10 (a++ was SKIPPED!)

// Scenario 2: Using Bitwise | on booleans
int b = 10;
System.out.println(b > 5 | b++ > 0);  // true
System.out.println("Value of b: " + b); // 11 (b++ was EXECUTED!)

8. Combining Multiple Logical Operators & Operator Precedence

When combining multiple boolean operators in compound expressions, Java follows a strict operator precedence hierarchy:

1. Unary NOT ( ! )  >  2. Logical AND ( && )  >  3. Logical OR ( || )
CompoundEvaluation.java 
public class CompoundEvaluation {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 22;
        boolean hasId = true;
        boolean isBlocked = false;

        // Compound verification check:
        if (age >= 18 && hasId && !isBlocked) {
            System.out.println("Security: Access Granted");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Security: Access Denied");
        }

        // Precedence demo:
        // false && false is evaluated FIRST due to higher precedence of && over ||
        // Expression becomes: true || (false && false) -> true || false -> true
        boolean result = true || false && false;
        System.out.println("Precedence result: " + result); // true

        // Forcing different evaluation order with parentheses:
        boolean groupedResult = (true || false) && false;
        System.out.println("Parenthesized result: " + groupedResult); // false
    }
}
💡 Pro-Tip (Clean Code): Never rely on reader memory for precedence between && and ||. Always use explicit grouping parentheses (A && B) || (C && D) to eliminate ambiguity and prevent defects during code maintenance.

9. Bonus: De Morgan's Laws in Java

De Morgan's Laws state how to distribute a negation across logical operators:

Law 1:
!(A && B)  ≡  !A || !B
Law 2:
!(A || B)  ≡  !A && !B

10. Comparison Operators vs. Logical Operators

Criterion Comparison (Relational) Operators Logical Operators
Primary Function Compare values or magnitudes of operands Combine or negate existing boolean conditions
Operands Accepted Numbers (int, double), char, references (==, !=) Strictly boolean values or expressions
Symbols ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= &&, ||, ! (and bitwise &, |)
Result Produced Always returns boolean Always returns boolean
RangeCheckIdiom.java 
int age = 20;

// Comparison operators (>=, <=) produce booleans; Logical AND (&&) joins them:
boolean isValidWorkingAge = (age >= 18) && (age <= 60);
System.out.println("Eligible working age: " + isValidWorkingAge); // true

11. Common Mistakes & Best Practices Matrix

Common Beginner Mistake Root Cause / Symptom Idiomatic Java Correction
Using single & instead of && in guards Disables short-circuiting; triggers NullPointerException or division by zero. Use conditional && for standard logic.
Using single | instead of || Forces unwanted evaluation of the right-side expression. Use conditional || for boolean conditions.
Writing mathematical ranges like 18 <= age <= 60 Compilation error: Java does not support chained relational operators. Decompose into two comparisons: age >= 18 && age <= 60.
Writing if (isLoggedIn == true) Redundant and unidiomatic boolean comparison. Simply write if (isLoggedIn) or if (!isLoggedIn).
Negation confusion: !a && b vs !(a && b) ! binds tightly to a alone; alters the entire logic. Use parentheses explicitly to express intent.

Chapter 2: Control Flow & Decision Making

The if Statement: Conditional Branching, else-if Ladders, Nested Logic & Best Practices

1. Introduction to Conditional Decision-Making

In computer programming, programs rarely execute in a purely linear sequence from top to bottom. The if statement is Java's foundational control flow construct for selection and decision-making. It instructs the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) to execute a specific block of statements only if a given predicate condition evaluates to true.

Real-World Conditional Analogies:
  • Academic Grading: If marks $\ge 40$, the student passes.
  • Civic Franchise: If age $\ge 18$, the citizen is eligible to vote.
  • Cybersecurity Authentication: If password matches hash, access is granted; otherwise, account lockout triggers.

2. Anatomy and Evaluation Mechanics of the if Statement

Syntax: if Statement 
if (condition) {
    // Statements execute ONLY when condition evaluates to true
}
1. Evaluate Predicate JVM computes boolean expression inside (condition)
➔
2. Check Truth Value Is the result true or false?
➔
3. Branch Execution If true: execute block
If false: skip block entirely

3. Basic if Statement Demonstration

VotingEligibility.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 20;

        // Condition evaluates to true (20 >= 18)
        if (age >= 18) {
            System.out.println("You are eligible to vote.");
        }

        // When condition evaluates to false:
        int minorAge = 16;
        if (minorAge >= 18) {
            System.out.println("This message will NEVER be printed.");
        }

        System.out.println("Program execution completed.");
    }
}
Console Output: 
You are eligible to vote.
Program execution completed.

4. Coupling Comparison Operators with if

Conditions are predominantly composed using the six standard relational operators:

Operator Relational Meaning Java Conditional Example Behavior
== Equal to if (status == 200) Executes if status holds the exact integer value 200
!= Not equal to if (accountType != null) Executes if accountType reference is non-null
> Strictly greater than if (balance > 0) Executes only if positive funds exist
< Strictly less than if (temperature < 0) Executes if temperature is sub-zero
>= Greater than or equal to if (marks >= 40) Executes for 40 and all higher values
<= Less than or equal to if (attempts <= 3) Executes while attempts do not exceed 3

5. Formulating Compound Predicates with Logical Operators

Real-world business rules frequently require multiple conditions to be checked simultaneously using &&, ||, or !:

CompoundConditions.java 
public class CompoundConditions {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Logical AND (&&): Both criteria must hold
        int driverAge = 22;
        boolean hasLicense = true;

        if (driverAge >= 18 && hasLicense) {
            System.out.println("Authorization: You are authorized to drive.");
        }

        // 2. Logical OR (||): At least one criterion must hold
        boolean isWeekend = false;
        boolean isHoliday = true;

        if (isWeekend || isHoliday) {
            System.out.println("Schedule: You can relax today.");
        }

        // 3. Logical NOT (!): Inverting a boolean condition
        boolean isLoggedIn = false;

        if (!isLoggedIn) {
            System.out.println("Security: Please log in to view protected resources.");
        }
    }
}

6. Binary Branching: The if-else Statement

When you need to perform mutually exclusive actions — one action when the condition is true and an alternative action when it is false — use the if-else construct:

PassFailCheck.java 
public class PassFailCheck {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int marks = 35;

        if (marks >= 40) {
            System.out.println("Result: Student Passed");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Result: Student Failed (Must Retake)");
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway: Exactly one of the two branches is guaranteed to execute. The JVM will never execute both, nor will it skip both.

7. Multi-Way Branching: The else-if Ladder

When an application needs to evaluate a cascade of multiple sequential conditions, the else-if ladder tests each condition from top to bottom. The first condition that evaluates to true triggers its corresponding block; all subsequent branches are completely skipped.

GradeCalculator.java 
public class GradeCalculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int marks = 85;

        if (marks >= 90) {
            System.out.println("Distinction: Grade A");
        } else if (marks >= 80) {
            System.out.println("First Division: Grade B");
        } else if (marks >= 70) {
            System.out.println("Second Division: Grade C");
        } else if (marks >= 40) {
            System.out.println("Passing Grade: Grade D");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Unsuccessful: Grade F (Fail)");
        }
    }
}
⚠️ Critical Design Rule: Sequence & Specificity
In an else-if ladder, order matters critically! Always test the most restrictive or highest threshold first. If you placed marks >= 40 at the top, a student with 98 marks would immediately receive Grade D because the first condition would trigger and exit the entire ladder!

8. Hierarchical Decision-Making: Nested if Statements

A nested if is an if block placed inside another if or else block. It is ideal for multi-stage verification where subsequent checks are logically meaningless unless preceding conditions have already passed:

TwoFactorAuth.java 
public class TwoFactorAuth {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        boolean usernameCorrect = true;
        boolean passwordCorrect = true;

        if (usernameCorrect) {
            // Evaluated ONLY IF username is valid
            if (passwordCorrect) {
                System.out.println("Authentication Status: Login successful! Welcome back.");
            } else {
                System.out.println("Security Alert: Incorrect password.");
            }
        } else {
            System.out.println("Security Alert: User does not exist in directory.");
        }
    }
}

9. Interactive User Input with Scanner and if

Combining conditional statements with dynamic keyboard input enables fully interactive console applications:

NumberSignClassifier.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class NumberSignClassifier {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter an integer value: ");
        int number = sc.nextInt();

        if (number > 0) {
            System.out.println("Classification: Positive integer");
        } else if (number < 0) {
            System.out.println("Classification: Negative integer");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Classification: Neutral Zero");
        }

        sc.close();
    }
}

10. Common Beginner Mistakes & Gotchas

Bug / Anti-Pattern Erroneous Code Snippet Consequence & Correct Idiom
Accidental Semicolon if (age >= 18); { ... } The semicolon terminates the if as an empty statement! The subsequent block executes unconditionally. Remove the semicolon.
Assignment in Predicate if (x = 10) { ... } Compilation error: = is assignment. Java requires a strict boolean predicate. Use ==.
Non-Boolean Predicate if (count) { ... } Unlike C/C++ where 0 is false and non-zero is true, Java rejects integers in conditionals. Must write if (count != 0).
Omitting Braces (Dangling Else) if (x > 0) a = 1; b = 2; Without braces, only a = 1; belongs to the if. b = 2; executes unconditionally. Always use explicit braces { ... }.

11. Architectural Comparison: if vs. if-else vs. Ladder vs. Nested

Control Flow Construct Number of Output Paths Primary Architectural Role
Single if 1 or 0 (optional execution) Single guard check (execute only on true; otherwise do nothing).
Binary if-else Exactly 1 of 2 alternatives Binary fork (mutually exclusive true/false branch execution).
else-if Ladder Exactly 1 of N alternatives Multi-range categorization (grades, tax brackets, tier classification).
Nested if Multi-stage dependent paths Hierarchical gating (authentication steps, dependent prerequisites).

Triggered: marks >= 80 (85 >= 80 is true)

Chapter 2: Control Flow & Decision Making

Simplifying If Statements: Clean Code Patterns, Ternary Idioms, Guard Clauses & De Morgan's Laws

1. Introduction to Conditional Refactoring

Writing working code is only the first step of software engineering; writing clean, idiomatic, and maintainable code is what distinguishes professional engineers. In Java, simplifying if statements involves refactoring verbose conditional branching into concise, expressive expressions without altering the program's observable behavior.

Key Advantages of Simplified Conditionals:
  • Eliminates Redundant Boilerplate: Removes redundant checks against boolean literals.
  • Flattens Nested Pyramids: Eliminates the "Arrow Anti-Pattern" of deeply indented blocks.
  • Enhances Cognitive Readability: Code reads naturally like standard English specifications.
  • Prevents Subtle Bugs: Fewer lines of branching logic directly correlates with fewer edge-case regressions.
❌ Verbose & Redundant 
boolean hasHighIncome = false;

if (hasHighIncome == true) {
    System.out.println("Eligible");
}
✅ Clean & Idiomatic 
boolean hasHighIncome = false;

if (hasHighIncome) {
    System.out.println("Eligible");
}

2. Rule 1: Eliminate Redundant Boolean Literal Comparisons

Because a boolean variable or expression already evaluates to either true or false, comparing it to a boolean literal (== true or == false) is completely unnecessary:

Redundant Expression Clean Idiomatic Equivalent Logical Behavior
if (x == true) if (x) Executes when x is true
if (x == false) if (!x) Executes when x is false
if (x != true) if (!x) Executes when x is not true (i.e. false)
if (x != false) if (x) Executes when x is not false (i.e. true)
BooleanLiteralRefactoring.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        boolean isLoggedIn = true;
        boolean isAvailable = false;

        // Clean positive check:
        if (isLoggedIn) {
            System.out.println("Welcome back to your dashboard!");
        }

        // Clean negative check using NOT (!):
        if (!isAvailable) {
            System.out.println("Item status: Out of stock / Not available");
        }
    }
}

3. Rule 2: Simplify if-else Boolean Assignments

A ubiquitous beginner antipattern is using an entire if-else block solely to assign true or false to a boolean variable.

Before (7 lines of code): 
int age = 20;
boolean isAdult;

if (age >= 18) {
    isAdult = true;
} else {
    isAdult = false;
}
After (1 single clean line): 
int age = 20;

// Relational expression directly yields a boolean:
boolean isAdult = age >= 18;
Why This Works: In Java, comparison operators like >=, ==, and < are expressions that return a primitive boolean. Assigning the evaluated expression directly avoids branching instructions in JVM bytecode.

4. Rule 3: Use the Ternary Operator for Value Selection

The conditional operator ? : (ternary operator) is a compact expression used to select between two values based on a boolean condition:

TernaryIdioms.java 
public class TernaryIdioms {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int marks = 75;

        // Refactoring if-else value assignment:
        String result = (marks >= 40) ? "Pass" : "Fail";
        System.out.println("Result: " + result); // Pass

        // Finding the greater of two numbers:
        int a = 10, b = 20;
        int max = (a > b) ? a : b;
        System.out.println("Maximum: " + max);    // 20
    }
}
💡 Architectural Best Practice on Ternaries: Use the ternary operator exclusively when assigning or returning a value. Avoid nesting ternary operators (e.g. a ? b : c ? d : e) as this degrades code scannability.

5. Rule 4: Flatten Nested if Statements with Logical Operators

When consecutive nested if statements do not contain intermediate else branches, they can be merged into a single clean predicate using &&:

FlatteningConditions.java 
// 1. Multi-Criteria Validation:
// BEFORE:
if (age >= 18) {
    if (hasId) {
        System.out.println("Eligible to vote");
    }
}

// AFTER (Flattened):
if (age >= 18 && hasId) {
    System.out.println("Eligible to vote");
}

// 2. Continuous Numeric Range Check:
// BEFORE:
if (marks >= 40) {
    if (marks <= 100) {
        System.out.println("Valid passing marks");
    }
}

// AFTER (Flattened):
if (marks >= 40 && marks <= 100) {
    System.out.println("Valid passing marks");
}

6. Rule 5: Simplify Inverted Logic with De Morgan's Laws

Negating complex compound expressions often leads to confusing syntax. De Morgan's Laws allow developers to distribute negations to create far more intuitive conditions:

Law 1:
!(A && B)  ≡  !A || !B
Law 2:
!(A || B)  ≡  !A && !B
DeMorganSimplification.java 
// Scenario 1: Access control
// Before (cumbersome negation over grouping):
if (!(isAdult && hasId)) {
    System.out.println("Access denied");
}

// After (clearer decomposed check):
if (!isAdult || !hasId) {
    System.out.println("Access denied");
}

// Scenario 2: Guarding underage permission
// Before:
if (!(age >= 18 || hasPermission)) {
    System.out.println("Access denied");
}

// After (naturally readable without outer negation):
if (age < 18 && !hasPermission) {
    System.out.println("Access denied");
}

7. Rule 6: Extract Repeated Conditions into Named Variables

When the same comparison expression appears repeatedly across several blocks, extracting it into an explanatory boolean variable documents the business logic and eliminates redundant recomputation:

ExplanatoryVariables.java 
int age = 25;
boolean hasLicense = true;

// Clean extraction of self-documenting intent:
boolean isAdult = age >= 18;

if (isAdult) {
    System.out.println("Classification: Adult");
}

if (isAdult && hasLicense) {
    System.out.println("Authorization: Can drive");
}

8. Rule 7: Guard Clauses & Early Returns (Eliminate Unnecessary else)

When a conditional branch terminates a function (e.g. using return, throw, or break), wrapping the remainder of the method inside an else block adds meaningless indentation:

Before (Deeply Nested else): 
public static void checkAge(int age) {
    if (age < 18) {
        System.out.println("Minor");
        return;
    } else {
        System.out.println("Adult");
    }
}
After (Guard Clause & Early Return): 
public static void checkAge(int age) {
    // Guard clause handles edge case:
    if (age < 18) {
        System.out.println("Minor");
        return;
    }

    // Main execution path remains unindented:
    System.out.println("Adult");
}

9. Golden Rule: Preserve Observable Logic & Short-Circuit Semantics

⚠️ Critical Warning during Refactoring:
Simplification is valid only if semantics remain 100% identical:
  • Never swap || and && casually: || requires at least one true; && requires both true.
  • Watch Short-Circuit Order: In user != null && user.isActive(), swapping the order or altering the structure will cause a runtime NullPointerException!
  • Beware Side Effects: If a method call modifies internal state (e.g. hasPermissions() && nextToken()), short-circuiting determines whether nextToken() ever executes.

10. Master Refactoring Matrix

Verbose Antipattern Clean Refactored Form Refactoring Principle
if (flag == true) if (flag) Boolean literal elimination
if (flag == false) if (!flag) Logical NOT inversion
if (c) x = true; else x = false; x = c; Direct boolean expression assignment
if (c) x = "A"; else x = "B"; x = c ? "A" : "B"; Ternary value selection
if (a) { if (b) { ... } } if (a && b) { ... } Nested branch flattening
if (err) { handle(); return; } else { doWork(); } if (err) { handle(); return; } doWork(); Guard clause / Early return

11. ⚡ Live Interactive Condition Simplifier & Tester

Toggle between Verbose and Simplified forms to verify identical execution:

✨ Live Conditional Refactoring Workbench

Direct Boolean Assignment: boolean isAdult = age >= 18;
Result: true
Ternary Status Resolution: isAdult ? "Eligible" : "Underage"
Ternary Result: Eligible
Flattened Voting Predicate: if (isAdult && hasId)
Voting Eligibility: Allowed to Vote
Chapter 2: Control Flow & Decision Making

The Ternary Operator: Inline Conditionals, Type Promotion, Nested Expressions & Discount Project

1. Introduction to the Conditional (Ternary) Operator

The ternary operator (? :) is Java's only three-operand operator. It serves as a concise, inline conditional expression that yields one of two values depending on the evaluation of a boolean predicate.

Unlike standard if-else blocks which are statements (they execute code actions without returning a value), the ternary operator is an expression: it evaluates to a concrete value that can be assigned, passed into methods, or returned directly.

Syntax: Ternary Operator 
variable = condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse;
1. Condition Check Evaluate predicate expression to true or false
➔
2. True Branch ( ? ) If true: evaluate & return left expression
➔
3. False Branch ( : ) If false: evaluate & return right expression

2. Basic Example: if-else vs. The Ternary Operator

Traditional if-else Statement: 
int age = 20;

if (age >= 18) {
    System.out.println("Adult");
} else {
    System.out.println("Minor");
}
Ternary Expression: 
int age = 20;

String result = (age >= 18) ? "Adult" : "Minor";

System.out.println(result); // Adult

3. Common Use Cases for Value Assignment

The ternary operator shines brightest when selecting between two scalar values:

TernaryAssignments.java 
public class TernaryAssignments {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Pass / Fail Evaluation
        int marks = 75;
        String examResult = marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";
        System.out.println("Result: " + examResult); // Pass

        // 2. Finding the Maximum of Two Numbers
        int a = 10, b = 20;
        int max = a > b ? a : b;
        System.out.println("Maximum: " + max); // 20

        // 3. Parity Check (Even vs Odd) via Modulus
        int number = 7;
        String parity = (number % 2 == 0) ? "Even" : "Odd";
        System.out.println(number + " is: " + parity); // 7 is: Odd
    }
}

4. Direct Inline Usage with System.out.println()

Because the ternary operator is a first-class expression, it can be passed directly as an argument to method invocations without creating an intermediate local variable:

InlinePrintTernary.java 
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 16;

        // Evaluated inline on the fly:
        System.out.println(age >= 18 ? "Eligible to vote" : "Not Eligible to vote");
    }
}

5. Combining Ternaries with Logical Operators (&&, ||)

Ternary predicates can incorporate compound boolean logic using &&, ||, and !:

CompoundTernary.java 
public class CompoundTernary {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int driverAge = 22;
        boolean hasLicense = true;

        String drivingStatus = (driverAge >= 18 && hasLicense)
                ? "Authorized to drive"
                : "Cannot drive";

        System.out.println(drivingStatus); // Authorized to drive
    }
}

6. Nested Ternary Operators & Readability Boundaries

A ternary operator can be nested inside another ternary expression to resolve three or more branches:

NestedTernaryMaxOfThree.java 
public class NestedTernaryMaxOfThree {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 25;
        int c = 15;

        // Nested ternary: checks (a > b), then cascades to find highest
        int largest = (a > b)
                ? (a > c ? a : c)
                : (b > c ? b : c);

        System.out.println("Largest = " + largest); // 25
    }
}
⚠️ Readability Warning on Nesting:
While nesting ternary operators is syntactically valid in Java, chaining multiple levels (e.g. a ? b : c ? d : e ? f : g) severely harms code maintainability. For more than two decision paths, prefer an else-if ladder or a switch statement.

7. Type Compatibility & Numeric Promotion Gotchas

The true and false expressions of a ternary operator must be type-compatible with each other and the receiving variable. When mixing primitive numeric types, Java applies binary numeric promotion:

NumericPromotionTrap.java 
// Both branches return compatible String types:
String message = (age >= 18) ? "Adult" : "Minor"; // OK

// Numeric Promotion Trap:
// int (10) vs double (20.5) forces promotion of 10 to 10.0!
var result = true ? 10 : 20.5;

System.out.println(result); // Outputs: 10.0 (Type inferred as double)

8. Architectural Comparison: if-else vs. The Ternary Operator

Architectural Feature if-else Statement Ternary Operator (? :)
Language Construct Control flow statement (blocks) Value-producing expression
Returns a Value No (cannot assign block to a variable) Yes (can be assigned, passed, returned)
Side-Effects & Multi-Statements Can contain loops, method calls, multiple statements Restricted to single value expressions per branch
Readability Best Fit Complex logic, mutations, ladders Simple, clean, two-way value selection

9. Common Mistakes & Compiler Pitfalls

Mistake Erroneous Code Corrected Code
Omitting the Colon (:) String s = (x > 0) ? "Positive"; String s = (x > 0) ? "Positive" : "Negative";
Assignment instead of Equality int s = (n = 5) ? 1 : 2; int s = (n == 5) ? 1 : 2;
Excessive Chained Nesting grade = m >= 90 ? "A" : m >= 80 ? "B" : "C"; Refactor into an else-if ladder or enhanced switch.

10. Mini Project: Simple Discount Calculator

A real-world console utility demonstrating ternary-based rate selection: applying a 10% discount when purchases reach or exceed ₹1,000.

DiscountCalculator.java 
import java.util.Scanner;

public class DiscountCalculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Enter purchase amount (₹): ");
        double amount = sc.nextDouble();

        // Ternary operator resolves discount rate cleanly:
        double discountRate = (amount >= 1000) ? 0.10 : 0.0;
        double discount = amount * discountRate;
        double finalAmount = amount - discount;

        System.out.println("\n--- Receipt Summary ---");
        System.out.printf("Original Amount: ₹%.2f%n", amount);
        System.out.printf("Discount (10%%):   ₹%.2f%n", discount);
        System.out.printf("Final Payable:   ₹%.2f%n", finalAmount);

        sc.close();
    }
}
Expected Console Session: 
Enter purchase amount (₹): 1500

--- Receipt Summary ---
Original Amount: ₹1500.00
Discount (10%):   ₹150.00
Final Payable:   ₹1350.00
