                  Part 2: Classes
                  
68. Introduction to Classes

                

              

              

                

                  In this section, we transition from writing sequential scripts inside a single main() method to building modular, maintainable software using Classes and Objects. You will master the fundamentals of Encapsulation, understand how the JVM manages memory for objects in the Heap, and learn how to minimize Coupling between software components.
                

              

            


            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming
                  
Classes and Objects in Java

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction

                

                  Classes and objects are the fundamental building blocks of Object-Oriented Programming in Java. A class defines the structure and behavior that its objects can have, while an object is a particular instance created from that class.
                

                
Memory anchor: A class is a blueprint; an object is something created using that blueprint.

                

                  
ConceptMeaningExample

                  
                    
ClassDefines fields and methods that objects can have.Car

                    
ObjectAn individual instance with its own state and identity.car1, car2, car3

                  
                

                
A Car class can define a brand, color, and start() method. Several car objects can then be created from the same class, each with different field values.


                
2. What Is a Class?

                
A class is a user-defined reference type that describes the fields, constructors, and methods associated with its objects. It acts as a blueprint for creating objects.

                

                  
Class Syntax

                  
class ClassName {
    // Fields (data)

    // Constructors

    // Methods (behavior)
}

                

                

                  
Student.java

                  
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    void study() {
        System.out.println(name + " is studying");
    }
}

                

                
    
                  
  • class Student declares a class named Student.
    • 
                  
  • String name and int age are instance fields.
    • 
                  
  • study() defines behavior for a student object.
    • 
                  
  • The declaration alone does not create a Student object.
    • 
                


                
3. What Is an Object?

                
An object is an instance of a class. It holds state through instance fields and provides behavior through methods. Objects of the same class share the class's method definitions but can have different field values.

                

                  
Object Creation

                  
ClassName referenceName = new ClassName();

Student student1 = new Student();

                

                

                  
ExpressionRole

                  
                    
StudentType of object that the reference can refer to.

                    
student1Reference variable that stores a reference to the object.

                    
new Student()Creates a new object and invokes its constructor.

                  
                

                
Important: student1 is a reference variable, not the object itself. The new expression creates the object, and the reference is used to access its members.


                
4. Complete Java Program: Classes and Objects

                
The same Student class can create multiple objects with independent field values.

                

                  
Main.java

                  
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    void displayInfo() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
        System.out.println();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student student1 = new Student();
        student1.name = "Abhinav";
        student1.age = 21;

        Student student2 = new Student();
        student2.name = "Rahul";
        student2.age = 22;

        student1.displayInfo();
        student2.displayInfo();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Name: Abhinav
Age: 21

Name: Rahul
Age: 22

                
    
                  
  1. Java defines the Student class with two fields and one method.
    2. 
                  
  2. new Student() creates each object.
    3. 
                  
  3. Each object receives its own name and age values.
    4. 
                  
  4. Calling displayInfo() uses the state of the object on which it is invoked.
    5. 
                


                
5. How Classes and Objects Work in Memory

                
Conceptually, each object has its own instance fields, and references allow the program to access those objects.

                

                  
main()student1 reference

                  ->
                  
Student Object 1name = "Abhinav", age = 21

                    
                  
student2 referenceseparate reference

                  ->
                  
Student Object 2name = "Rahul", age = 22

                

                
    
                  
  • Local reference variables are often stored in a method's stack frame.
    • 
                  
  • Objects are typically allocated on the heap.
    • 
                  
  • Instance fields belong to individual objects.
    • 
                  
  • Methods are defined by the class and invoked on objects.
    • 
                

                
This is a conceptual model. The JVM may optimize allocation and object representation, so the physical layout is implementation-dependent.


                
6. Instance Variables and Instance Methods

                
Instance Variables

                
Instance variables are declared inside a class but outside its methods and constructors. Every object has its own copy of these fields.

                

                  
Employee Fields

                  
class Employee {
    String name;
    double salary;
}

                

                
Instance Methods

                
Instance methods define behavior and can access the fields of the object on which they are invoked.

                

                  
Employee Behavior

                  
class Employee {
    String name;

    void work() {
        System.out.println(name + " is working");
    }
}

Employee emp = new Employee();
emp.name = "Abhinav";
emp.work(); // Abhinav is working

                


                
7. Default Values of Instance Variables

                
When an object is created, its instance fields receive default values before explicit assignments or constructor initialization change them.

                

                  
Data TypeDefault Value

                  
                    
byte, short, int, long0

                    
float, double0.0

                    
char'\u0000'

                    
booleanfalse

                    
Reference types, including Stringnull

                  
                

                

                  
DefaultValues.java

                  
class Demo {
    int number;
    boolean status;
    String message;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Demo d = new Demo();
        System.out.println(d.number);  // 0
        System.out.println(d.status);  // false
        System.out.println(d.message); // null
    }
}

                

                
Remember: Local variables inside methods do not automatically receive these default values. They must be definitely assigned before use.


                
8. Accessing Object Members

                
Use the dot operator (.) to access accessible fields and call methods through an object reference.

                

                  
Member Access

                  
objectName.fieldName;
objectName.methodName();

class Calculator {
    int number = 10;

    void showNumber() {
        System.out.println(number);
    }
}

Calculator c = new Calculator();
System.out.println(c.number); // 10
c.showNumber();               // 10

                


                
9. Multiple Objects of the Same Class

                
A single class can be used to create many independent objects. Each object maintains its own instance state while using the same class behavior.

                

                  
ReferenceObject State

                  
                    
student1Name: Abhinav, Age: 21

                    
student2Name: Rahul, Age: 22

                  
                

                
General rule: The same pattern applies to products, employees, bank accounts, orders, and other entities in Java applications.


                
10. Class vs Object

                

                  
FeatureClassObject

                  
                    
MeaningBlueprint or type definitionInstance of a class

                    
Contains or representsFields, constructors, methods, and declarationsState and identity; behavior is accessed through its class

                    
Declaration / creationDeclared using classCommonly created using new

                    
CountOne class can define many objectsMany objects can be created from one class

                    
Exampleclass Student {}new Student()

                  
                


                
11. Common Mistakes

                
Mistake 1: Using an object without creating it

                

                  
Uninitialized Reference

                  
Student s;
s.name = "Abhinav"; // Compilation error

// Correct
Student s = new Student();
s.name = "Abhinav";

                

                
The local variable s has not been initialized with a reference in the first example.

                
Mistake 2: Assuming objects share instance variables

                

                  
Independent State

                  
Student s1 = new Student();
Student s2 = new Student();

s1.age = 20;
s2.age = 25;
// s1.age is 20 and s2.age is 25

                

                
Mistake 3: Confusing a reference with an object

                

                  
Shared Reference

                  
Student s1 = new Student();
Student s2 = s1;

// Only one Student object exists.
// s1 and s2 refer to the same object.

                


                
12. Interview Questions

                
    
                  
  1. What is a class in Java? A user-defined reference type that defines the structure and behavior of its instances.
    2. 
                  
  2. What is an object? An instance of a class with its own identity and instance state.
    3. 
                  
  3. Can we create multiple objects from one class? Yes, subject to available system resources.
    4. 
                  
  4. What is the difference between an object and a reference variable? An object is an instance; a reference variable identifies or refers to that object.
    5. 
                  
  5. What happens in Student s = new Student();? Java creates a Student object using its constructor and assigns its reference to s.
    6. 
                  
  6. What are default instance values? Numeric primitives default to zero, boolean to false, char to '\u0000', and references to null.
    7. 
                  
  7. Can two references point to the same object? Yes. Assigning one reference to another copies the reference, not the object.
    8.

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming
                  
Creating Classes in Java

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction

                
A Java class is a user-defined reference type that defines the structure and behavior of objects. A class can contain fields, constructors, methods, initializer blocks, and nested types.

                
Creating classes allows us to represent real-world entities such as students, employees, products, bank accounts, and orders. An e-commerce application might contain Product, Customer, Cart, and Order classes.


                
2. Basic Syntax of a Class

                

                  
Class Syntax

                  
class ClassName {
    // Fields (data)

    // Constructors

    // Methods (behavior)
}

                

                

                  
Student.java

                  
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    void study() {
        System.out.println(name + " is studying.");
    }
}

                

                

                  
PartPurpose

                  
                    
classKeyword used to declare a class.

                    
StudentName of the class.

                    
name, ageInstance fields that store data.

                    
study()Instance method that defines behavior.

                    
{ }Delimit the class body.

                  
                

                
Important: Declaring a class does not create an object. An object must be created separately, usually with the new keyword.


                

                
3. Creating a Class and Its Object

                
To use an ordinary class's instance fields and methods, create an object and store its reference in a variable.

                

                  
Main.java

                  
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;

    void displayInfo() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student();
        s1.name = "Abhinav";
        s1.age = 21;
        s1.displayInfo();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Name: Abhinav
Age: 21

                
    
                  
  1. Student declares the class.
    2. 
                  
  2. new Student() creates an object and invokes its constructor.
    3. 
                  
  3. s1 stores a reference to that object.
    4. 
                  
  4. s1.name and s1.age assign values to instance fields.
    5. 
                  
  5. s1.displayInfo() invokes the object's method.
    6. 
                


                
4. Components of a Class

                

                  
ComponentPurposeExample

                  
                    
FieldsStore object or class data.name, id, salary

                    
ConstructorsInitialize objects when they are created.Employee()

                    
MethodsDefine operations and behavior.displayDetails()

                    
Other declarationsProvide class-level or nested structure.Static members, initializer blocks, nested classes, interfaces

                  
                


                
5. Naming Rules for Classes

                
    
                  
  • A class name cannot begin with a digit.
    • 
                  
  • It cannot be a Java keyword such as class, int, or public.
    • 
                  
  • Spaces are not allowed in class names.
    • 
                  
  • Class names conventionally use PascalCase.
    • 
                  
  • A public top-level class must have the same name as its source file.
    • 
                

                

                  
Class NameValid?Reason

                  
                    
StudentYesUses standard PascalCase.

                    
EmployeeDetailsYesUses PascalCase.

                    
Student1YesDigits are allowed after the first character.

                    
1StudentNoStarts with a digit.

                    
classNoIt is a Java keyword.

                    
Student DetailsNoContains a space.

                  
                


                
6. Creating Multiple Classes in One File

                
Java allows multiple top-level classes in one source file, but an ordinary source file can contain at most one public top-level class. The public class name must match the filename.

                

                  
Main.java

                  
class Student {
    String name = "Abhinav";

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Student: " + name);
    }
}

class Teacher {
    String subject = "Java";

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Subject: " + subject);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        Teacher t = new Teacher();
        s.display();
        t.display();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Student: Abhinav
Subject: Java

                
Student, Teacher, and Main are separate classes. The Main class creates objects of the other two classes.


                
7. Creating Classes in Separate Files

                
For larger applications, a common practice is to place each public top-level class in its own source file.

                
MyJavaProject/
|-- Main.java
|-- Student.java
|-- Teacher.java

                

                  
Student.java

                  
public class Student {
    String name;

    public void display() {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

                

                

                  
Main.java

                  
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        s.name = "Abhinav";
        s.display();
    }
}

                

                
If both files are in the same package, Main.java can use Student without an import statement.


                
8. Instance Members vs Static Members

                

                  
Instance and Static Members

                  
class Student {
    String name;                    // Instance field
    static String college = "AIMT"; // Static field

    void display() {                // Instance method
        System.out.println(name);
    }

    static void showCollege() {     // Static method
        System.out.println(college);
    }
}

Student s = new Student();
s.name = "Abhinav";
s.display();
Student.showCollege();

                

                

                  
FeatureInstance MemberStatic Member

                  
                    
Belongs toEach objectThe class

                    
AccessUsually through an object referenceUsually through the class name

                    
Examples.nameStudent.college

                    
Memory behaviorPer-object valuesOne shared class-level value

                  
                

                
Rule of thumb: Use instance members for data or behavior that varies per object. Use static members for data or behavior shared by the class.


                
9. Common Mistakes When Creating Classes

                
Mistake 1: Forgetting class braces

                
// Incorrect
class Student
    String name;

// Correct
class Student {
    String name;
}

                
Mistake 2: Using a class name as an object

                
// Invalid for a non-static instance field
Student.name = "Abhinav";

// Correct
Student s = new Student();
s.name = "Abhinav";

                
Mistake 3: Incorrect public class filename

                
If a source file declares public class Student, its filename must be Student.java.

                
Mistake 4: Confusing declaration with object creation

                
class Student {
    String name;
} // Class declaration only

Student s = new Student(); // Object creation


                
10. Practice Exercise

                
Create an Employee class with fields name, employeeId, and salary. Add a displayDetails() method, create two employee objects, and display both employees' details.

                

                  
Practice Solution

                  
class Employee {
    String name;
    int employeeId;
    double salary;

    void displayDetails() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("ID: " + employeeId);
        System.out.println("Salary: " + salary);
        System.out.println();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee e1 = new Employee();
        e1.name = "Abhinav";
        e1.employeeId = 101;
        e1.salary = 35000.0;

        Employee e2 = new Employee();
        e2.name = "Rahul";
        e2.employeeId = 102;
        e2.salary = 40000.0;

        e1.displayDetails();
        e2.displayDetails();
    }
}

                

                
Expected output:

                
Name: Abhinav
ID: 101
Salary: 35000.0

Name: Rahul
ID: 102
Salary: 40000.0


                
11. Interview Questions

                
    
                  
  1. What is a class in Java? A user-defined reference type that defines fields, constructors, methods, and other members.
    2. 
                  
  2. Can a Java file contain multiple classes? Yes. It can contain multiple top-level classes, but at most one can be public in an ordinary source file, and that public class must match the filename.
    3. 
                  
  3. What is the difference between a class and an object? A class defines a type and structure; an object is an instance of that class.
    4. 
                  
  4. What is the difference between instance and static members? Instance members belong to individual objects, while static members belong to the class.
    5. 
                  
  5. Can a class be created without creating an object? Yes. A class can be declared without objects, and static members can be used without creating an instance.
    6. 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming
                  
Memory Allocation in Java

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction

                
Memory allocation in Java is the process of reserving memory for objects, variables, method calls, and other runtime data. The JVM manages allocation and reclamation, so developers usually do not manually allocate and free application memory.

                
Understanding memory allocation helps explain where data is stored, how references point to objects, how method calls work, how garbage collection reclaims memory, and why errors such as StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError occur.


                
2. Main JVM Memory Areas

                
The JVM runtime is divided into several runtime data areas. For classes and objects, the most important areas are the stack and heap.

                

                  
StackFrames, locals, references

                  +
                  
HeapObjects and arrays

                  +
                  
Method AreaClass metadata and runtime structures

                  +
                  
Other AreasPC registers, native method stacks

                

                
This is a conceptual overview. The JVM specification defines runtime data areas, but the exact physical layout depends on the JVM implementation.


                
2.1 Stack Memory

                
Each thread has its own JVM stack. The stack contains frames for active method calls. A frame typically holds local variables, intermediate computation data, and information required to return from a method.

                

                  
Stack Frame Example

                  
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 21;
        double salary = 35000.0;

        System.out.println(age);
        System.out.println(salary);
    }
}

                

                
Here, age and salary are local primitive variables associated with the main() method's stack frame.


                
2.2 Heap Memory

                
The heap is the runtime area from which memory for objects and arrays is typically allocated.

                

                  
Heap Object Example

                  
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        s.name = "Abhinav";
        s.age = 21;
    }
}

                

                
    
                  
  • new Student() creates a Student object.
    • 
                  
  • The object's instance fields are part of its state.
    • 
                  
  • s is a local reference variable associated with the main() stack frame.
    • 
                  
  • The object is typically allocated on the heap.
    • 
                


                
3. Stack vs Heap Memory

                

                  
FeatureStackHeap

                  
                    
Main purposeMethod execution and local dataObjects and arrays

                    
OrganizationStack frames per threadShared runtime allocation area

                    
StoresLocal variables, references, intermediate dataObject and array data

                    
LifetimeFrames exist while methods are activeObjects remain while reachable or otherwise needed

                    
ManagementFrames are pushed and popped during executionManaged by the JVM and garbage collector

                    
Common problemStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError

                  
                


                
4. Practical Allocation Example

                

                  
Student References and Objects

                  
class Student {
    String name;
    int age;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int number = 10;

        Student s1 = new Student();
        s1.name = "Abhinav";
        s1.age = 21;

        Student s2 = new Student();
        s2.name = "Rahul";
        s2.age = 22;
    }
}

                

                

                  
main() stack framenumber = 10, s1, s2

                  ->
                  
Student Object 1Abhinav, 21

                    
                  
Student Object 2Rahul, 22

                

                
    
                  
  1. The JVM creates a stack frame for main().
    2. 
                  
  2. The local primitive number receives 10.
    3. 
                  
  3. Each new Student() creates a separate object and returns a reference.
    4. 
                  
  4. s1 and s2 refer to separate objects with separate field values.
    5. 
                  
  5. When main() returns, its stack frame is removed. Objects that are no longer reachable may later be reclaimed.
    6. 
                

                
String fields hold references to string objects; the simplified diagram does not show those additional objects.


                
5. Two References Pointing to One Object

                

                  
Reference Assignment

                  
class Student {
    String name;
}

Student s1 = new Student();
s1.name = "Abhinav";

Student s2 = s1; // Copies the reference, not the object
s2.name = "Rahul";

System.out.println(s1.name); // Rahul
System.out.println(s2.name); // Rahul

                

                
Output:

                
Rahul
Rahul

                

                  
s1Reference

                  ↘
                  
One Shared Student Objectname = "Rahul"

                  ↗
                  
s2Reference

                

                
Why? The statement Student s2 = s1; copies the reference, not the object. Both variables refer to the same Student object.


                
6. Null References

                
A reference variable can contain null, meaning that it does not currently refer to an object.

                
Student s = null;
System.out.println(s.name); // NullPointerException

                
The code compiles if Student declares name, but it throws a NullPointerException at runtime because no object is referenced.

                

                  
Null Check

                  
Student s = null;

if (s != null) {
    System.out.println(s.name);
} else {
    System.out.println("Student object does not exist.");
}

                

                
Output:

                
Student object does not exist.


                
7. Static Memory and Class Information

                

                  
Static and Instance Fields

                  
class Student {
    static String college = "AIMT";
    String name;
}

Student s1 = new Student();
Student s2 = new Student();
s1.name = "Abhinav";
s2.name = "Rahul";

System.out.println(Student.college);
System.out.println(s1.name);
System.out.println(s2.name);

                

                
Output:

                
AIMT
Abhinav
Rahul

                
    
                  
  • college is a static field shared by instances of Student.
    • 
                  
  • name is an instance field with a separate value for each object.
    • 
                  
  • Class metadata is managed in JVM runtime structures associated with the method area; HotSpot commonly uses Metaspace.
    • 
                  
  • A static reference field and the object it references are separate; the referenced object is typically allocated on the heap.
    • 
                


                
8. Garbage Collection

                
Garbage collection (GC) is the JVM's automatic process for reclaiming memory used by objects that are no longer reachable and therefore no longer needed by the application.

                

                  
Eligible for Garbage Collection

                  
class Student {
    String name;
}

Student s = new Student();
s.name = "Abhinav";

s = null; // The object may now be eligible for GC

                

                
    
                  
  • Setting a reference to null does not immediately destroy the object.
    • 
                  
  • The object becomes eligible only if no other reachable reference points to it.
    • 
                  
  • The JVM decides when collection occurs.
    • 
                  
  • System.gc() only requests garbage collection; it does not guarantee immediate collection.
    • 
                


                
9. Memory Errors in Java

                

                  
ErrorMeaningCommon Cause

                  
                    
StackOverflowErrorA thread's stack cannot grow further.Excessive or infinite recursion.

                    
OutOfMemoryErrorThe JVM cannot satisfy a memory allocation request.Excessive memory use or insufficient available memory.

                    
NullPointerExceptionCode uses a null reference where an object is required.Accessing a field or method through null.

                  
                

                

                  
StackOverflowError Example

                  
public class Main {
    static void display() {
        display();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        display();
    }
}

                

                
Because display() calls itself without a terminating condition, stack frames keep accumulating until the available stack capacity is exhausted.


                
10. Quick Revision

                
    
                  
  • Stack: Supports method calls and local execution data.
    • 
                  
  • Heap: Typically stores objects and arrays.
    • 
                  
  • Reference variable: Holds a reference to an object or null.
    • 
                  
  • Instance field: Stores object-specific state.
    • 
                  
  • Static field: Represents class-level state.
    • 
                  
  • Garbage collection: Reclaims memory from unreachable objects.
    • 
                  
  • StackOverflowError: Commonly associated with excessive recursion.
    • 
                  
  • OutOfMemoryError: Occurs when the JVM cannot satisfy a memory allocation request.
    •

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming & Paradigms
                  
Procedural Programming in Java: Architecture, Characteristics & OOP Comparison

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Procedural Programming

                

                  Procedural Programming is a programming paradigm in which a program is organized into a sequence of instructions and procedures (functions or methods) that perform specific tasks.
                

                

                  In this approach, a large problem is divided into smaller, manageable procedures. Each procedure performs a particular operation, and the program executes those procedures in sequence or according to control logic to produce the desired result.
                

                

                  Procedural programming primarily focuses on functions, step-by-step instructions, and the flow of control.
                

                

                  Examples of procedural programming languages include C, Pascal, and BASIC. Java supports procedural-style programming through static methods and sequential instructions, although Java itself is fundamentally class-based.
                


                
2. Basic Structure of Procedural Programming

                
A procedural program generally follows a structured execution pipeline:

                

                  
Start

                  →
                  
Input DataAccept values

                  →
                  
Process DataCalculations & checks

                  →
                  
Call ProceduresExecute methods

                  →
                  
Display OutputShow result

                  →
                  
End

                

                
This is a simplified flow. Actual programs utilize loops, conditional branches, and repeated method invocations.


                
3. Example of Procedural Programming in Java

                
Suppose we want to calculate the sum of two numbers using a procedural method design:

                

                  
Main.java

                  
public class Main {

    static int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int num1 = 10;
        int num2 = 20;

        int result = add(num1, num2);

        System.out.println("Sum = " + result);
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Sum = 30


                
Code Explanation

                
    
                  
  1. public class Main defines a class container because all Java code must reside inside a class structure.
    2. 
                  
  2. add(int a, int b) defines a static procedure/method that performs addition.
    3. 
                  
  3. main() serves as the application's starting execution point.
    4. 
                  
  4. Variables num1 and num2 store input data in the stack frame.
    5. 
                  
  5. add(num1, num2) invokes the procedure with the two arguments.
    6. 
                  
  6. return a + b returns the calculated integer value back to the caller.
    7. 
                  
  7. System.out.println() displays the final computed result.
    8. 
                

                
Important: This example demonstrates a procedural programming style inside Java. It does not mean Java is a purely procedural language.


                
4. Main Characteristics of Procedural Programming

                

                  
#CharacteristicDescription

                  
                    
1Step-by-step executionInstructions are executed in a sequential, top-to-bottom order unless control-flow statements alter execution.

                    
2Functions or proceduresComplex problems are decomposed into smaller sub-tasks implemented as reusable functions or methods.

                    
3Code reusabilityA procedure can be invoked multiple times across the program without rewriting identical logic.

                    
4Control structuresEmploys sequence, selection (if, switch), and iteration (for, while) to direct program flow.

                    
5Separation of data & operationsProcedures operate on data passed through parameters or accessed via shared variables rather than encapsulating state.

                  
                


                
5. Example: A Procedural Program Using Multiple Methods

                
A procedural program calculating the area and perimeter of a rectangle through modular procedures:

                

                  
RectangleCalculator.java

                  
public class RectangleCalculator {

    static int calculateArea(int length, int width) {
        return length * width;
    }

    static int calculatePerimeter(int length, int width) {
        return 2 * (length + width);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int length = 10;
        int width = 5;

        int area = calculateArea(length, width);
        int perimeter = calculatePerimeter(length, width);

        System.out.println("Area = " + area);
        System.out.println("Perimeter = " + perimeter);
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Area = 50
Perimeter = 30


                
Here, the overarching task is cleanly modularized into specialized methods:

                
    
                  
  • calculateArea() calculates the rectangle's area.
    • 
                  
  • calculatePerimeter() calculates the perimeter.
    • 
                  
  • main() coordinates data initialization and execution order.
    • 
                

                
This separation makes the codebase significantly easier to read, test, and maintain.


                
6. Advantages of Procedural Programming

                
    
                  
  • Easy to understand: Programs follow a straightforward, linear sequence of instructions.
    • 
                  
  • Simple for small problems: Ideal for mathematical calculations, utility scripts, and straightforward workflows.
    • 
                  
  • Code reuse: Methods can be called repeatedly without duplicating logic.
    • 
                  
  • Easy debugging: Errors can be quickly isolated to a specific method.
    • 
                  
  • Structured development: Large problems are systematically broken down into bite-sized procedures.
    • 
                  
  • Low conceptual overhead: Simpler learning curve compared to complex object-oriented class hierarchies for small programs.
    • 
                


                
7. Disadvantages of Procedural Programming

                
    
                  
  • Difficult to maintain in large programs: As the codebase expands, managing hundreds of interacting procedures becomes complex.
    • 
                  
  • Limited data protection: Shared or global state can be inadvertently altered by any procedure.
    • 
                  
  • Cascading modifications: Changing a data structure often forces alterations across multiple dependent procedures.
    • 
                  
  • Less natural real-world modeling: Real-world entities inherently combine data with behavior, which procedural models decouple.
    • 
                  
  • Shared-state risks: Uncontrolled mutations to shared variables make tracking bugs difficult.
    • 
                

                
These are common trade-offs rather than absolute limitations. Disciplined procedural design can still produce robust software.


                
8. Procedural Programming vs Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

                

                  
BasisProcedural ProgrammingObject-Oriented Programming (OOP)

                  
                    
Main focusProcedures and functionsObjects and classes

                    
Program organizationFunctions or proceduresClasses and their objects

                    
Data and methodsOften organized separatelyBundled together through encapsulation

                    
ApproachEmphasizes step-by-step operationsModels entities with state and behavior

                    
ReusabilityFunction reuseMethods, composition, inheritance, and interfaces

                    
Data protectionDepends on language features and manual designSupports encapsulation and access control modifiers

                    
Common examplesC, Pascal, BASICJava, C++, C#, Python

                  
                

                
Interview Point: Procedural programming emphasizes what operations the program performs and in what order. OOP emphasizes organizing state and behavior into objects.


                
9. Procedural Programming in Java: Important Notes

                
Java is an object-oriented language, but you can write methods that adhere strictly to procedural principles:

                

                  
Calculator.java

                  
public class Calculator {

    static int square(int number) {
        return number * number;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(square(5));
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
25


                
Key JVM and Java architectural realities:

                
    
                  
  • Class enclosing requirement: Every method declaration must reside within a class, record, enum, or interface.
    • 
                  
  • Static methods: static methods can be invoked directly on the class without instantiating an object (e.g., Math.max(a, b)).
    • 
                  
  • No free-standing global functions: Java does not permit top-level global functions outside of a class like C does.
    • 
                  
  • Hybrid paradigm: Real-world Java applications frequently combine procedural helper utilities (like Collections.sort()) with rich OOP domain models.
    • 
                


                
10. Interview Questions

                
    
                  
  1. What is procedural programming?
    A programming paradigm that organizes a program around procedures or functions that execute a sequence of operations.
    2. 
                  
  2. Give examples of procedural programming languages.
    C, Pascal, and BASIC are classic procedural languages.
    3. 
                  
  3. Is Java a procedural programming language?
    Java is primarily a class-based object-oriented language, but it fully supports procedural-style programming through static methods and control-flow statements.
    4. 
                  
  4. What is the main difference between procedural programming and OOP?
    Procedural programming focuses on procedures, functions, and sequential operations, whereas OOP models software as objects combining state (fields) and behavior (methods).
    5. 
                  
  5. What are the main advantages of procedural programming?
    Simplicity, clear execution flow, easy debugging for small programs, and low conceptual overhead.
    6. 
                  
  6. What is a procedure in Java?
    In Java, a procedure is implemented as a method. A void method performs an operation without returning a value:
                    
    
                      
    static void greet() {
    System.out.println("Hello Java");
}
    
                    
    
                  
    7. 
                

              

            



            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming & Core Pillars
                  
Encapsulation in Java: Data Hiding, Getters/Setters & Domain Validation

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Encapsulation

                

                  Encapsulation is one of the four foundational pillars of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), alongside Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction.
                

                

                  Encapsulation is the process of bundling data (variables) and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class), while strictly controlling external access to internal state.
                

                
In Java, encapsulation is standardly implemented by:

                
    
                  
  1. Declaring instance variables with the private access modifier.
    2. 
                  
  2. Providing public accessor (getter) and mutator (setter) methods when appropriate.
    3. 
                  
  3. Validating business constraints and boundary conditions before allowing updates.
    4. 
                

                
In Simple Words: Encapsulation shields an object's internal representation from arbitrary, uncontrolled external tampering.


                
Real-Life Analogy: The ATM Machine

                

                  Consider an Automated Teller Machine (ATM). You cannot directly reach into the bank's internal vaults or modify the centralized ledger numbers directly. Instead, you interact through a strictly controlled interface (screen buttons, card slot, PIN authentication). The ATM validates your PIN, verifies account balance, and dispenses cash through controlled methods.
                

                

                  Similarly in Java, an object safeguards its raw fields as private and exposes only approved, validated operations via public methods.
                


                
2. Why Do We Need Encapsulation?

                
Suppose we create a Student class with raw public fields:

                

                  
StudentWithoutEncapsulation.java

                  
class Student {
    public int age;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();

        s.age = -10; // Corrupted state!

        System.out.println(s.age);
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
-10


                

                  The code compiles and runs, but a negative age is biologically impossible and corrupts application integrity. 
                  The root defect is that the field can be modified directly without business logic validation.
                

                
The Architectural Fix: Mark variables private and route state changes through validating methods.


                
3. How to Achieve Encapsulation in Java

                
Let's construct a properly encapsulated Student class featuring defensive validation:

                

                  
EncapsulatedStudent.java

                  
class Student {

    private String name;
    private int age;

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        if (age > 0 && age <= 120) {
            this.age = age;
        } else {
            System.out.println("Invalid age!");
        }
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student s = new Student();

        s.setName("Rahul");
        s.setAge(20);

        System.out.println(s.getName());
        System.out.println(s.getAge());

        s.setAge(-10); // Rejected by defensive validation
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Rahul
20
Invalid age!


                
Step-by-Step Architectural Mechanics

                
    
                  
  • private String name; and private int age; forbid direct member access from external classes. Direct calls like s.age = -10; trigger compilation errors.
    • 
                  
  • setName(String name) provides a controlled pathway to update the student's name.
    • 
                  
  • getName() returns the stored name value.
    • 
                  
  • setAge(int age) enforces boundary constraints (age > 0 && age <= 120) before applying the mutation.
    • 
                  
  • getAge() provides safe read-only access to the field.
    • 
                  
  • this.age = age; uses the this reference to distinguish the instance field from the incoming method parameter.
    • 
                


                
4. Understanding private, public, and the this Keyword

                
A. The private Access Modifier

                
Restricts member visibility strictly to the declaring top-level class. External classes cannot read or write to private members directly:

                

                  
PrivateAccess.java

                  
class Account {
    private double balance;
}

// Inside Main class:
Account a = new Account();
// a.balance = 5000; // COMPILATION ERROR: balance has private access in Account

                


                
B. The public Access Modifier

                
Allows unrestricted access from any package and class where the enclosing type is accessible:

                

                  
PublicAccess.java

                  
public double getBalance() {
    return balance;
}

                


                
C. The this Keyword

                
this is an explicit reference to the current object instance. It resolves shadowing when parameter names mirror field names:

                

                  
ThisKeyword.java

                  
public void setAge(int age) {
    this.age = age; // 'this.age' = instance field; 'age' = method parameter
}

                

                
Without this, writing age = age; assigns the parameter to itself, leaving the instance field uninitialized!


                
5. Getters and Setters

                
Getters and setters are conventional accessor/mutator methods used to read and manipulate private state:

                

                  
Method TypePurposeConvention Example

                  
                    
Getter (Accessor)Returns field value without exposing the raw storagepublic int getAge() { return age; }

                    
Setter (Mutator)Updates field value with validation guardrailspublic void setAge(int age) { ... }

                  
                

                

                  
Standard Getter/Setter Syntax

                  
class Example {
    private int value;

    public int getValue() {
        return value;
    }

    public void setValue(int value) {
        this.value = value;
    }
}

                

                
Architectural Best Practice: Encapsulation does not mean mindlessly generating getters and setters for every private field! Only expose methods that make logical sense for your domain model. For instance, a bank account should expose deposit() and withdraw() methods rather than a raw setBalance() setter that allows arbitrary overwrite.


                
6. Real-World Domain Example: Bank Account

                
A resilient banking class that enforces deposit thresholds and overdraft protection:

                

                  
BankAccount.java

                  
class BankAccount {

    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        if (initialBalance >= 0) {
            balance = initialBalance;
        }
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0) {
            balance += amount;
            System.out.println("Deposit successful.");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Invalid deposit amount.");
        }
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            System.out.println("Invalid withdrawal amount.");
        } else if (amount > balance) {
            System.out.println("Insufficient balance.");
        } else {
            balance -= amount;
            System.out.println("Withdrawal successful.");
        }
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        BankAccount account = new BankAccount(5000);

        account.deposit(2000);
        account.withdraw(1000);
        account.withdraw(10000);

        System.out.println("Balance: " + account.getBalance());
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Deposit successful.
Withdrawal successful.
Insufficient balance.
Balance: 6000.0


                
How Encapsulation Operates in this System

                

                  
Main / CallerRequests operation

                  →
                  
Public Methodsdeposit() • withdraw()

                  →
                  
Validation BarrierEnforce business rules

                  →
                  
Private balanceControlled safe update

                

                

                  The caller cannot directly execute account.balance = -5000;. Instead, every operation must pass through domain validation logic.
                


                
7. Encapsulation vs Data Hiding

                
While frequently used interchangeably, they represent two distinct architectural aspects:

                

                  
BasisEncapsulationData Hiding

                  
                    
DefinitionBundles data (state) and related methods (behavior) in a cohesive class unitShields internal implementation details and raw state from direct external access

                    
How AchievedThrough class declaration, modular methods, and member packagingPrimarily via access modifiers (private, protected)

                    
Primary FocusStructural organization and controlled public interactionRestricting visibility and preventing unauthorized mutation

                  
                

                
Interview Anchor: Encapsulation is the packaging of data and behavior together with controlled access. Data hiding is the security mechanism (using private) used to achieve that control.


                
8. Key Advantages of Encapsulation

                
    
                  
  • Data Protection: Eliminates rogue direct modifications to sensitive state variables.
    • 
                  
  • Active Validation: Intercepts invalid input values before state corruption occurs.
    • 
                  
  • High Maintainability: You can refactor private internal representations without breaking consumer code that relies on the public API.
    • 
                  
  • Granular Access Control: Easily design write-only, read-only, or strictly authorized fields.
    • 
                  
  • Loose Coupling: External classes interact strictly through stable method contracts rather than fragile internal field names.
    • 
                  
  • Invariable Object Integrity: Ensures an object is never left in an inconsistent runtime state.
    • 
                


                
9. Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

                

                  
Anti-PatternWhy It Breaks EncapsulationCorrect Approach

                  
                    
Public FieldsExposes fields directly without validation guardrails.Declare fields private; provide controlled methods.

                    
Blind SettersProviding a setter that accepts any argument without sanity checks.Add validation guards (e.g. if (age > 0)) inside mutators.

                    
Leaking Mutable ReferencesReturning a direct reference to a mutable object (like Date or List).Return a defensive copy (e.g., Collections.unmodifiableList()).

                    
Over-AccessorizingAuto-generating getters and setters for internal flags that shouldn't be exposed.Only expose methods that represent genuine domain actions.

                  
                


                
10. Encapsulation in Enterprise & Spring Boot Architecture

                
In modern Spring Boot and microservice architectures, encapsulation is used everywhere in DTOs, entities, and service boundaries:

                

                  
ProductDTO.java

                  
public class Product {

    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private double price;

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public double getPrice() {
        return price;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        if (name != null && !name.isBlank()) {
            this.name = name;
        }
    }

    public void setPrice(double price) {
        if (price >= 0) {
            this.price = price;
        }
    }
}

                

                

                  In production Spring Boot applications, this encapsulated logic works alongside Bean Validation annotations (such as @NotBlank, @PositiveOrZero) and transactional service layers.
                


                
11. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is encapsulation in Java?
    Encapsulation is the OOP pillar of bundling data fields and behavioral methods into a single class unit while controlling external access to internal state.
    2. 
                  
  2. How do you achieve encapsulation in Java?
    By declaring instance variables as private and providing suitable public getter and setter methods with validation checks.
    3. 
                  
  3. Why are variables declared private?
    To prevent direct, uncontrolled access from external classes and guarantee that mutations adhere to business rules.
    4. 
                  
  4. What is the difference between a getter and a setter?
    A getter (accessor) safely returns a field's value without exposing the raw variable. A setter (mutator) updates the field's value after verifying input validity.
    5. 
                  
  5. Is encapsulation possible without setters?
    Yes! A class can be made read-only (immutable) with only getters, or expose domain-specific methods (like deposit()) without generic setters.
    6. 
                  
  6. What is the relationship between encapsulation and data hiding?
    Encapsulation is the broader organizational concept of binding state and behavior; data hiding is the specific security tactic of restricting visibility via access modifiers like private.
    7. 
                  
  7. Can we achieve encapsulation using only public variables?
    No. While public variables bundle data within a class, they fail to provide data hiding or access control, leaving the state vulnerable to arbitrary corruption.
    8. 
                

              

            



            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming & Core Pillars
                  
Getters and Setters in Java: Accessor/Mutator Patterns, Validation & Best Practices

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Getters and Setters

                

                  Getters and setters (also known as accessors and mutators) are public methods used to read and modify the private fields of a class safely.
                

                
    
                  
  • Getter (Accessor): Retrieves the current value of a private field without exposing the field itself.
    • 
                  
  • Setter (Mutator): Updates the value of a private field, optionally after enforcing validation rules.
    • 
                

                

                  They represent the standard programming idiom for implementing encapsulation in Java, decoupling how data is stored internally from how it is accessed externally.
                

                

                  
Method TypeRoleReturn TypeParametersJava Naming Convention

                  
                    
GetterReads dataMatches field typeNonegetField() or isFlag()

                    
SetterModifies datavoidNew valuesetField(DataType value)

                  
                


                
2. Basic Implementation Example

                
Consider a Student class where name and age are private, and setAge() protects against negative numbers:

                

                  
Student.java

                  
class Student {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    // Setter for name
    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    // Getter for name
    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    // Setter with defensive validation
    public void setAge(int age) {
        if (age > 0) {
            this.age = age;
        }
    }

    // Getter for age
    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student student = new Student();

        student.setName("Rahul");
        student.setAge(20);

        System.out.println(student.getName());
        System.out.println(student.getAge());
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Rahul
20


                
Execution Flow

                

                  
Callerstudent.setAge(20)

                  →
                  
Setter MethodReceives age = 20

                  →
                  
Validation Guardif (age > 0)

                  →
                  
Internal Statethis.age = 20

                


                
3. Standard Naming Conventions & Syntax

                
Java follows standard JavaBeans naming conventions for accessor and mutator methods:

                

                  
Standard Getter/Setter Template

                  
// Standard Getter Syntax
public DataType getFieldName() {
    return fieldName;
}

// Standard Setter Syntax
public void setFieldName(DataType fieldName) {
    this.fieldName = fieldName;
}

// Boolean Getter Syntax (Special convention: uses 'is' instead of 'get')
public boolean isActive() {
    return active;
}

                

                
Memory Anchor: Getters read data; setters change data.


                
4. Key Architectural Takeaways

                
    
                  
  • Declare fields as private: Always restrict raw field access to prevent uncontrolled direct mutations from outside the class.
    • 
                  
  • Use getters to retrieve field values: Provides a controlled, read-only window into the object's current state.
    • 
                  
  • Use setters to update field values: Routes all mutations through a single method where business logic can intercept errors.
    • 
                  
  • Use the this keyword: Disambiguates instance fields from incoming parameters when they share the exact same identifier (e.g., this.name = name;).
    • 
                  
  • Defensive validation in setters: Check boundary conditions, nullity, or range limits before committing changes to internal state.
    • 
                  
  • Avoid over-accessorizing: Not every private field requires both a getter and a setter. If a field should never change after construction, provide only a getter (immutable read-only property). If an operation is a complex business workflow (like paying a bill), prefer domain methods like payBill() over generic setters.
    • 
                

              

            



            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming & Core Pillars
                  
Abstraction in Java: Abstract Classes, Interfaces & Polymorphic Contracts

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Abstraction

                

                  Abstraction is one of the four foundational pillars of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP).
                

                

                  Abstraction is the architectural process of hiding internal implementation details and exposing only the essential features and operations of an object to the outside world.
                

                
In Simple Words: Abstraction focuses on what an object does rather than how it accomplishes it.


                
Real-Life Analogies

                
    
                  
  • The ATM Machine: You insert a debit card, enter your PIN, and withdraw cash. You interact solely with a clean user interface without needing to understand the underlying database queries, RPC network sockets, encryption engines, or hardware actuators.
    • 
                  
  • Driving an Automobile: A driver accelerates using the pedal and navigates with the steering wheel without having to calculate fuel injection ratios, combustion valve timings, or torque distribution curves.
    • 
                


                
2. Why Do We Need Abstraction?

                
Without abstraction, client code would have to be tightly coupled to low-level implementation details, leading to fragile, unmaintainable architectures. Abstraction provides:

                
    
                  
  • Complexity Reduction: Hides intricate internal mechanics so developers consume clean, high-level APIs.
    • 
                  
  • Separation of Concerns: Decouples the operation contract from the underlying execution algorithms.
    • 
                  
  • Architectural Flexibility: Multiple distinct classes can fulfill the same contract in completely different ways without breaking caller code.
    • 
                  
  • Enhanced Maintainability: Internal implementation code can be completely rewritten or optimized without affecting consuming systems.
    • 
                


                
3. How to Achieve Abstraction in Java

                
Java delivers abstraction primarily through two fundamental language mechanisms:

                

                  
Abstraction in Java

                  →
                  
Abstract Classes0% to 100% Abstraction (Partial)

                  +
                  
Interfaces100% Contractual Abstraction

                


                
4. Abstract Classes

                

                  An abstract class is declared using the abstract modifier. It serves as an incomplete blueprint that cannot be directly instantiated and can contain both abstract methods (without bodies) and concrete methods (with full implementations).
                

                

                  
Abstract Class Syntax

                  
abstract class ClassName {
    // Abstract method: specifies WHAT to do
    abstract void methodName();

    // Concrete method: specifies HOW to do
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Concrete method implementation");
    }
}

                

                
Key Rules for Abstract Classes

                
    
                  
  • No Direct Instantiation: You cannot execute new ClassName() on an abstract class.
    • 
                  
  • Constructors Allowed: An abstract class can define constructors, which are called via super() during concrete subclass construction.
    • 
                  
  • Instance State: Can hold instance fields, static variables, and constants.
    • 
                  
  • Subclass Obligation: Any non-abstract subclass extending an abstract class must provide concrete implementations for all inherited abstract methods.
    • 
                


                
Practical Implementation: The Shape Hierarchy

                

                  
ShapeHierarchy.java

                  
abstract class Shape {

    abstract double calculateArea();

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Calculating area...");
    }
}

class Circle extends Shape {

    private double radius;

    Circle(double radius) {
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    @Override
    double calculateArea() {
        return Math.PI * radius * radius;
    }
}

class Rectangle extends Shape {

    private double length;
    private double width;

    Rectangle(double length, double width) {
        this.length = length;
        this.width = width;
    }

    @Override
    double calculateArea() {
        return length * width;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Shape circle = new Circle(5);
        Shape rectangle = new Rectangle(10, 4);

        circle.display();
        System.out.println("Circle Area: " + circle.calculateArea());

        rectangle.display();
        System.out.println("Rectangle Area: " + rectangle.calculateArea());
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Calculating area...
Circle Area: 78.53981633974483
Calculating area...
Rectangle Area: 40.0


                
Code Explanation

                
    
                  
  • Shape defines the common contract (calculateArea()) without prescribing formula specifics.
    • 
                  
  • Circle and Rectangle provide their own mathematical implementations.
    • 
                  
  • The caller executes calculations via polymorphic Shape reference variables without needing to know internal shape geometry details.
    • 
                


                
5. Interfaces

                

                  An interface is an absolute contract specification. A class agrees to implement the interface using the implements keyword, promising to fulfill all declared methods.
                

                

                  
Interface Syntax

                  
interface InterfaceName {
    void methodName(); // public abstract by default
}

                


                
Practical Implementation: Payment Processing System

                

                  
PaymentSystem.java

                  
interface Payment {
    void pay(double amount);
}

class UpiPayment implements Payment {

    @Override
    public void pay(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Paid ₹" + amount + " using UPI");
    }
}

class CardPayment implements Payment {

    @Override
    public void pay(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Paid ₹" + amount + " using Card");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Payment payment = new UpiPayment();
        payment.pay(500);

        payment = new CardPayment();
        payment.pay(1000);
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Paid ₹500.0 using UPI
Paid ₹1000.0 using Card


                

                  The caller interacts strictly with the Payment interface. Whether an order is settled via UPI or Card, the caller simply invokes pay(), leaving payment gateway mechanics completely abstracted.
                

                
Modern Java Note: Since Java 8 and 9, interfaces can also declare default, static, and private helper methods with concrete implementations!


                
6. Abstract Class vs Interface

                

                  
FeatureAbstract ClassInterface

                  
                    
Declaration Keywordabstract classinterface

                    
Inheritance Keywordextendsimplements

                    
ConstructorsAllowed (invoked by subclass)Not allowed

                    
Instance FieldsAllowed (can store object state)Not allowed (fields are public static final)

                    
Abstract MethodsAllowedAllowed

                    
Concrete MethodsAllowed (regular methods)Allowed (default, static, private)

                    
Multiple InheritanceSingle inheritance only (extends OneClass)Multiple inheritance supported (implements A, B, C)

                    
Primary Architectural PurposeShare common state and partial implementation among closely related classesDefine a public contract or functional capability across disparate classes

                  
                

                
Interview Tip: Choose an abstract class when closely related classes share state, constructors, and code. Choose an interface when establishing a capability or contract that completely unrelated classes can adopt.


                
7. Abstraction vs Encapsulation

                

                  
BasisAbstractionEncapsulation

                  
                    
Primary ObjectiveHides implementation complexityRestricts direct access to internal state

                    
Core FocusFocuses on what an object doesFocuses on how state is protected and controlled

                    
Implementation VehicleAbstract classes and interfacesPrivate access modifiers, getters, and mutators

                    
Real-World ExamplePayment.pay() hides gateway routing protocolsBankAccount.balance cannot be directly altered without validation

                  
                

                
Synergy: Abstraction and Encapsulation work hand-in-hand! A well-designed Java class exposes clean abstract operations while encapsulating internal state defensively.


                
8. Key Advantages of Abstraction

                
    
                  
  • Reduced Cognitive Load: Clients only navigate the operations they need to interact with.
    • 
                  
  • Long-Term Maintainability: Refactoring internal algorithms never disrupts downstream consumers adhering to the abstraction.
    • 
                  
  • Polymorphic Flexibility: Enables interchangeable strategies and plug-and-play components (e.g. swapping payment providers).
    • 
                  
  • Code Reusability: Common foundational logic lives in shared abstract classes, minimizing duplicate code.
    • 
                  
  • Loose Coupling: High-level application modules depend on abstractions rather than brittle concrete classes (Dependency Inversion Principle).
    • 
                


                
9. Common Mistakes & Misconceptions

                
    
                  
  • Attempting to directly instantiate an abstract class with new Shape().
    • 
                  
  • Writing class Dog extends AnimalInterface instead of using the implements keyword.
    • 
                  
  • Assuming an abstract class is invalid if it does not contain any abstract methods.
    • 
                  
  • Believing interfaces can never contain executable code (forgetting default and static methods in Java 8+).
    • 
                  
  • Confusing abstraction (contract/complexity hiding) with encapsulation (state validation/data hiding).
    • 
                


                
10. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is abstraction in Java?
    Abstraction is the OOP pillar of hiding implementation complexity and exposing only the essential operational contract to the user.
    2. 
                  
  2. How can abstraction be achieved in Java?
    Primarily through abstract classes (0–100% abstraction) and interfaces (100% contractual specification).
    3. 
                  
  3. Can we instantiate an abstract class?
    No, direct instantiation via new is forbidden by the compiler. However, you can declare reference variables of the abstract type pointing to concrete subclass instances.
    4. 
                  
  4. Can an abstract class have a constructor?
    Yes. An abstract class constructor is executed as part of the subclass instantiation chain via super().
    5. 
                  
  5. What is the primary difference between an abstract class and an interface?
    An abstract class supports instance variables, constructors, and single inheritance; an interface supports multiple implementation contracts without instance state.
    6. 
                  
  6. Give a real-world software example of abstraction.
    Java's java.sql.Connection is an interface. Developers write generic SQL queries against it without knowing whether the underlying driver connects to PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Oracle.
    7. 
                  
  7. Is abstraction possible without abstract classes?
    Yes! Pure interfaces, method signatures, and clean API boundaries deliver abstraction without requiring abstract classes.
    8. 
                


                
11. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Abstraction: Core OOP pillar focusing on what an object does rather than how.
    • 
                  
  • Abstract Class: Class with abstract keyword; cannot be instantiated directly; holds constructors and fields.
    • 
                  
  • Interface: Contractual specification implemented using implements; supports multiple inheritance.
    • 
                  
  • Abstraction vs Encapsulation: Abstraction hides complexity; encapsulation protects internal state.
    • 
                

              

            



            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Design & Architecture
                  
Coupling in Java: Tight vs. Loose Coupling, Dependency Injection & Spring Boot Architecture

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Coupling

                

                  Coupling is the degree of direct interdependence and knowledge between two classes, packages, or software subsystems.
                

                

                  In Java software engineering, coupling measures how strongly one class relies on another class's concrete implementation to accomplish its tasks:
                

                
    
                  
  • Low (Loose) Coupling: Classes interact through minimal, stable abstractions and contracts without depending on internal implementation details.
    • 
                  
  • High (Tight) Coupling: Classes depend intimately on the concrete classes and specific implementation nuances of other classes.
    • 
                

                
Architectural Gold Standard: In production enterprise development, loose coupling is always preferred because it dramatically improves testability, maintainability, agility, and modular scalability.


                
Real-Life Analogy: The Automobile Driver

                

                  Imagine a driver operating a car. The driver controls speed via the accelerator pedal and steers via the steering wheel. The driver does not depend on whether the car has a 4-cylinder petrol engine, a turbo diesel, or an electric battery motor. If the mechanics replace a combustion engine with an electric motor, the driver's interface (pedal and wheel) remains identical!
                

                

                  In Java, we achieve this exact decoupling by programming to interfaces rather than depending directly on concrete classes.
                


                
2. Types of Coupling

                

                  
Tight (High) CouplingDirect concrete new dependencies • Avoid!

                  ↔
                  
Loose (Low) CouplingInterface contracts & Dependency Injection • Preferred!

                


                
3. Example of High (Tight) Coupling in Java

                
Consider an application notification pipeline where Notification directly instantiates EmailService:

                

                  
TightCouplingDemo.java

                  
class EmailService {

    public void sendEmail(String message) {
        System.out.println("Email sent: " + message);
    }
}

class Notification {

    // TIGHT COUPLING: Hard-coded concrete dependency!
    private EmailService emailService = new EmailService();

    public void notifyUser(String message) {
        emailService.sendEmail(message);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Notification notification = new Notification();
        notification.notifyUser("Your order has been shipped.");
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Email sent: Your order has been shipped.


                
Why Is This Code Anti-Pattern Tight Coupling?

                
    
                  
  • Hard-coded Instantiation: Notification directly invokes new EmailService(), cementing a rigid dependency.
    • 
                  
  • Rigid Extensibility: If business rules require sending an SMS or WhatsApp notification instead of an Email, the Notification class must be modified, violating the Open-Closed Principle (OCP).
    •
