            "Mortgage 1: " + calculator1.calculateMortgage()
        );

        System.out.println(
            "Mortgage 2: " + calculator2.calculateMortgage()
        );
    }
}

                


                
6. Before vs. After Refactoring Matrix

                

                  
Architectural DimensionBefore RefactoringAfter Refactoring

                  
                    
Formula PlacementDuplicated multiple times across code blocksCentralized in exactly one authoritative location

                    
Maintenance FootprintAltering math rules requires editing every copyModifications are isolated strictly to a single method

                    
Code Volume & ClutterRepetitive, bloated, high cognitive loadConcise, self-descriptive, highly expressive

                    
Behavioral ConsistencyHigh risk of subtle copy-paste discrepancies100% deterministic calculation parity guaranteed

                    
Automated TestingImpossible to test logic without running driverCan be unit-tested directly across edge cases

                  
                


                
7. When to Extract vs. When to Tolerate Similarity

                

                  Critical Architectural Nuance: Genuine Duplication vs. Accidental Duplication
                  
    
                    
  • Extract When: The repeated blocks represent the same business concept or domain rule. If the underlying business rule evolves, all usages should logically evolve together.
    • 
                    
  • Do NOT Over-Extract When: Two code blocks merely look similar by coincidence but represent fundamentally different business concepts. Forcing them into a single polymorphic Frankenstein method couples unrelated domains and creates fragile abstractions.
    • 
                  

                


                
8. Common Mistakes & Gotchas

                
    
                  
  • Copy-Paste Laziness: Copying code blocks across methods instead of taking 30 seconds to extract a reusable function.
    • 
                  
  • The Kitchen-Sink Method: Packing too many unrelated operations into the extracted method, violating the Single Responsibility Principle.
    • 
                  
  • Global Variable Reliance: Reading static or class-level variables inside the extracted method rather than passing clean, explicit method arguments.
    • 
                  
  • Neglecting Regression Tests: Extracting logic without validating that existing caller outputs and corner-case behaviors remain 100% identical.
    • 
                


                
9. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is the "Extracting Duplicate Logic" refactoring pattern?
    Moving repetitive code into a unified, reusable method or class to eliminate redundancy and adhere to the DRY principle.
    2. 
                  
  2. What is the DRY Principle and why does it matter?
    DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. It states that every piece of domain knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system.
    3. 
                  
  3. What are the primary architectural benefits of eliminating duplicate logic?
    Enhanced code readability, centralized maintenance, eliminated divergent bugs, and isolated unit testability.
    4. 
                  
  4. Should every repeated line of code be extracted immediately?
    No. Premature abstraction on accidental duplication can cause harmful coupling. Logic should be extracted when it shares a unified business responsibility.
    5. 
                  
  5. How does method extraction improve unit testing?
    Extracted methods can be tested independently with parameter matrices (e.g. zero values, negative numbers, maximum bounds) without executing entire application workflows.
    6. 
                


                
10. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Identify repeated code blocks across the system.
    • 
                  
  • Determine which parameters fluctuate and which formulas stay invariant.
    • 
                  
  • Extract the invariant calculation into a dedicated method with explicit parameters.
    • 
                  
  • Promote the method to a cohesive domain class (e.g. MortgageCalculator) when appropriate.
    • 
                  
  • Strictly verify that externally observable runtime behavior remains completely unchanged.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 4: Object-Oriented Programming & Class Architecture
                  
Refactoring: Extracting getRemainingBalances() & Loan Amortization Schedule Architecture

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Extracting getRemainingBalances()

                

                  Extracting getRemainingBalances() is an advanced refactoring technique in which the mathematical logic for computing ongoing loan balances across the entire life of a loan is encapsulated inside the domain calculator and exposed as a clean, queryable data structure.
                

                

                  In a real-world mortgage system, borrowers need to know their amortization schedule: exactly how much principal is still owed after payment month 1, month 2, ..., up to month 360.
                


                

                  The Architectural Objective: Decouple balance calculations from terminal rendering. Rather than iterating loops and calculating balances inside MortgageReport, MortgageCalculator exposes a pure method getRemainingBalances() returning an array of balances (double[]).
                


                
2. The Mathematical Loan Balance Formula

                

                  The remaining loan balance $B$ after making $p$ monthly payments on a principal loan $P$ with monthly interest rate $r$ over $n$ total payments is governed by:
                

                

                  B = P × [ (1 + r)n - (1 + r)p ] / [ (1 + r)n - 1 ]
                

                
    
                  
  • p = 0: Initial state before any payments; $B = P$ (full loan balance owed).
    • 
                  
  • p = n: Final payment month; $B = 0$ (loan completely paid off).
    • 
                


                
3. Encapsulating Balance Logic inside MortgageCalculator

                

                  We add two cohesive methods to MortgageCalculator: a helper calculateBalance() for a specific month, and getRemainingBalances() to return the complete lifetime schedule:
                


                

                  
MortgageCalculator.java

                  
public class MortgageCalculator {

    private final double principal;
    private final float annualInterestRate;
    private final int years;

    public MortgageCalculator(
        double principal,
        float annualInterestRate,
        int years
    ) {
        this.principal = principal;
        this.annualInterestRate = annualInterestRate;
        this.years = years;
    }

    public double calculateMortgage() {
        double monthlyRate = annualInterestRate / 100 / 12;
        int payments = years * 12;
        if (monthlyRate == 0) return principal / payments;
        double factor = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, payments);
        return principal * monthlyRate * factor / (factor - 1);
    }

    // Calculates remaining balance after p monthly payments
    public double calculateBalance(short numberOfPaymentsMade) {
        double monthlyRate = annualInterestRate / 100 / 12;
        int payments = years * 12;

        double totalPaymentsFactor = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, payments);
        double paidPaymentsFactor = Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, numberOfPaymentsMade);

        return principal * (totalPaymentsFactor - paidPaymentsFactor)
            / (totalPaymentsFactor - 1);
    }

    // Returns the complete amortization schedule as pure data
    public double[] getRemainingBalances() {
        int totalPayments = years * 12;
        double[] balances = new double[totalPayments];
        for (short month = 1; month <= totalPayments; month++) {
            balances[month - 1] = calculateBalance(month);
        }
        return balances;
    }
}

                


                
4. Integrating getRemainingBalances() into MortgageReport

                

                  Now, MortgageReport solely handles the formatting and terminal rendering of the schedule without knowing anything about exponentiation formulas:
                


                

                  
MortgageReport.java

                  
public class MortgageReport {

    private final MortgageCalculator calculator;

    public MortgageReport(MortgageCalculator calculator) {
        this.calculator = calculator;
    }

    public void printPaymentSchedule() {
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("PAYMENT SCHEDULE");
        System.out.println("----------------");

        double[] balances = calculator.getRemainingBalances();
        for (int month = 0; month < balances.length; month++) {
            System.out.printf("Month %d: $%.2f%n", (month + 1), balances[month]);
        }
    }
}

                


                
5. Architectural Benefits of This Extraction

                

                  
MortgageCalculatorComputes double[] balances array

                  → Pure Data →
                  
MortgageReportFormats CLI terminal output

                  +
                  
Future Web/JSON APICan serialize same double[] to JSON

                


                

                  Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) Realized: If you switch the application from a console program to a React web app or Android mobile app, MortgageCalculator requires zero changes. It returns raw numbers; the presentation layer decides how to render them.

Notice how clean it is now: it contains only a few lines to instantiate our classes and call report.printMortgage() and report.printPaymentSchedule(). All complexity is neatly encapsulated in dedicated classes!

                  Part 2: Inheritance
                  
98. Introduction to Inheritance

                

              

              

                

                  Inheritance is a core mechanism in Object-Oriented Programming that allows a new class (subclass) to inherit attributes and methods from an existing class (superclass). It promotes code reusability and forms the foundation for Polymorphism.
                

              

            


            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Inheritance in Java: Superclasses, Subclasses, Constructor Chaining & Runtime Polymorphism

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Inheritance

                

                  Inheritance is one of the four fundamental pillars of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java.
                

                

                  Inheritance allows a new class (the subclass or child class) to inherit the accessible fields and methods of an existing class (the superclass or parent class) using the extends keyword.
                

                

                  Inheritance models an is-a relationship. For example, a Car is a type of Vehicle. A car naturally inherits foundational vehicle capabilities (such as start() and stop()) while introducing specialized car features (such as drive() and openTrunk()).
                


                
2. Why Do We Need Inheritance?

                

                  Suppose we are building an automotive system managing Car and Bike entities. Both share attributes like brand and methods like start(). Without inheritance, identical fields and routines are duplicated across every vehicle class:
                


                

                  Core Engineering Benefits of Inheritance:
                  
    
                    
  • Code Reusability: Common properties and behaviors are defined once in a superclass and shared across all subclasses.
    • 
                    
  • Centralized Maintenance: Bug fixes or enhancements in the superclass automatically propagate across all child classes.
    • 
                    
  • Extensibility: New specialized subclasses can be introduced without modifying existing tested classes.
    • 
                    
  • Polymorphism: Code can operate uniformly on a general superclass reference while dynamically executing specialized subclass logic.
    • 
                  

                


                
3. Basic Terminology & Conceptual Model

                

                  
Superclass / Parent Class (Vehicle)brand, start(), stop()

                  ⇓ extends ⇓
                  
Subclass 1 (Car)drive(), openTrunk()

                  
Subclass 2 (Bike)ride(), kickStand()

                


                
    
                  
  • Parent Class (Superclass / Base Class): The class whose accessible members are inherited.
    • 
                  
  • Child Class (Subclass / Derived Class): The class that extends and inherits from the parent.
    • 
                  
  • extends: The dedicated Java keyword that establishes the inheritance relationship.
    • 
                


                
4. Java Syntax of Inheritance

                

                  
InheritanceSyntax.java

                  
// Superclass
class Parent {
    // Shared fields and methods
}

// Subclass inheriting from Parent
class Child extends Parent {
    // Child inherits all accessible members of Parent
    // and defines additional specialized members
}

                


                
5. Example 1: Basic Inheritance (Animal Hierarchy)

                

                  
BasicInheritanceDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Animal is eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Dog is barking");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Dog dog = new Dog();

        dog.eat();  // Inherited method from Animal!
        dog.bark(); // Specialized method defined in Dog
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal is eating
Dog is barking


                
Step-by-Step Execution Breakdown:

                
    
                  
  1. Animal defines the generic method eat().
    2. 
                  
  2. Dog extends Animal establishes the child-parent relationship.
    3. 
                  
  3. new Dog() allocates a Dog object in the JVM Heap.
    4. 
                  
  4. Because Dog inherits accessible members, it calls eat() directly without reimplementing it.
    5. 
                


                
6. Example 2: Inheritance with Fields and Methods

                

                  
EmployeeHierarchy.java

                  
class Employee {

    String name;
    double salary;

    void displayDetails() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Salary: " + salary);
    }
}

class Developer extends Employee {

    String programmingLanguage;

    void writeCode() {
        System.out.println(
            name + " is writing " + programmingLanguage + " code."
        );
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Developer developer = new Developer();

        // Accessing inherited fields from Employee:
        developer.name = "Abhinav";
        developer.salary = 50000;

        // Accessing specialized field from Developer:
        developer.programmingLanguage = "Java";

        // Invoking inherited and child methods:
        developer.displayDetails();
        developer.writeCode();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Name: Abhinav
Salary: 50000.0
Abhinav is writing Java code.


                

                  Production Note: In production enterprise code, fields are declared private to maintain encapsulation, with child classes accessing parent state via public/protected getters or constructor parameters.
                


                
7. Supported and Unsupported Types of Inheritance in Java

                

                  
Inheritance TypeStructureJava Class SupportExplanation & Workaround

                  
                    

                      1. Single Inheritance
                      A → B
                      Supported
                      A child class extends exactly one direct parent class.
                    

                    

                      2. Multilevel Inheritance
                      A → B → C
                      Supported
                      A child inherits from a class that itself extends another class.
                    

                    

                      3. Hierarchical Inheritance
                      A → B & A → C
                      Supported
                      Multiple subclasses independently extend a single shared superclass.
                    

                    

                      4. Multiple Inheritance
                      (A, B) → C
                      NOT Supported for Classes
                      Java bars class C extends A, B to prevent the Deadly Diamond Problem. Supported via Interfaces (implements A, B).
                    

                    

                      5. Hybrid Inheritance
                      Combination of above
                      Supported via Interfaces
                      Permitted in Java through a combination of class inheritance and interface implementations.
                    

                  
                


                
8. Inheritance with Constructors & Constructor Chaining

                

                  Critical Rule: Constructors are NOT inherited in Java! However, when an instance of a child class is created, the parent class constructor is automatically executed first before the child constructor executes.
                


                

                  
ConstructorChainingDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    Animal() {
        System.out.println("Animal constructor (Parent executed 1st)");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    Dog() {
        // Implicit super() invoked here by compiler
        System.out.println("Dog constructor (Child executed 2nd)");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal constructor (Parent executed 1st)
Dog constructor (Child executed 2nd)


                
Calling Parameterized Parent Constructors with super(...)

                

                  To invoke a specific parameterized parent constructor, use super(...) as the very first statement inside the child constructor:
                


                

                  
ExplicitSuperConstructor.java

                  
class Animal {

    String name;

    Animal(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    Dog(String name) {
        super(name); // Explicitly calls Animal(String name)
    }
}

                


                
9. Method Overriding & Runtime Polymorphism

                

                  Method Overriding occurs when a subclass provides its own specific implementation of an instance method already defined in its parent class, matching the exact name, parameter list, and compatible return type:
                


                

                  
MethodOverridingDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Upcasting: Animal reference pointing to Dog heap object
        Animal animal = new Dog();

        // Resolves to Dog.sound() at runtime!
        animal.sound();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Dog barks


                

                  Dynamic Method Dispatch (Runtime Polymorphism): Even though the reference variable animal is of type Animal, the JVM evaluates the actual underlying heap object (which is a Dog) at runtime and invokes Dog's overridden sound() method.
                


                
10. The super Keyword: 3 Primary Use Cases

                

                  
1. super(...)Invoke parent constructor

                  ↔
                  
2. super.method()Invoke overridden parent method

                  ↔
                  
3. super.fieldAccess shadowed parent field

                


                

                  
SuperMethodDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        super.sound(); // Invokes parent Animal.sound()
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
        dog.sound();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal sound
Dog barks


                
11. Master Rules Matrix of Java Inheritance

                

                  
Inheritance ElementRule & Compiler Enforcement

                  
                    
extendsThe mandatory keyword used to establish class-to-class inheritance.

                    
Private Membersprivate parent fields and methods are not directly accessible by subclasses.

                    
ConstructorsConstructors are never inherited; they participate via chaining.

                    
final classA class declared final cannot be extended by any subclass.

                    
final methodA method declared final cannot be overridden by subclasses.

                    
Static MethodsStatic methods are hidden, not overridden (they do not participate in dynamic dispatch).

                    
Single SuperclassJava classes can extend only one direct class (no multiple class inheritance).

                    
InterfacesA single Java class can implement unlimited interfaces simultaneously.

                  
                


                
12. Common Mistakes & Gotchas

                
    
                  
  • Assuming Private Members are Accessible: Thinking child classes can directly mutate private fields of the parent.
    • 
                  
  • Assuming Constructors are Inherited: Writing child code expecting parent constructor signatures without writing child constructors.
    • 
                  
  • Confusing Overloading with Overriding: Overriding requires exact matching parameter lists; overloading requires different parameter lists.
    • 
                  
  • Inheritance Without "Is-A" Reality: Subclassing purely to steal code (e.g., Stack extends ArrayList) rather than modeling genuine conceptual hierarchy. Favor composition over inheritance when "is-a" does not apply.
    • 
                  
  • Attempting Multiple Class Extension: Writing class Child extends Parent1, Parent2, which is an immediate syntax error in Java.
    • 
                  
  • Omitting @Override: Forgetting the @Override annotation prevents the compiler from alerting you if you accidentally mistype the parent method name.
    • 
                


                
13. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is inheritance in Java?
    An OOP mechanism where a subclass derives accessible fields and methods from a superclass using the extends keyword, establishing an "is-a" relationship.
    2. 
                  
  2. What are the core advantages of inheritance?
    Code reusability, reduced boilerplate, unified maintenance, and support for runtime polymorphism.
    3. 
                  
  3. Does Java support multiple inheritance?
    Not through classes (to prevent the Deadly Diamond Problem). It is fully supported through interfaces.
    4. 
                  
  4. Are constructors inherited in Java?
    No. Constructors are not inherited. A child constructor invokes a parent constructor via implicit or explicit super(...).
    5. 
                  
  5. What is the difference between this and super?
    this refers to the current object instance; super refers to the superclass portion of the current object.
    6. 
                  
  6. What is method overriding?
    When a subclass provides a tailored implementation of an instance method already declared in its superclass, using the identical signature.
    7. 
                  
  7. Can a final class be inherited?
    No. A final class (e.g. java.lang.String) cannot be extended.
    8. 
                  
  8. What is the difference between inheritance and encapsulation?
    Inheritance enables specialization and code reuse between hierarchical types; encapsulation bundles state with behavior and protects data behind access controls.
    9. 
                


                
14. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Inheritance represents an authentic is-a relationship.
    • 
                  
  • Java uses the extends keyword for class inheritance.
    • 
                  
  • Subclasses inherit accessible members and can introduce specialized fields and methods.
    • 
                  
  • Parent constructors always execute prior to child constructors.
    • 
                  
  • Method overriding enables dynamic method dispatch (Runtime Polymorphism).
    • 
                  
  • Java enforces single class inheritance but permits multiple interface implementation.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
The Object Class in Java: Root Hierarchy, Core Methods & Equality Contracts

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to the Object Class

                

                  In the Java programming language, java.lang.Object sits at the apex of the class hierarchy as the cosmic root superclass. The package java.lang is imported automatically by the Java compiler into every single .java compilation unit.
                

                

                  Every class in Java—whether a built-in standard library class like String, Scanner, or custom user-defined classes—directly or indirectly extends Object.
                


                

                  The Foundational Guarantee: Because every class derives from Object, every object in the JVM inherits an essential baseline of universal methods, notably toString(), equals(), hashCode(), and getClass().
                


                
2. Why Do We Need the Object Class?

                

                  The Object class establishes a unified contract of common behaviors that all reference types can utilize or customize.
                

                

                  For example, if we declare an Employee class without writing any custom methods, it immediately inherits the default toString() implementation:
                


                

                  
DefaultObjectMethods.java

                  
class Employee {
    String name = "Abhinav";
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee employee = new Employee();

        // Calling inherited toString() from java.lang.Object:
        System.out.println(employee.toString());
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Employee@5acf9800


                

                  Deconstructing the Default Output: The default implementation returns getClass().getName() + '@' + Integer.toHexString(hashCode()). While informative for debugging heap memory identity, it is not human-readable without being overridden.
                


                
3. How Inheritance from Object Works in the JVM

                
When you declare an ordinary class without specifying an extends clause:

                
class Animal { }

                
The Java compiler implicitly transforms it at bytecode level into:

                
class Animal extends Object { }


                
Multilevel Inheritance Chain to Root

                

                  
Objectjava.lang.Object (Root Superclass)

                  ⇓ Implicit extends ⇓
                  
AnimalIntermediate parent class

                  ⇓ Explicit extends ⇓
                  
DogLeaf child class (inherits from Animal & Object)

                


                
4. Master Catalog of java.lang.Object Methods

                

                  
Method SignaturePrimary Purpose & ContractOverride Frequency

                  
                    
public String toString()Returns a textual representation of the object.Very High (recommended for all domain entities)

                    
public boolean equals(Object obj)Evaluates logical equivalence based on internal state.High (required for identity & collections)

                    
public int hashCode()Generates an integer hash code for hash buckets (e.g. HashMap).High (mandatory when overriding equals)

                    
public final Class<?> getClass()Returns the runtime Class object reflecting runtime type.Cannot be overridden (declared final)

                    
protected Object clone()Creates a field-by-field shallow copy (requires Cloneable).Medium (copy constructor usually preferred)

                    
public final void wait()Causes current thread to wait on object monitor.Final (concurrency synchronization)

                    
public final void notify()Wakes up a single thread waiting on this object monitor.Final (concurrency synchronization)

                    
public final void notifyAll()Wakes up all threads waiting on this object monitor.Final (concurrency synchronization)

                    
protected void finalize()Invoked before garbage collection; deprecated for removal.Never use (deprecated since Java 9)

                  
                


                
5. Overriding the toString() Method

                

                  To convert cryptic memory identifiers (Student@36baf30c) into descriptive domain data, override toString():
                


                

                  
OverridingToStringDemo.java

                  
class Student {
    int id;
    String name;

    Student(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Student{id=" + id + ", name='" + name + "'}";
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student student = new Student(101, "Rahul");

        // Automatically calls student.toString() under the hood!
        System.out.println(student);
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Student{id=101, name='Rahul'}


                

                  Implicit Invocations: Whenever you pass an object to System.out.println(), string concatenation ("Value: " + obj), or logging libraries, Java automatically evaluates String.valueOf(obj), which delegates directly to obj.toString().
                


                
6. The equals() Method & Logical Equivalence

                

                  By default, Object.equals() performs reference equality (identical to ==). Two distinct heap objects are considered unequal even if all their internal fields match identically:
                


                

                  
DefaultEqualsFailure.java

                  
class Student {
    int id;
    Student(int id) { this.id = id; }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student(101);
        Student s2 = new Student(101);

        System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // Prints: false (Different heap addresses!)
    }
}

                


                
Overriding equals() Correctly (Modern Java Pattern)

                

                  To compare internal state logically, override equals() using modern pattern matching for instanceof alongside java.util.Objects:
                


                

                  
OverridingEqualsAndHashCode.java

                  
import java.util.Objects;

class Student {
    int id;
    String name;

    Student(int id, String name) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        // 1. Reflexive check: compare references
        if (this == obj) return true;

        // 2. Pattern matching check: null safe and type safe
        if (!(obj instanceof Student other)) return false;

        // 3. Significant fields comparison
        return id == other.id && Objects.equals(name, other.name);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(id, name);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student(101, "Rahul");
        Student s2 = new Student(101, "Rahul");

        System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // Prints: true!
    }
}

                


                
7. The hashCode() Contract

                

                  The hashCode() method generates an integer integer digest used by hash-based collections like HashMap, HashSet, and Hashtable to determine storage buckets:
                


                

                  The Holy equals-hashCode Contract:
                  
    
                    
  • Equal Objects MUST Have Equal Hash Codes: If a.equals(b) == true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must unconditionally be true.
    • 
                    
  • Unequal Objects CAN Share Hash Codes: If a.equals(b) == false, their hash codes may collide (hash collision), but distinct values improve hash table performance.
    • 
                    
  • Golden Rule: If you override equals(), you must always override hashCode(). Failing to do so breaks collection lookups in HashSet and HashMap.
    • 
                  

                


                

                  
HashCodeContractDemo.java

                  
String a = new String("Java");
String b = new String("Java");

System.out.println(a.equals(b));                  // true
System.out.println(a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()); // true (Matching hash codes!)

                


                
8. The getClass() Method: Runtime Type Introspection

                

                  Declared as public final Class<?> getClass(), this method returns the active runtime class metadata representing the heap object, ignoring the declared variable reference type:
                


                

                  
GetClassDemo.java

                  
class Animal { }
class Dog extends Animal { }

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal animal = new Dog(); // Declared type: Animal; Runtime type: Dog

        System.out.println(animal.getClass().getName()); // Output: Dog
    }
}

                


                
9. The clone() and finalize() Methods

                
clone() (Shallow Copying)

                

                  clone() is a protected method that performs a shallow field-by-field copy. For classes to use it, they must implement the marker interface Cloneable and override clone() as public. In modern Java, copy constructors or static factory methods (new Student(originalStudent)) are overwhelmingly preferred over clone().
                


                
finalize() (Deprecated for Removal)

                

                  Historically invoked by the JVM Garbage Collector before reclaiming memory. It is deprecated because execution is completely non-deterministic and leads to severe memory leaks and deadlocks. Always use AutoCloseable and try-with-resources for managing file handles, network sockets, and database connections.
                


                
10. == Operator vs. equals() Method Master Comparison

                

                  
Feature== Operatorequals() Method

                  
                    
Primitive TypesCompares actual primitive bit values (e.g. 10 == 10 is true)Cannot be used on primitive types directly

                    
Reference TypesCompares memory addresses (Object Identity)Compares logical state equivalence

                    
Overriding CapabilityCannot be overridden (fixed Java language operator)Fully customizable via method overriding

                    
Default Object BehaviorReturns true only if both pointers point to same memory addressDefault Object implementation delegates to this == obj

                  
                


                

                  
EqualityComparisonDemo.java

                  
String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);      // false (Different memory addresses)
System.out.println(s1.equals(s2));  // true  (Equal character sequences)

                


                
11. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is the Object class in Java?
    The ultimate root superclass of all classes in Java, located in the auto-imported package java.lang.
    2. 
                  
  2. Which package contains the Object class?
    java.lang.
    3. 
                  
  3. Is the Object class inherited automatically?
    Yes. Any class that does not explicitly declare extends AnotherClass implicitly extends java.lang.Object.
    4. 
                  
  4. What is the difference between toString() and getClass()?
    toString() returns a human-readable string representation of the object's state; getClass() returns the java.lang.Class metadata reflecting its runtime type.
    5. 
                  
  5. Why must hashCode() be overridden whenever equals() is overridden?
    To uphold the contract that equal objects must have identical hash codes. Violating this breaks hash-based data structures like HashMap and HashSet.
    6. 
                  
  6. Can we override the getClass() method?
    No. getClass() is declared with the final keyword in java.lang.Object.
    7. 
                  
  7. Is the clone() method public in the Object class?
    No. It is declared as protected and requires implementing the Cloneable interface to expose publicly.
    8. 
                


                
12. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Object is the cosmic root superclass of every class in Java.
    • 
                  
  • Auto-imported from java.lang without requiring an import statement.
    • 
                  
  • Override toString() to deliver meaningful text representations.
    • 
                  
  • Override equals() and hashCode() together to support logical equality and hash collections.
    • 
                  
  • Use == for memory address identity and equals() for domain value equivalence.
    • 
                  
  • getClass() identifies runtime instance type and cannot be overridden.
    • 
                  
  • Avoid finalize(); manage resources via try-with-resources and AutoCloseable.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Constructors and Inheritance in Java: Super Chaining, Initialization Order & this() vs. super()

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Constructors in Inheritance

                

                  In Java, constructors and inheritance interact closely whenever an object of a derived child class is instantiated.
                

                

                  A constructor initializes an object's memory. When a subclass object is created, Java guarantees that the parent-class portion of the object is fully initialized first by executing the superclass constructor before the body of the child constructor executes.
                


                

                  The Golden Rule: Constructors are NOT inherited! Subclasses do not inherit constructors from their parents. Instead, child constructors invoke parent constructors using the super() keyword via Constructor Chaining.
                


                
2. Basic Implementation Example

                
Observe how both parent and child constructors execute during object creation:


                

                  
BasicConstructorChain.java

                  
class Animal {

    Animal() {
        System.out.println("Animal constructor (Parent executed 1st)");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    Dog() {
        System.out.println("Dog constructor (Child executed 2nd)");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Creates a Dog object in the JVM Heap:
        Dog dog = new Dog();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal constructor (Parent executed 1st)
Dog constructor (Child executed 2nd)


                
Execution Sequence:

                
    
                  
  1. new Dog() allocates memory on the Heap for the complete Dog instance (including inherited Animal state).
    2. 
                  
  2. The Dog() constructor starts, but immediately invokes the Animal() constructor first.
    3. 
                  
  3. The Animal() constructor finishes initializing parent fields and logs its output.
    4. 
                  
  4. Control returns to Dog(), which executes its own body.
    5. 
                


                
3. The super() Keyword & Implicit Compiler Injection

                

                  The super() keyword explicitly calls a constructor of the immediate superclass. If you do not write an explicit constructor call in a child constructor, the Java compiler automatically injects an implicit no-argument super(); call as the first line:
                


                

                  
ExplicitSuperCall.java

                  
class Animal {

    Animal() {
        System.out.println("Animal created");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    Dog() {
        super(); // Explicit call to parent's no-arg constructor
        System.out.println("Dog created");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal created
Dog created


                
4. Parameterized Constructors in Parent Classes

                

                  A critical trap occurs when a parent class defines only a parameterized constructor and no default no-argument constructor:
                


                

                  
ParameterizedParentDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    // Only parameterized constructor defined (no-arg constructor is NOT provided)
    Animal(String name) {
        System.out.println("Animal name: " + name);
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    Dog() {
        // MANDATORY: Must explicitly supply the required argument!
        super("Tommy");
        System.out.println("Dog constructor");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal name: Tommy
Dog constructor


                

                  Critical Compilation Trap: If you omit super("Tommy") from Dog(), the compiler will attempt to inject super();. Because Animal has no no-argument constructor, compilation immediately fails: constructor Animal in class Animal cannot be applied to given types: required: String, found: no arguments.
                


                
5. Constructor Execution Order in Multilevel Inheritance

                

                  In a deep inheritance hierarchy, constructor execution flows hierarchically from the highest root ancestor downwards to the most specialized leaf subclass:
                


                

                  
1. Animal ConstructorRoot ancestor (Level 1)

                  ⇓ Initializes 1st ⇓
                  
2. Dog ConstructorIntermediate parent (Level 2)

                  ⇓ Initializes 2nd ⇓
                  
3. Puppy ConstructorLeaf subclass (Level 3)

                


                

                  
MultilevelChainDemo.java

                  
class Animal {
    Animal() {
        System.out.println("Animal constructor");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    Dog() {
        System.out.println("Dog constructor");
    }
}

class Puppy extends Dog {
    Puppy() {
        System.out.println("Puppy constructor");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Puppy puppy = new Puppy();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal constructor
Dog constructor
Puppy constructor


                
6. Passing Arguments Through Constructor Chaining

                

                  Subclasses delegate parent state initialization upward by passing constructor parameters through super(...), ensuring proper encapsulation:
                


                

                  
PassingArgumentsDemo.java

                  
class Person {

    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        System.out.println("Person constructor");
    }
}

class Student extends Person {

    int rollNumber;

    Student(String name, int rollNumber) {
        super(name); // Delegate parent field 'name' to Person constructor
        this.rollNumber = rollNumber; // Initialize child-specific field
        System.out.println("Student constructor");
    }

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Roll Number: " + rollNumber);
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student student = new Student("Abhinav", 101);
        student.display();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Person constructor
Student constructor
Name: Abhinav
Roll Number: 101


                
7. this() vs. super() Constructor Chaining Master Comparison

                

                  
Featurethis()super()

                  
                    
Target ConstructorCalls an overloaded constructor in the same classCalls a constructor of the immediate parent class

                    
Architectural ScopeIntra-class constructor overloadingInter-class inheritance initialization

                    
Placement RuleMust be the first statement in constructor bodyMust be the first statement in constructor body

                    
Mutual ExclusivityA single constructor cannot call both this() and super() directly.

                  
                


                
Example of this() Constructor Overload Delegation

                

                  
ThisConstructorChain.java

                  
class Student {

    Student() {
        this("Unknown"); // Delegates to Student(String name)
        System.out.println("No-argument constructor");
    }

    Student(String name) {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Name: Unknown
No-argument constructor


                

                  Modern Java Evolution Note: In traditional Java, this() or super() had to be strictly on Line 1. Modern Java (JEP 447 / JEP 482 - Flexible Constructor Bodies) permits pre-initialization statements (such as parameter validation or defensive checks) prior to calling super(...), but still prohibits invoking both in the same constructor.
                


                
8. Common Mistakes & Traps

                
    
                  
  • Forgetting Explicit super(args): When the parent lacks a default constructor, omitting super(args) triggers immediate compilation failure.
    • 
                  
  • Believing Constructors are Inherited: Writing child code assuming parent constructor signatures are automatically inherited by subclasses.
    • 
                  
  • Expecting Subclass to Run First: Forgetting that parent constructors always execute before the child constructor body.
    • 
                  
  • Misplacing super(): Placing super() on line 2 or inside an if block triggers a compilation error.
    • 
                  
  • Confusing super() with super.method(): super() calls a parent constructor; super.someMethod() invokes an overridden parent instance method.
    • 
                


                
9. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. Are constructors inherited by child classes in Java?
    No. Constructors are never inherited. Subclasses must declare their own constructors and chain to parent constructors via super().
    2. 
                  
  2. Why is the super() keyword used in constructors?
    To invoke an appropriate constructor of the immediate superclass to initialize parent-owned fields.
    3. 
                  
  3. What happens if a parent class only defines a parameterized constructor?
    The compiler does not supply a default no-argument constructor. Therefore, every child constructor must explicitly call super(...) with appropriate arguments.
    4. 
                  
  4. In what order do constructors execute during object creation?
    Hierarchically from top to bottom: starting from java.lang.Object down to the instantiated child subclass.
    5. 
                  
  5. Can a constructor be overridden in Java?
    No. Because constructors are not inherited, they cannot be overridden. However, constructors can be overloaded within the same class.
    6. 
                  
  6. Can an abstract class have a constructor?
    Yes. While an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly via new, its constructor runs when a concrete subclass is instantiated to initialize inherited state.
    7. 
                  
  7. Can a constructor be declared static or final?
    No. Constructors cannot be static (they initialize instances) or final (they are never inherited or overridden).
    8. 
                


                
10. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Constructors initialize objects; they are never inherited by subclasses.
    • 
                  
  • super() calls the immediate parent's no-argument constructor.
    • 
                  
  • super(args) calls a matching parameterized parent constructor.
    • 
                  
  • Parent constructors always execute completely before child constructor bodies.
    • 
                  
  • this() delegates to an overloaded constructor in the same class.
    • 
                  
  • Neither static nor final modifiers can be applied to constructors.
    • 
                  
  • Constructor chaining guarantees full, orderly state initialization across the inheritance tree.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Access Modifiers in Java: Visibility Matrix, Encapsulation & Protected Inheritance

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Access Modifiers

                

                  Access Modifiers in Java are essential access control keywords that govern the scope, visibility, and accessibility of classes, constructors, methods, and instance variables.
                

                

                  They form the foundational barrier of Encapsulation, safeguarding sensitive object state against unauthorized external corruption and establishing clear API boundaries between interacting modules.
                

                
Java defines four distinct access visibility levels:


                

                  
1. publicUnrestricted global visibility

                  →
                  
2. protectedPackage + Subclasses

                  →
                  
3. Default (Package-Private)Same package only (no keyword)

                  →
                  
4. privateEnclosing class only

                


                
2. The Four Access Modifiers Deconstructed

                
    
                  
  • public: Accessible from any class anywhere in the application (subject to module/package accessibility).
    • 
                  
  • protected: Accessible within the same package, and accessible across different packages only by subclasses through inheritance.
    • 
                  
  • Default (Package-Private): No keyword is written. Accessible strictly by classes residing within the identical package.
    • 
                  
  • private: The most restrictive modifier. Accessible only within the body of the declaring top-level class (and its nested inner classes).
    • 
                


                
3. Master Visibility Matrix

                

                  
Access LocationpublicprotectedDefault (Package-Private)private

                  
                    
Same ClassYesYesYesYes

                    
Same Package, Other ClassYesYesYesNo

                    
Different Package, SubclassYesYes*NoNo

                    
Different Package, Non-SubclassYesNoNoNo

                  
                


                

                  *Subtle Protected Nuance: Cross-package protected access is permitted only through inheritance inside the subclass itself. Code outside the package cannot access protected members using an arbitrary parent reference (e.g., Animal a = new Animal(); a.eat(); will fail if called from a different package).
                


                
4. Comprehensive Implementation Example

                
Observe all four visibility tiers declared in a single Student class:


                

                  
AccessModifierDemo.java

                  
class Student {

    public String name = "Abhinav";
    protected int age = 21;
    int marks = 90;                // Default access (package-private)
    private String password = "abc123";

    public void display() {
        // All 4 members are directly accessible inside declaring class:
        System.out.println(name);
        System.out.println(age);
        System.out.println(marks);
        System.out.println(password);
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Student student = new Student();

        System.out.println(student.name);   // VALID: public
        System.out.println(student.age);    // VALID: protected (same package)
        System.out.println(student.marks);  // VALID: default (same package)

        // System.out.println(student.password); // COMPILATION ERROR: password has private access in Student!

        student.display(); // VALID: public method printing private state safely
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Abhinav
21
90
Abhinav
21
90
abc123


                
5. Understanding protected in Inheritance Hierarchies

                

                  The primary purpose of protected is enabling parent classes to share implementation mechanics with subclasses while concealing them from arbitrary outside callers:
                


                

                  
ProtectedInheritanceDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    // Protected method: visible to subclasses
    protected void eat() {
        System.out.println("Animal is eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void play() {
        eat(); // Invoking inherited protected method directly
        System.out.println("Dog is playing");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Dog dog = new Dog();
        dog.play();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal is eating
Dog is playing


                
6. Permissible Access Modifiers for Classes

                

                  Java applies strict constraints on top-level classes versus nested classes:
                


                
Top-Level Classes

                
Top-level classes (classes declared directly inside a .java file) can ONLY be:

                
    
                  
  • public: Accessible from any other package.
    • 
                  
  • Default (Package-Private): Omit modifier; accessible only within the containing package.
    • 
                

                

                  Compiler Rule: You cannot declare a top-level class as private or protected! The compiler rejects private class MyClass immediately.
                


                
Nested Inner Classes

                

                  Nested classes declared inside an enclosing class can leverage all four modifiers (public, protected, default, or private).
                


                
7. Access Modifiers as the Enforcers of Encapsulation

                

                  The gold standard of software design is declaring state fields private and channeling mutations through validating public mutators (setters/methods):
                


                

                  
BankAccountEncapsulation.java

                  
class BankAccount {

    // Private field: shielded from outside tampering
    private double balance;

    // Controlled mutation with business invariant validation
    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0) {
            balance += amount;
        }
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        BankAccount account = new BankAccount();
        account.deposit(1000);

        System.out.println(account.getBalance());
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
1000.0


                
8. Common Mistakes & Gotchas

                
    
                  
  • Confusing Default with Public: Assuming leaving off a modifier makes it globally accessible. Default limits visibility to the current package.
    • 
                  
  • Direct Private Field Mutation: Trying to write obj.privateField = value; from an external class instead of using getters/setters.
    • 
                  
  • Over-Assuming Protected Reach: Believing protected allows anyone in another package to call methods on arbitrary object references.
    • 
                  
  • Declaring Top-Level Classes Private: Writing private class Foo triggers a compilation error.
    • 
                  
  • Assuming Modifiers Validate Logic: Access modifiers only control visibility; your methods must still enforce boundary and invariant validations.
    • 
                


                
9. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. How many access levels are available in Java?
    Four visibility levels: public, protected, Default (package-private), and private.
    2. 
                  
  2. Which access modifier provides the most restrictive visibility?
    private (accessible only within the declaring top-level class).
    3. 
                  
  3. What is the keyword for default access in Java?
    There is no keyword. If no access modifier is declared, Java applies package-private visibility by default.
    4. 
                  
  4. Can a private method be overridden?
    No. A private method is invisible to subclasses, so it cannot participate in polymorphism or method overriding.
    5. 
                  
  5. Can a constructor be declared private?
    Yes. Private constructors prevent external instantiation, a pattern used in Singleton architectures, Factory methods, and static utility classes (e.g. java.lang.Math).
    6. 
                  
  6. Can interface methods be private?
    Yes. Since Java 9, interfaces support private and private static helper methods to share common routines between default interface methods.
    7. 
                  
  7. Why do software engineers make fields private?
    To enforce encapsulation, prevent external state corruption, and maintain the freedom to alter internal implementation without breaking client code.
    8. 
                


                
10. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • public: Globally visible to any class.
    • 
                  
  • protected: Visible within package and to subclasses across packages.
    • 
                  
  • Default (package-private): Visible only within the declaring package.
    • 
                  
  • private: Visible strictly inside the declaring class.
    • 
                  
  • Top-level classes can only be public or package-private.
    • 
                  
  • Private fields + validated public methods form the cornerstone of object-oriented encapsulation.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Method Overriding in Java: Runtime Polymorphism, Dynamic Dispatch & Covariant Returns

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Method Overriding

                

                  Method Overriding is a core Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) mechanism in Java where a subclass provides its own specialized implementation of an instance method that it inherits from a superclass.
                

                

                  Overriding allows child classes to refine, customize, or completely replace inherited behavior while preserving a uniform method contract across a class hierarchy.
                

                

                  Method overriding is the technical foundation of Runtime Polymorphism (Dynamic Method Dispatch). For instance, a base class Animal defines a generic sound() method; a Dog overrides it to bark, while a Cat overrides it to meow.
                


                

                  Key Motivations for Method Overriding:
                  
    
                    
  • Customized Subclass Behavior: Specializes general parent behavior for distinct child domains.
    • 
                    
  • Enables Runtime Polymorphism: Upcasted parent references dynamically route to the actual heap object's implementation.
    • 
                    
  • Unified API Contracts: Eliminates fragmented names like dogSound(), catSound(), or cowSound() in favor of a clean, universal sound() method.
    • 
                    
  • Extensible Open/Closed Architecture: New animal types can be added without modifying existing caller code.
    • 
                  

                


                
2. Basic Syntax & The @Override Annotation

                

                  
OverridingSyntax.java

                  
class Parent {

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Parent method");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {

    // Mandatory Best Practice: Compile-time check
    @Override
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Child method");
    }
}

                


                

                  Why You Must Always Use @Override: While optional, @Override instructs the Java compiler to verify that the method actually matches an inherited method signature. If you make a typo (e.g. void displaay()), the compiler alerts you immediately with an error instead of silently treating it as a new unrelated method!
                


                
3. Example 1: Basic Method Overriding

                

                  
BasicOverridingDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Animal animal = new Animal();
        Dog dog = new Dog();

        animal.sound(); // Parent version executes
        dog.sound();    // Subclass overridden version executes
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal makes a sound
Dog barks


                
4. Example 2: Runtime Polymorphism (Dynamic Method Dispatch)

                

                  The true power of method overriding emerges when polymorphism is leveraged: parent reference variables point to child heap instances at runtime:
                


                

                  
RuntimePolymorphismDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

class Cat extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Cat meows");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Upcasting: Generic Animal reference
        Animal animal;

        animal = new Dog();
        animal.sound(); // Dynamically dispatches to Dog.sound()

        animal = new Cat();
        animal.sound(); // Dynamically dispatches to Cat.sound()
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Dog barks
Cat meows


                
JVM Virtual Table (vtable) Dynamic Dispatch Architecture

                

                  
Compile-Time CheckReference type (Animal) determines visible method signatures

                  → Runtime vtable Lookup →
                  
JVM Heap InspectionIdentifies actual concrete instance (Dog / Cat)

                  → Dynamic Dispatch →
                  
Subclass ExecutionExecutes specialized overridden body

                


                
5. Master Rules Matrix of Method Overriding

                

                  
Rule CategoryCompiler Enforcement & Requirement

                  
                    
Method SignatureMust be identical: Same method name, same parameter count, types, and sequence.

                    
Inheritance RelationshipMandatory: Can only override an accessible inherited method from a superclass.

                    
Return TypeMust be identical or a Covariant Subtype (narrower reference type).

                    
Access ModifiersCannot reduce visibility: May expand visibility (e.g. protected → public), but cannot restrict it.

                    
Exception HandlingCannot declare new or broader checked exceptions. May throw fewer, narrower, or unchecked exceptions.

                    
final MethodsCannot be overridden under any circumstance.

                    
private MethodsCannot be overridden: Invisible to subclasses; any identical name in child is a completely new method.

                    
static MethodsCannot be overridden: Static methods participate in Method Hiding, not polymorphic dispatch.

                    
ConstructorsCannot be overridden: Constructors are never inherited.

                  
                


                
6. Access Modifiers & Visibility Invariants

                

                  A child class cannot reduce the accessibility of an inherited method. Doing so breaks the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP):
                


                

                  
VisibilityRulesDemo.java

                  
class Parent {
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {

    // COMPILATION ERROR: Cannot reduce visibility from public to protected!
    // @Override
    // protected void display() { }

    // VALID: Retaining public visibility
    @Override
    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}

                


                

                  Visibility Expansion Rule: You can always broaden accessibility (e.g. overriding a protected method as public), but you can never narrow it (e.g. overriding a public method as protected or private).
                


                
7. Covariant Return Types (Subtype Returns)

                

                  Introduced in Java 5, a subclass method can declare a return type that is a subtype (more specific type) of the parent method's return type:
                


                

                  
CovariantReturnDemo.java

                  
class Animal { }
class Dog extends Animal { }

class Parent {
    Animal getAnimal() {
        return new Animal();
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {

    // VALID COVARIANT RETURN: Dog is a subtype of Animal!
    @Override
    Dog getAnimal() {
        return new Dog();
    }
}

                

                

                  Advantage: Callers invoking child.getAnimal() directly receive a strongly typed Dog reference without needing explicit downcasting!
                


                
8. Invoking Parent Implementation via the super Keyword

                

                  Subclasses often want to augment rather than completely discard the parent's work. Use super.methodName():
                


                

                  
SuperOverridingDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        super.sound(); // Delegate to parent logic first
        System.out.println("Dog barks"); // Specialized child behavior
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
        dog.sound();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal makes a sound
Dog barks


                
9. Method Overriding vs. Method Overloading Master Comparison

                

                  
FeatureMethod OverridingMethod Overloading

                  
                    
ScopeOccurs across parent-child inheritanceOccurs within the same class (or hierarchy)

                    
Method SignatureMust be identical (name & parameters)Must differ in count, types, or order

                    
Polymorphism TypeRuntime Polymorphism (Dynamic Binding)Compile-Time Polymorphism (Static Binding)

                    
Return TypeMust be identical or covariant subtypeCan differ freely provided parameters differ

                    
Static / PrivateCannot override static or private methodsCan overload static and private methods freely

                    
PurposeCustomizes / replaces inherited behaviorProvides multiple convenient input ways to call a method

                  
                


                
10. Common Mistakes & Gotchas

                
    
                  
  • Omitting @Override: Mistyping parameter types (e.g. float instead of double) creates an accidental overload instead of an override if @Override is omitted.
    • 
                  
  • Narrowing Visibility: Trying to make an overridden method private or protected when the parent method was public.
    • 
                  
  • Attempting to Override static Methods: Writing an identical static method in a subclass hides the parent method; it does not participate in polymorphic dispatch.
    • 
                  
  • Attempting to Override final or private Methods: The compiler strictly prohibits overriding final methods. private methods are not inherited and cannot be overridden.
    • 
                  
  • Assuming Reference Type Determines Method: For instance methods, the JVM always dispatches based on the actual runtime heap object, never the variable reference type.
    • 
                


                
11. Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is method overriding in Java?
    The OOP process where a subclass provides a specialized implementation of an inherited instance method sharing the exact same signature.
    2. 
                  
  2. Why is the @Override annotation recommended?
    It triggers compile-time verification, ensuring the method actually overrides an existing superclass method and catching signature typos.
    3. 
                  
  3. Can static methods be overridden in Java?
    No. Static methods belong to the class, not object instances. Defining the same static method in a child class is called Method Hiding.
    4. 
                  
  4. Can a final method be overridden?
    No. The final keyword explicitly prohibits subclasses from modifying the method implementation.
    5. 
                  
  5. Can a private method be overridden?
    No. Private methods are invisible outside their declaring class; a child class declaring a method with the same name simply creates an unrelated new method.
    6. 
                  
  6. What is runtime polymorphism?
    The dynamic selection and invocation of an overridden method at runtime based on the actual object's type on the heap.
    7. 
                  
  7. What are the rules regarding exception handling in method overriding?
    An overriding method cannot throw checked exceptions that are broader than those declared by the superclass method. It can throw narrower checked exceptions, fewer checked exceptions, or any unchecked (runtime) exceptions.
    8. 
                  
  8. Can constructors be overridden?
    No. Constructors are never inherited, so they cannot be overridden.
    9. 
                


                
12. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Method overriding customizes inherited instance method behavior.
    • 
                  
  • Requires identical method names and parameter lists.
    • 
                  
  • Always annotate with @Override for compiler safety.
    • 
                  
  • Enables Dynamic Method Dispatch (Runtime Polymorphism).
    • 
                  
  • Overriding methods cannot reduce visibility or throw broader checked exceptions.
    • 
                  
  • Supports Covariant Returns (narrower reference return types).
    • 
                  
  • final, private, and static methods cannot be overridden.
    • 
                  
  • Use super.method() to delegate to the superclass implementation.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Upcasting and Downcasting in Java: Type Hierarchy, ClassCastException & Pattern Matching

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Reference Type Casting

                

                  In Java, Upcasting and Downcasting refer to converting an object reference from one class type to another along an established inheritance hierarchy.
                

                

                  Reference casting controls what members the compiler permits you to see and invoke through a reference variable.
                


                

                  The Golden Rule of Casting: Type casting a reference variable never modifies or transforms the underlying object in heap memory. The object remains 100% identical in structure and class identity; only the "lens" (the reference type) through which you inspect it changes.
                


                

                  
Superclass (Animal)General parent type

                  ↑ UPCASTING (Implicit & Safe) ↑
                  
Subclass (Dog)Specialized child type

                  ↓ DOWNCASTING (Explicit & Guarded) ↓
                


                
2. Upcasting in Java (Widening Reference Conversion)

                

                  Upcasting occurs when a child-class reference is assigned to a parent-class reference variable. Because a child is-a parent, upcasting is completely automatic (implicit) and guaranteed to be type-safe by the JVM.
                


                

                  
UpcastingDemo.java

                  
class Animal {

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Animal is eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Dog is barking");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Dog dog = new Dog();

        // UPCASTING: Assigning child Dog to parent Animal reference
        Animal animal = dog; // Automatic & Implicit

        animal.eat(); // Valid: eat() is declared in Animal
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal is eating


                
Heap Memory & Compiler Scope Limitation

                

                  
Reference 1: Dog dogCan see eat() AND bark()

                  ↘ Both point to same object ↙
                  
Single Heap Object: new Dog()Actual concrete instance in JVM Heap

                  ↙ Both point to same object ↘
                  
Reference 2: Animal animalCan ONLY see eat()

                


                

                  Critical Compiler Restriction: Even though the object in memory is a Dog, writing animal.bark(); triggers an immediate compilation error! The Java compiler checks method availability based on the declared reference type (Animal), which has no knowledge of bark().
                


                
3. Downcasting in Java (Narrowing Reference Conversion)

                

                  Downcasting converts a parent-class reference back down to a child-class reference. Because the compiler cannot verify whether an arbitrary Animal reference actually points to a Dog at runtime, downcasting requires an explicit cast operator (TargetType):
                


                

                  
DowncastingDemo.java

                  
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // 1. Upcasting
        Animal animal = new Dog();

        // 2. EXPLICIT DOWNCASTING back to Dog
        Dog dog = (Dog) animal;

        dog.eat();  // Inherited method
        dog.bark(); // Specialized Dog method now accessible!
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Animal is eating
Dog is barking


                
4. The Danger: Runtime ClassCastException

                

                  Downcasting is only valid if the actual underlying heap object is genuinely an instance of the target type. Downcasting to an incompatible sibling class causes a fatal runtime crash:
                


                

                  
InvalidDowncastCrash.java

                  
class Animal { }
class Dog extends Animal { }
class Cat extends Animal { }

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Animal animal = new Cat(); // Upcasting Cat to Animal (Valid)

        // RUNTIME DISASTER: Cat cannot be cast to Dog!
        Dog dog = (Dog) animal; // Compiles cleanly, but throws ClassCastException!
    }
}
