In your Main class, create polymorphic Vehicle references pointing to both objects and invoke both methods!
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Dependency Injection (DI) in Java: Inversion of Control, Testability & Enterprise Spring Boot Architecture

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to Dependency Injection

                

                  Dependency Injection (DI) is a software architectural design pattern in which an object receives its collaborating dependencies from an external entity rather than instantiating them internally using the new operator.
                

                

                  Instead of a class hardcoding its collaborators, control is inverted: external configuration or a container "injects" the required objects into the dependent class.
                


                

                  
Without DI (Hardcoded & Brittle)OrderService directly instantiates new PaymentService()

                  ↔ VS ↔
                  
With DI (Inverted & Flexible)External Container injects PaymentService into OrderService

                


                

                  The Real-World Analogy: Think of a modern laptop. If the battery were welded directly onto the motherboard, replacing a dead battery would require buying a brand-new laptop (tight coupling). Instead, modern hardware provides a standardized modular slot where external batteries are "injected" (loose coupling).
                


                
2. What is a "Dependency"?

                

                  A dependency is any collaborating service, repository, utility, or data source that a class requires to execute its business responsibility.
                


                

                  
DependencyConcept.java

                  
class PaymentService {

    void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed");
    }
}

class OrderService {

    // OrderService DEPENDS ON PaymentService
    private PaymentService paymentService;

    void placeOrder() {
        // NullPointerException if paymentService is not initialized!
        paymentService.pay();
    }
}

                


                

                  In the naive snippet above, paymentService is uninitialized. Calling placeOrder() throws an immediate NullPointerException. How we supply this object is the core problem Dependency Injection solves.
                


                
3. Dependency Injection Without Frameworks (Pure Core Java)

                

                  Dependency Injection is an architectural principle, not a Spring-exclusive feature. It can be implemented cleanly in pure Java:
                


                
A. The Anti-Pattern: Tightly Coupled Hardcoded Instantiation

                

                  
TightlyCoupledOrderService.java

                  
class PaymentService {

    void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed");
    }
}

class OrderService {

    // ANTI-PATTERN: OrderService controls its own dependency creation
    private PaymentService paymentService = new PaymentService();

    void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        OrderService orderService = new OrderService();
        orderService.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                

                  Why this fails in enterprise code: You cannot unit test OrderService in isolation. It is permanently married to PaymentService. You cannot substitute a mock or staging payment provider without modifying the source code of OrderService!
                


                
B. The Clean Architecture Pattern: Constructor Dependency Injection

                

                  
ConstructorInjectionDemo.java

                  
class PaymentService {

    void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed");
    }
}

class OrderService {

    // CLEAN: Immutable, explicitly declared dependency
    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    // Constructor Injection: Supplied from the outside
    OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // 1. Dependency created outside
        PaymentService paymentService = new PaymentService();

        // 2. Dependency injected into dependent class
        OrderService orderService = new OrderService(paymentService);

        orderService.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment processed
Order placed


                
4. The Three Types of Dependency Injection

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Injection Type
                        Implementation Syntax
                        Pros & Best Use Cases
                        Cons & Architectural Pitfalls
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Constructor Injection
(Strongly Recommended)		
                        
                          public OrderService(PaymentService ps) { this.ps = ps; }
                        
                        Allows fields to be declared final (immutable), guarantees objects cannot be constructed in a half-initialized state, easily unit-tested.
                        Can suffer from verbose constructor signatures if classes violate the Single Responsibility Principle.
                      

                      

                        Setter Injection
(Optional Collaborators)		
                        
                          public void setPaymentService(PaymentService ps) { this.ps = ps; }
                        
                        Allows dynamic reconfiguration or swapping of dependencies at runtime.
                        Objects can be instantiated in an incomplete/broken state; cannot declare fields final.
                      

                      

                        Field Injection
(Anti-Pattern in Modern Java)		
                        
                          @Autowired private PaymentService ps;
                        
                        Less boilerplate in legacy codebases.
                        Hides dependencies, breaks encapsulation, prevents standalone unit tests without launching reflection/Spring container.
                      

                    
                  

                


                
5. Combining DI with Interfaces: The Holy Grail of Loose Coupling

                

                  When Dependency Injection is paired with polymorphic interfaces, application flexibility reaches its zenith. The consumer class depends solely on an abstract contract:
                


                

                  
InterfaceDrivenDI.java

                  
// 1. Common contract
interface PaymentService {
    void pay();
}

// 2. Concrete Implementation A
class UpiPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through UPI");
    }
}

// 3. Concrete Implementation B
class CardPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through Card");
    }
}

// 4. Consumer depends ONLY on interface
class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    // Constructor injection accepting the interface contract
    OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Seamlessly inject UpiPayment
        PaymentService upi = new UpiPayment();
        OrderService order1 = new OrderService(upi);
        order1.placeOrder();

        // Seamlessly switch to CardPayment without touching a single line of OrderService!
        PaymentService card = new CardPayment();
        OrderService order2 = new OrderService(card);
        order2.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment through UPI
Order placed
Payment through Card
Order placed


                
6. Enterprise Dependency Injection in Spring Boot (IoC Container)

                

                  In Spring Boot, you do not write manual new wiring in Main. The Spring Inversion of Control (IoC) Container automatically discovers classes annotated with @Service, @Repository, or @RestController, instantiates them as singleton beans, and wires them together via Constructor Injection:
                


                

                  
UserController@RestController (HTTP Layer)

                  ↓ Injects ↓
                  
UserService@Service (Business Layer)

                  ↓ Injects ↓
                  
UserRepository@Repository (Database JPA Layer)

                


                

                  
SpringBootDIArchitecture.java

                  
// 1. Data Access Repository
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
}

// 2. Business Service Interface
public interface UserService {
    User getUserById(Long id);
}

// 3. Service Implementation with Constructor Injection
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class UserServiceImpl implements UserService {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    // Spring Boot automatically autowires single constructors without needing @Autowired!
    public UserServiceImpl(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    @Override
    public User getUserById(Long id) {
        return userRepository.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("User not found"));
    }
}

// 4. Web Controller Layer
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserController {

    private final UserService userService;

    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.getUserById(id);
    }
}

                


                

                  Spring Boot Modern Best Practice: If a Spring bean class has only one constructor, Spring 4.3+ automatically treats it as the @Autowired constructor. Explicitly typing @Autowired on the constructor is no longer required.
                


                
7. Dependency Injection vs. Inversion of Control (IoC)

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Comparison Dimension
                        Dependency Injection (DI)
                        Inversion of Control (IoC)
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Conceptual Scope
                        A specific design pattern and technique.
                        A broad architectural philosophy / principle.
                      

                      

                        Core Mechanism
                        Supplying collaborators from external callers.
                        Transferring execution control or lifecycle to a framework.
                      

                      

                        Relationship
                        DI is a concrete implementation of the IoC principle.
                        IoC can be realized via DI, Template Method, or Event Listeners.
                      

                    
                  

                


                
8. How DI Revolutionizes Automated Unit Testing

                

                  The paramount advantage of Dependency Injection is making code trivially testable. Because dependencies are passed into constructors, unit tests can supply lightweight fakes or mocks without firing up databases, networks, or payment gateways:
                


                

                  
UnitTestWithMockDI.java

                  
// Fast, offline fake payment provider for unit testing
class FakePaymentService implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Fake payment completed in memory");
    }
}

public class OrderServiceTest {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // In unit test: Inject the fake dependency!
        PaymentService fakePayment = new FakePaymentService();
        OrderService order = new OrderService(fakePayment);

        order.placeOrder(); // Runs in milliseconds without network calls!
    }
}

                


                
9. Common Anti-Patterns & Developer Mistakes

                

                  Critical Mistakes to Avoid:
                  
    
                    
  • Calling new Everywhere: Hardcoding new Service() inside business classes destroys testability and enforces tight coupling.
    • 
                    
  • Over-relying on Field Injection (@Autowired on fields): Prevents immutability (fields cannot be final), hides class dependencies, and requires reflection hacks to test.
    • 
                    
  • Uninitialized Dependencies: Forgetting to assign the dependency in constructors or setters triggers NullPointerException at runtime.
    • 
                    
  • Coupling to Concrete Classes Instead of Interfaces: Always inject interfaces (e.g., PaymentService) rather than concrete classes (e.g., UpiPayment).
    • 
                  

                


                
10. Core Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is Dependency Injection in Java?
    A design pattern where an object's dependencies are provided by an external caller or container rather than created internally by the object itself.
    2. 
                  
  2. What are the three primary types of Dependency Injection?
    Constructor Injection, Setter Injection, and Field Injection.
    3. 
                  
  3. Why is Constructor Injection overwhelmingly preferred in Spring Boot?
    It enables dependencies to be declared final (immutable), guarantees full object initialization at instantiation time, and allows seamless mock injection during unit tests.
    4. 
                  
  4. What is the difference between DI and Inversion of Control (IoC)?
    IoC is the broad design principle of delegating control (lifecycle, object creation) to an external framework. DI is the specific design pattern used to implement IoC by injecting collaborating objects.
    5. 
                  
  5. Does Dependency Injection require a framework like Spring?
    No. Pure Java can implement DI manually via standard parameterized constructors and setters (known as "Pure DI" or "Manual DI").
    6. 
                  
  6. What happens when multiple Spring beans implement the same interface?
    Spring throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless resolved using @Qualifier("beanName") or @Primary on the preferred bean.
    7. 
                


                
11. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • A dependency is any collaborating object a class needs to function.
    • 
                  
  • DI supplies collaborating objects from the outside.
    • 
                  
  • Constructor Injection is the industry standard for mandatory dependencies.
    • 
                  
  • Always pair DI with interfaces for ultimate loose coupling and polymorphism.
    • 
                  
  • Spring Boot's IoC container manages bean lifecycle and wires dependencies automatically.
    • 
                  
  • DI eliminates tightly coupled code and makes unit testing effortless.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Constructor Injection in Java: Architecture, Immutable Fields & Spring Boot Best Practices

                

              

              

                
1. What is Constructor Injection?

                

                  Constructor Injection is the gold standard implementation of Dependency Injection (DI) in which a class receives all required collaborator dependencies directly through its constructor parameters at instantiation time.
                

                

                  Instead of a class hardcoding or self-instantiating dependencies via new, the surrounding application runtime or DI container explicitly supplies those dependencies during object construction.
                


                

                  
PaymentServiceExternal Collaborator

                  ⇒ passed into ⇒
                  
OrderService(PaymentService ps)Constructor receives and binds dependency

                  ⇒ executes ⇒
                  
orderService.placeOrder()Leverages injected collaborator safely

                


                
2. Basic Syntax & The final Invariance Guarantee

                

                  The canonical syntax for Constructor Injection stores dependencies in private final instance fields:
                


                

                  
ConstructorInjectionSyntax.java

                  
class ServiceA {
    // Collaborating dependency
}

class ServiceB {

    // 1. Declare as private final to guarantee immutability
    private final ServiceA serviceA;

    // 2. Supply dependency via constructor parameter
    public ServiceB(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA; // Bind parameter to instance variable
    }
}

                


                

                  Why final Matters: Marking fields final guarantees that the dependency reference cannot be reassigned or mutated after construction. It also ensures thread-safety without requiring synchronization blocks.
                


                
3. Complete Pure Java Step-by-Step Walkthrough

                

                  Let us trace the complete three-tier architectural lifecycle in standalone Java without third-party frameworks:
                


                

                  
StepByStepConstructorInjection.java

                  
// Step 1: Declare the dependency service
class PaymentService {

    public void processPayment() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed successfully");
    }
}

// Step 2: Declare the client class receiving dependency via constructor
class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    // Constructor Injection
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.processPayment();
        System.out.println("Order placed successfully");
    }
}

// Step 3: Instantiate and wire in the consumer/bootstrap layer
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // 1. Instantiate the dependency externally
        PaymentService paymentService = new PaymentService();

        // 2. Inject dependency into OrderService
        OrderService orderService = new OrderService(paymentService);

        // 3. Execute business logic
        orderService.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment processed successfully
Order placed successfully


                
4. Constructor Injection vs. Internal Instantiation

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Architectural Dimension
                        Without Constructor Injection (Internal new)
                        With Constructor Injection
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Dependency Origin
                        Internally instantiated inside the class.
                        Externally supplied by caller / IoC container.
                      

                      

                        Coupling Level
                        Tightly coupled to one concrete implementation.
                        Loosely coupled; easily swappable.
                      

                      

                        Testability
                        Extremely difficult to mock in unit tests.
                        Trivially tested by passing mock/fake objects.
                      

                      

                        Visibility
                        Hidden dependencies embedded in class body.
                        Explicit dependencies declared right on constructor signature.
                      

                      

                        Immutability
                        Often mutable; cannot enforce external binding.
                        Fields can be marked final.
                      

                    
                  

                


                
5. Constructor Injection Paired with Interfaces

                

                  Combining Constructor Injection with interfaces decouples client classes from concrete implementations, unleashing pure polymorphic substitution:
                


                

                  
PolymorphicConstructorInjection.java

                  
// 1. Contract
interface PaymentService {
    void pay();
}

// 2. Providers
class UpiPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through UPI");
    }
}

class CardPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through Card");
    }
}

// 3. Client receiving interface contract
class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Easily switch providers without touching OrderService!
        PaymentService payment = new UpiPayment();
        OrderService order = new OrderService(payment);
        order.placeOrder();

        // Switch to CardPayment:
        PaymentService card = new CardPayment();
        OrderService order2 = new OrderService(card);
        order2.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment through UPI
Order placed
Payment through Card
Order placed


                
6. Constructor Injection in Enterprise Spring Boot

                

                  In modern Spring Boot development, Constructor Injection is the official recommended paradigm over field injection (@Autowired on fields):
                


                

                  
SpringBootConstructorInjection.java

                  
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

// 1. Service Contract
public interface PaymentService {
    void pay();
}

// 2. Service Implementation managed as Spring Bean
@Service
public class PaymentServiceImpl implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed");
    }
}

// 3. Client Service utilizing Constructor Injection
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    // Spring 4.3+: @Autowired is OPTIONAL when there is only one constructor!
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

                


                

                  How the Spring Container Wires This:
                  
    
                    
  1. Spring scans components and discovers PaymentServiceImpl and OrderService.
    2. 
                    
  2. Spring inspects the constructor of OrderService and notes it requires a PaymentService bean.
    3. 
                    
  3. Spring instantiates PaymentServiceImpl first and injects it into OrderService.
    4. 
                    
  4. If multiple implementations exist, annotate with @Qualifier("beanName") or mark one with @Primary.
    5. 
                  

                


                
7. Why Use the final Keyword with Constructor Injection?

                

                  Using final on constructor-injected fields provides four mission-critical guarantees:
                

                
    
                  
  • Compile-Time Enforcement: The Java compiler forces you to initialize the field in every constructor path; you cannot forget to bind it.
    • 
                  
  • Reference Immutability: Once bound, no rogue setter or internal method can accidentally point the field to null or another instance.
    • 
                  
  • Thread-Safety: In concurrent multithreaded environments, final fields guarantee visibility across threads without synchronization locks (JMM safe publication).
    • 
                  
  • Fail-Fast Initialization Guard: Pair with Objects.requireNonNull() to reject null dependencies instantly:
    • 
                


                

                  
DefensiveNullCheck.java

                  
import java.util.Objects;

class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;

    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        // Rejects null immediately upon construction rather than throwing NPE later!
        this.paymentService = Objects.requireNonNull(paymentService, "PaymentService cannot be null");
    }
}

                


                
8. Six Core Architectural Advantages

                
    
                  
  1. Explicit Collaborators: A class clearly declares everything it needs up front in its public constructor signature.
    2. 
                  
  2. True Immutability: Dependencies can be marked final, ensuring stable state across the application lifecycle.
    3. 
                  
  3. No Incomplete Objects: Prevents objects from ever existing in an uninitialized, half-constructed state.
    4. 
                  
  4. Frictionless Unit Testing: In JUnit tests, pass mocks (e.g., Mockito mocks) directly into new OrderService(mockPayment) without needing Spring reflection tools.
    5. 
                  
  5. Circular Dependency Detection: Constructor injection enables Spring to detect circular bean dependencies immediately at startup rather than failing at runtime.
    6. 
                  
  6. Framework Agnostic: Code written with constructor injection can be used in Spring, Quarkus, Micronaut, or standalone Java without modifications.
    7. 
                


                
9. Common Developer Mistakes & Gotchas

                

                  Watch Out for These Errors:
                  
    
                    
  • Shadowing Parameter Error (Missing this.):
    
                      OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) { paymentService = paymentService; } → Assigns the parameter to itself; the instance field remains uninitialized! Always write this.paymentService = paymentService;.
                    
    • 
                    
  • Calling Deleted Default Constructor: Once you define a parameterized constructor, Java suppresses the default no-arg constructor. Writing new OrderService() without arguments causes a compile error.
    • 
                    
  • Injecting Unregistered Spring Beans: If PaymentService is not annotated with @Service or registered via @Bean, Spring fails at startup with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
    • 
                  

                


                
10. Core Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is Constructor Injection?
    A Dependency Injection pattern where an object's required dependencies are supplied as arguments to its constructor during instantiation.
    2. 
                  
  2. Why is Constructor Injection overwhelmingly favored over Field Injection in Spring Boot?
    It promotes immutable fields (final), avoids hidden dependencies, eliminates circular dependency traps, and enables fast unit testing without reflection or Spring test runners.
    3. 
                  
  3. Is @Autowired required on a single constructor in modern Spring Boot?
    No. Starting from Spring 4.3+, if a class declares a single constructor, Spring automatically uses it for dependency injection without requiring @Autowired.
    4. 
                  
  4. What happens if someone passes null to a constructor-injected class?
    Java permits null unless guarded. Best practice is to use Objects.requireNonNull(dependency, "message") inside the constructor to fail fast.
    5. 
                  
  5. How does Spring resolve ambiguity when multiple constructors exist?
    If a class defines multiple constructors, you must annotate the intended injection constructor with @Autowired, or configure bean factory methods.
    6. 
                  
  6. What is the relationship between Dependency Injection and Constructor Injection?
    Dependency Injection is the general architectural pattern; Constructor Injection is one specific, highly recommended implementation mechanism.
    7. 
                


                
11. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Constructor Injection supplies dependencies at instantiation time.
    • 
                  
  • Always declare dependency fields as private final.
    • 
                  
  • Always use this.field = param to bind dependencies safely.
    • 
                  
  • Prefer programming to interfaces to allow effortless swapping and mocking.
    • 
                  
  • Spring Boot automatically autowires single constructors without @Autowired.
    • 
                  
  • Use Objects.requireNonNull() to guard against null dependencies.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Setter Injection in Java: Post-Creation Binding, Dynamic Reconfiguration & Spring Boot Patterns

                

              

              

                
1. What is Setter Injection?

                

                  Setter Injection is a form of Dependency Injection (DI) in which an object's collaborator dependencies are supplied through public setter methods after the object has been instantiated.
                

                

                  Unlike Constructor Injection where dependencies are mandatory at instantiation time, Setter Injection decouples object allocation from dependency configuration, allowing dependencies to be supplied, modified, or swapped dynamically throughout the object's lifecycle.
                


                

                  Simple Definition: In Setter Injection, the object is created first (often via a no-argument constructor), and its required collaborators are "injected" afterward by invoking one or more setter methods.
                


                
2. Basic Syntax & Mechanics

                

                  The dependent class exposes a standard JavaBean setter method (setCollaboratorName()) to receive and assign the dependency:
                


                

                  
SetterInjectionSyntax.java

                  
class ServiceA {

    void show() {
        System.out.println("Service A is working");
    }
}

class ServiceB {

    // Dependency field (cannot be declared final if initialized via setter!)
    private ServiceA serviceA;

    // Setter method for injection
    public void setServiceA(ServiceA serviceA) {
        this.serviceA = serviceA;
    }

    void execute() {
        serviceA.show();
    }
}

                


                
3. Complete Pure Java Step-by-Step Implementation

                

                  Let us trace the complete three-tier architectural lifecycle of Setter Injection with defensive null-checking:
                


                

                  
SetterInjectionDemo.java

                  
// Step 1: Create the dependency class
class PaymentService {

    public void processPayment() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed successfully");
    }
}

// Step 2: Create the dependent class with a setter and defensive guard
class OrderService {

    private PaymentService paymentService;

    // Setter Injection method
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        // Defensive guard against uninitialized state
        if (paymentService == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                "PaymentService has not been configured. Call setPaymentService() first."
            );
        }

        paymentService.processPayment();
        System.out.println("Order placed successfully");
    }
}

// Step 3: Main execution demonstrating post-creation injection
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // 1. Instantiate dependency
        PaymentService paymentService = new PaymentService();

        // 2. Instantiate dependent object first
        OrderService orderService = new OrderService();

        // 3. Inject dependency via setter
        orderService.setPaymentService(paymentService);

        // 4. Execute business operation
        orderService.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment processed successfully
Order placed successfully


                
4. Architectural Flow: The Lifecycle of Setter Injection

                

                  
Step 1: Instantiate CollaboratorPaymentService ps = new PaymentService();

                  ⇒
                  
Step 2: Allocate Target ObjectOrderService os = new OrderService();

                  ⇒
                  
Step 3: Inject Via Setteros.setPaymentService(ps);

                  ⇒
                  
Step 4: Execute Methodos.placeOrder();

                


                
5. Setter Injection vs. Constructor Injection: Architectural Face-Off

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Architectural Dimension
                        Constructor Injection
                        Setter Injection
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Injection Timing
                        During object creation.
                        After object creation.
                      

                      

                        Mandatory Dependencies
                        Best suited: Guarantees class is fully formed upon return from new.
                        Risky: Object can exist in an invalid/incomplete half-state.
                      

                      

                        Optional Dependencies
                        Clunky: Requires telescoping constructors or builder pattern.
                        Ideal: Setters can be invoked selectively as needed.
                      

                      

                        final Field Immutability
                        Fully supported (private final Service s;).
                        Impossible: Java prohibits assigning final fields inside setters.
                      

                      

                        Dynamic Reconfiguration
                        Immutable: Cannot re-point references after construction.
                        Supported: Call setter again at runtime to swap collaborators.
                      

                      

                        Spring Recommendation
                        Strongly recommended for all mandatory enterprise beans.
                        Recommended only for optional configurations or circular dependency workarounds.
                      

                    
                  

                


                
6. Dynamic Runtime Reconfiguration: Swapping Strategies

                

                  A notable advantage of Setter Injection is the ability to mutate an object's strategy at runtime without discarding the existing object instance:
                


                

                  
DynamicSetterSwapping.java

                  
interface PaymentService {
    void pay();
}

class UpiPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through UPI");
    }
}

class CardPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through Card");
    }
}

class OrderService {

    private PaymentService paymentService;

    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        OrderService order = new OrderService();

        // 1. Initial strategy: UPI
        order.setPaymentService(new UpiPayment());
        order.placeOrder();

        // 2. Dynamically reconfigured strategy: Card
        order.setPaymentService(new CardPayment());
        order.placeOrder();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment through UPI
Payment through Card


                

                  Multithreading Hazard: Mutating dependencies at runtime via setters introduces severe race conditions in concurrent enterprise environments. If thread A mutates paymentService while thread B is midway through placeOrder(), undefined state corruption can occur.
                


                
7. Setter Injection in Spring Boot

                

                  Spring Boot supports Setter Injection by annotating the setter method with @Autowired:
                


                

                  
SpringBootSetterInjection.java

                  
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed");
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private PaymentService paymentService;

    // Spring invokes this setter automatically after bean instantiation
    @Autowired
    public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

                


                

                  Spring Container Lifecycle:
                  
    
                    
  1. Spring allocates OrderService via its default no-arg constructor.
    2. 
                    
  2. Spring resolves the PaymentService bean from the ApplicationContext.
    3. 
                    
  3. Spring executes setPaymentService(paymentService) to inject the bean.
    4. 
                    
  4. The bean is fully configured and ready to service incoming traffic.
    5. 
                  

                


                
8. Architectural Advantages and Disadvantages

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Architectural Advantages
                        Architectural Disadvantages & Trade-offs
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Flexible Optionality: Cleanly handles optional dependencies without bloated constructors.
                        Incomplete Object Vulnerability: An object can be instantiated but left in a broken state if the setter is omitted.
                      

                      

                        Dynamic Reconfiguration: Dependencies can be swapped at runtime via simple method calls.
                        NullPointerExceptions: Invoking business methods before setters execute throws runtime NPEs.
                      

                      

                        Resolves Circular Dependencies: Can resolve circular references between beans where constructor injection fails.
                        Breaks Immutability: Injected fields cannot be marked final, opening doors to mutable bugs.
                      

                    
                  

                


                
9. Common Mistakes & Gotchas

                

                  Watch Out for These Errors:
                  
    
                    
  • Omitting the Setter Invocation: Calling new OrderService().placeOrder() without calling setPaymentService() results in an immediate NullPointerException or IllegalStateException.
    • 
                    
  • Shadowing Parameter in Setter (Missing this.):
    
                      public void setPaymentService(PaymentService paymentService) { paymentService = paymentService; } → Leaves the instance field untouched! Always write this.paymentService = paymentService;.
                    
    • 
                  

                


                
10. Core Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is Setter Injection in Java?
    A Dependency Injection pattern where collaborators are supplied through public setter methods after the object has been instantiated.
    2. 
                  
  2. Which annotation is used for Setter Injection in Spring Boot?
    The @Autowired annotation placed directly above the setter method.
    3. 
                  
  3. Can a final field be initialized via Setter Injection?
    No. Java language specification dictates that final instance fields must be bound at declaration or inside constructors; ordinary setter methods cannot assign to final fields.
    4. 
                  
  4. When should an architect choose Setter Injection over Constructor Injection?
    When dependencies are genuinely optional, when dependencies must be reconfigured dynamically at runtime, or as a workaround for legacy circular bean dependencies.
    5. 
                  
  5. Why is Constructor Injection preferred for mandatory dependencies?
    Constructor Injection enforces full, atomic object initialization and allows fields to be immutable (final), eliminating partial-state bugs.
    6. 
                  
  6. Can Setter Injection cause concurrency issues?
    Yes. Because setter-injected fields are mutable, reassigning dependencies in a multi-threaded application without synchronization can lead to memory visibility issues and race conditions.
    7. 
                


                
11. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Setter Injection supplies dependencies post-construction via setter methods.
    • 
                  
  • The object is instantiated first, then configured.
    • 
                  
  • Allows dynamic dependency swapping at runtime.
    • 
                  
  • Fields cannot be declared final.
    • 
                  
  • Object risks living in an incomplete, uninitialized state if setters are missed.
    • 
                  
  • Use Constructor Injection for required dependencies; reserve Setter Injection for optional collaborators.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Method Injection in Java: Operation-Scoped Dependencies, Ephemeral Binding & Spring Factory Methods

                

              

              

                
1. What is Method Injection?

                

                  Method Injection is an operational form of Dependency Injection (DI) in which a collaborator dependency is supplied directly as a parameter to an individual method at invocation time.
                

                

                  Unlike Constructor Injection (where dependencies are bound permanently to the instance) or Setter Injection (where dependencies are stored in mutable fields), Method Injection provides ephemeral, operation-scoped dependencies: the dependency exists only for the duration of that method's execution stack frame.
                


                

                  Conceptual Intuition: Suppose an OrderService only needs a PaymentService when executing the placeOrder() action. Storing a payment gateway instance inside the long-lived OrderService might be wasteful or undesirable. Passing the payment gateway directly as placeOrder(paymentService) provides precise, just-in-time injection.
                


                
2. Basic Syntax & Mechanics

                

                  The dependent class does not hold an instance variable for the collaborator. Instead, the method signature accepts the required dependency:
                


                

                  
MethodInjectionSyntax.java

                  
class ServiceA {

    void execute() {
        System.out.println("Service A is working");
    }
}

class ServiceB {

    // Method Injection: Dependency received as a parameter
    void performTask(ServiceA serviceA) {
        serviceA.execute();
    }
}

                


                
3. Complete Pure Java Step-by-Step Implementation

                

                  Let us trace the complete three-tier architectural lifecycle of Method Injection in standard Java:
                


                

                  
MethodInjectionDemo.java

                  
// Step 1: Create the collaborator dependency class
class PaymentService {

    public void processPayment() {
        System.out.println("Payment processed successfully");
    }
}

// Step 2: Create the service class accepting dependency via method parameter
class OrderService {

    // Method Injection
    public void placeOrder(PaymentService paymentService) {

        // Validate and utilize injected dependency
        paymentService.processPayment();

        System.out.println("Order placed successfully");
    }
}

// Step 3: Main execution passing dependency directly at invocation
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        PaymentService paymentService = new PaymentService();
        OrderService orderService = new OrderService();

        // Dependency injected specifically for this method execution
        orderService.placeOrder(paymentService);
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment processed successfully
Order placed successfully


                
4. Method Injection with Polymorphic Interfaces

                

                  By typing the method parameter to an interface rather than a concrete class, callers can supply completely different algorithms on successive invocations of the same method:
                


                

                  
PolymorphicMethodInjection.java

                  
// 1. Contract
interface PaymentService {
    void pay();
}

// 2. Concrete Strategy A
class UpiPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through UPI");
    }
}

// 3. Concrete Strategy B
class CardPayment implements PaymentService {

    @Override
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Payment through Card");
    }
}

// 4. Client service accepting polymorphic method injection
class OrderService {

    public void placeOrder(PaymentService paymentService) {
        paymentService.pay();
        System.out.println("Order placed");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        OrderService orderService = new OrderService();

        // Call 1: Injecting UPI strategy
        orderService.placeOrder(new UpiPayment());

        // Call 2: Injecting Card strategy on the exact same instance!
        orderService.placeOrder(new CardPayment());
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Payment through UPI
Order placed
Payment through Card
Order placed


                
5. The Three Primary DI Flavors: Comprehensive Matrix

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Architectural Feature
                        Constructor Injection
                        Setter Injection
                        Method Injection
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        How Dependency is Supplied
                        Constructor argument
                        Setter method argument
                        Business method argument
                      

                      

                        When Supplied
                        At object instantiation
                        After object instantiation
                        On every method call
                      

                      

                        Stored in Instance Field?
                        Yes (typically final)
                        Yes (mutable field)
                        No (stack-scoped / ephemeral)
                      

                      

                        Ideal Use Case
                        Mandatory, core dependencies
                        Optional / dynamically reconfigurable
                        Operation-specific or varying strategies
                      

                      

                        Invocation Signature
                        new OrderService(payment)
                        order.setPayment(payment)
                        order.placeOrder(payment)
                      

                    
                  

                


                
6. Core Java Method Injection vs. Spring Framework Mechanisms

                

                  It is crucial for enterprise Java developers not to confuse standard Java method-parameter injection with specialized Spring framework features:
                


                
A. Spring @Bean Factory Method Injection

                

                  In Spring @Configuration classes, parameters passed to @Bean methods are resolved and injected automatically by the IoC container:
                


                

                  
SpringConfigurationFactory.java

                  
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    PaymentService paymentService() {
        return new UpiPayment();
    }

    // Spring resolves PaymentService from ApplicationContext and injects it here!
    @Bean
    OrderService orderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        return new OrderService(paymentService);
    }
}

                


                

                  Spring "Lookup Method Injection" Note: In advanced Spring scenarios where a singleton bean must acquire a new prototype bean instance on each method call, Spring uses CGLIB bytecode proxies via @Lookup (known as Lookup Method Injection). This is distinct from standard method parameter passing.
                


                
7. Core Architectural Advantages

                
    
                  
  1. Operation-Scoped Decoupling: The receiving object does not maintain long-lived memory references to dependencies it only needs sporadically.
    2. 
                  
  2. Stateless & Thread-Safe Services: Because dependencies are not stored in mutable instance fields, the service class remains stateless and inherently thread-safe across concurrent web requests.
    3. 
                  
  3. Strategy Pattern Realization: Easily fulfills the GoF Strategy Pattern by allowing callers to swap algorithms per invocation without altering class state.
    4. 
                  
  4. Simple Unit Testing: In JUnit tests, pass mock or dummy dependencies directly to the method under test without configuring reflection or mocking frameworks.
    5. 
                


                
8. Limitations & Architectural Trade-offs

                

                  When Method Injection Becomes a Design Flaw:
                  
    
                    
  • Caller Burden: The calling code must carry or look up dependencies on every single method call, creating leaky abstractions.
    • 
                    
  • Parameter Clutter: If an operation requires 3 or 4 collaborating services, method signatures become unwieldy (parameter smell).
    • 
                    
  • Global Dependencies: If nearly every method in the class requires PaymentService, passing it to every method is redundant; Constructor Injection should be used instead.
    • 
                  

                


                
9. Common Developer Mistakes

                

                  Watch Out for These Errors:
                  
    
                    
  • Instantiating Dependency Inside the Method:
    
                      public void placeOrder() { PaymentService ps = new PaymentService(); } → This is hardcoded internal instantiation, NOT Method Injection! Always declare the dependency as a parameter.
                    
    • 
                    
  • Omitting Mandatory Arguments: Calling orderService.placeOrder() without arguments when the method requires a parameter causes an immediate compile-time error.
    • 
                  

                


                
10. Core Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is Method Injection in Java?
    A Dependency Injection pattern where an external dependency is supplied as a parameter to an individual method rather than through a constructor or setter.
    2. 
                  
  2. How does Method Injection differ from Constructor Injection?
    Constructor Injection binds dependencies to the object during instantiation and stores them in fields; Method Injection supplies dependencies on-demand for specific method calls without storing them.
    3. 
                  
  3. Does Method Injection require Spring Boot or any third-party framework?
    No. Method Injection is a pure object-oriented design technique natively supported by Java method parameters.
    4. 
                  
  4. When should an architect select Method Injection?
    When a dependency is needed only for a single operation, when callers must dynamically provide varying strategies per call, or when designing stateless singleton services.
    5. 
                  
  5. How does Method Injection relate to the Strategy Pattern?
    Method Injection is the standard Java idiom for implementing the Strategy Pattern, allowing different behavioral strategies (e.g., payment algorithms) to be plugged into execution methods dynamically.
    6. 
                


                
11. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • Method Injection supplies collaborators via method parameters.
    • 
                  
  • Dependencies are ephemeral and exist only during the method call's stack frame.
    • 
                  
  • Keeps classes stateless, lightweight, and thread-safe.
    • 
                  
  • Combine with interfaces for dynamic runtime polymorphic strategy swapping.
    • 
                  
  • Avoid when a dependency is universally required by all methods in a class (use Constructor Injection instead).
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphic Architecture
                  
Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): SOLID Design, Lean Contracts & Decoupled Architecture

                

              

              

                
1. Introduction to the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

                

                  The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) is the fourth principle of the renowned SOLID architectural framework in Object-Oriented Software Engineering.
                

                

                  The Foundational Law of ISP (Robert C. Martin):
                  
"Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use."
                

                

                  In traditional, poorly factored systems, developers often construct large, monolithic "fat" interfaces that accumulate dozens of disparate operations. ISP dictates that we must decompose these monolithic contracts into smaller, client-specific, and highly cohesive role interfaces.
                


                
2. Real-World Analogy: The Worker Domain Dilemma

                

                  Imagine designing an enterprise resource system catering to diverse workforce categories:
                

                
    
                  
  • Human Developers: Write enterprise software and require lunch breaks.
    • 
                  
  • UI/UX Designers: Craft wireframes and prototypes, and require lunch breaks.
    • 
                  
  • Automated Robot Workers: Execute batch computing algorithms 24/7, but do not eat.
    • 
                

                

                  If an architect declares a single "fat" Worker interface with writeCode(), designUI(), and eat(), classes are forced to implement nonsensical, irrelevant methods.
                


                
3. Architectural Anti-Pattern: Violating ISP

                

                  The following code illustrates the disastrous consequences of a bloated, non-segregated interface:
                


                

                  
IspViolationDemo.java

                  
// ANTI-PATTERN: Monolithic "Fat" Interface
interface Worker {
    void writeCode();
    void designUI();
    void eat();
}

class Developer implements Worker {

    @Override
    public void writeCode() {
        System.out.println("Developer writes code");
    }

    @Override
    public void designUI() {
        // VIOLATION: Developer doesn't design UI!
        // Leaves empty or throws UnsupportedOperationException
    }

    @Override
    public void eat() {
        System.out.println("Developer eats lunch");
    }
}

class RobotWorker implements Worker {

    @Override
    public void writeCode() {
        System.out.println("Robot writes automated scripts");
    }

    @Override
    public void designUI() {
        // VIOLATION: Unused
    }

    @Override
    public void eat() {
        // CRITICAL VIOLATION: Robots do not eat!
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Robots do not consume food");
    }
}

                


                

                  Symptoms of an ISP Violation:
                  
    
                    
  • Classes containing empty {} method bodies solely to satisfy the Java compiler.
    • 
                    
  • Methods throwing UnsupportedOperationException.
    • 
                    
  • Modifying a method in an interface forces unrelated classes across the entire project to recompile and redeploy.
    • 
                  

                


                
4. Clean Architecture: Applying the Interface Segregation Principle

                

                  We segregate the monolithic Worker interface into three focused, cohesive role interfaces:
                


                

                  
interface Codervoid writeCode();

                  &
                  
interface Designervoid designUI();

                  &
                  
interface Eatervoid eat();

                


                

                  
CleanIspImplementation.java

                  
// 1. Segregated, cohesive role interfaces
interface Coder {
    void writeCode();
}

interface Designer {
    void designUI();
}

interface Eater {
    void eat();
}

// 2. Developer implements only relevant contracts
class Developer implements Coder, Eater {

    @Override
    public void writeCode() {
        System.out.println("Developer writes code");
    }

    @Override
    public void eat() {
        System.out.println("Developer eats");
    }
}

// 3. UI/UX Designer implements only relevant contracts
class UIUXDesigner implements Designer, Eater {

    @Override
    public void designUI() {
        System.out.println("Designer creates UI");
    }

    @Override
    public void eat() {
        System.out.println("Designer eats");
    }
}

// 4. RobotWorker implements only relevant technical contracts
class RobotWorker implements Coder, Designer {

    @Override
    public void writeCode() {
        System.out.println("Robot writes code");
    }

    @Override
    public void designUI() {
        System.out.println("Robot designs UI");
    }
}

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Developer developer = new Developer();
        developer.writeCode();
        developer.eat();

        UIUXDesigner designer = new UIUXDesigner();
        designer.designUI();

        RobotWorker robot = new RobotWorker();
        robot.writeCode();
        robot.designUI();
    }
}

                

                
Output:

                
Developer writes code
Developer eats
Designer creates UI
Robot writes code
Robot designs UI


                
5. Enterprise Spring Boot Architecture: Refactoring Monolithic Services

                

                  In enterprise web backends, bloated service interfaces are an epidemic. Consider a legacy, poorly factored UserService:
                


                

                  
MonolithicUserServiceViolation.java

                  
// BLOATED MONOLITHIC INTERFACE (Violates ISP)
public interface UserService {
    void createUser();
    void deleteUser();
    void sendWelcomeEmail();
    void generatePdfReport();
    void exportToExcelSpreadsheet();
}

                


                

                  The ISP Refactoring: Segregate into specialized, purpose-driven contracts aligned with consumer needs:
                


                

                  
SegregatedEnterpriseServices.java

                  
// 1. Core CRUD Lifecycle Contract
public interface UserManagementService {
    void createUser();
    void deleteUser();
}

// 2. Notification Contract
public interface EmailNotificationService {
    void sendWelcomeEmail();
}

// 3. Document Reporting Contract
public interface ReportGenerationService {
    void generatePdfReport();
}

// 4. Data Export Contract
public interface ExcelExportService {
    void exportToExcelSpreadsheet();
}

// Dedicated implementation focused strictly on identity management
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class UserManagementServiceImpl implements UserManagementService {

    @Override
    public void createUser() {
        System.out.println("User record committed to database");
    }

    @Override
    public void deleteUser() {
        System.out.println("User soft-deleted");
    }
}

                


                

                  Architectural Payoff: A lightweight registration controller now injects UserManagementService without being forced to drag in Excel spreadsheet dependencies or heavy PDF reporting engines!
                


                
6. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) vs. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

                

                  

                    
                      

                        Comparison Dimension
                        Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
                        Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Core Focus
                        Focuses on the internal cohesive responsibilities of a class.
                        Focuses on the contracts exposed to external clients / consumers.
                      

                      

                        Primary Rule
                        A class should have only one reason to change.
                        Clients should not depend on methods they never invoke.
                      

                      

                        Primary Target
                        Class implementations and algorithmic cohesion.
                        Interface boundaries, API granularity, and public signatures.
                      

                      

                        Violation Symptom
                        "God Class" doing database, parsing, and networking.
                        Classes forced to write empty {} implementations or dummy stubs.
                      

                    
                  

                


                
7. Core Architectural Advantages

                
    
                  
  1. Total Decoupling: Clients interact exclusively with the slim slice of functionality they actually care about.
    2. 
                  
  2. Eliminates Dead & Dummy Code: Classes never implement dummy stubs or throw UnsupportedOperationException.
    3. 
                  
  3. Isolated Recompilation: Changing an email signature does not trigger recompilation of user creation or database modules.
    4. 
                  
  4. Laser-Focused Test Mocks: Unit test suites only mock 2 methods instead of 30, speeding up CI/CD pipelines dramatically.
    5. 
                


                
8. Common Misconceptions & Anti-Patterns

                

                  Watch Out for These Errors:
                  
    
                    
  • The "One Method Per Interface" Extremism (Interface Explosion): ISP does not mandate that every single method must have its own interface! Group methods that naturally cohere to the same domain responsibility (e.g., save() and delete() belong together).
    • 
                    
  • Monolithic Interfaces: Stuffing billing, logging, and notifications into one interface.
    • 
                    
  • Confusing ISP with Dependency Injection: ISP designs the granular shape of contracts; DI injects concrete providers of those contracts.
    • 
                  

                


                
9. Core Interview Questions & Answers

                
    
                  
  1. What is the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?
    The fourth SOLID principle, stating that clients should never be forced to depend upon methods or contracts that they do not use.
    2. 
                  
  2. How can you quickly identify an ISP violation during code reviews?
    When classes implement interfaces by leaving empty method bodies {}, returning dummy null values, or throwing UnsupportedOperationException.
    3. 
                  
  3. How does ISP relate to multiple inheritance of type in Java?
    Java classes can implement multiple interfaces (e.g., implements Coder, Eater), allowing classes to assemble precise capabilities like building blocks.
    4. 
                  
  4. Does ISP demand single-method interfaces?
    No. ISP advocates for cohesive, client-oriented interfaces, not fragmented single-method micro-interfaces.
    5. 
                  
  5. What is the primary difference between SRP and ISP?
    SRP addresses class responsibilities and internal cohesion ("one reason to change"), whereas ISP addresses external client contracts and API design ("clients only see what they use").
    6. 
                


                
10. Quick Revision Summary

                
    
                  
  • ISP = 4th SOLID Principle ("Clients should not depend on methods they don't use").
    • 
                  
  • Decompose monolithic "fat" interfaces into cohesive role interfaces.
    • 
                  
  • Classes should implement only the interfaces relevant to their domain role.
    • 
                  
  • Prevents empty stubs and UnsupportedOperationException.
    • 
                  
  • Enhances maintainability, speeds up unit testing, and decouples enterprise architectures.
    • 
                

              

            


            
            

              

                

                  Chapter 5: Capstone Project — Architecture & Production Engineering
                  
Project: MyTube Video Platform — Spring Boot, MySQL & SOLID Architecture Capstone

                

              

              

                
1. Project Overview & Architectural Vision

                

                  MyTube is a production-grade, enterprise video-sharing platform inspired by modern video hubs like YouTube. This capstone project integrates all core disciplines mastered throughout Object-Oriented Programming: OOP Pillars, SOLID Principles, Interface-Driven Design, Constructor Dependency Injection, and full-stack backend development with Java 21, Spring Boot, and MySQL.
                

                

                  The backend micro-architecture is structured as a modular monolith responsible for user identity, media metadata, interactions (likes, comments, subscriptions), and transactional database operations. Actual high-volume binary video assets are segregated into an abstract file storage provider rather than stored as BLOBs in MySQL.
                


                

                  Architectural Core: Why a modular monolith instead of microservices? For solo developers and growing platforms, a modular monolith minimizes network latency, simplifies distributed transaction debugging, eliminates deployment overhead, and permits straightforward extraction into microservices when traffic demands.

6. Relational Database Schema Design

                

                  The core relational schema is designed with foreign key constraints, indexing for high-frequency queries, and unique composite indexes to prevent duplicate interactions:
                


                

                  

                    
                      

                        Table Name
                        Columns & Types
                        Keys & Integrity Constraints
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        users
                        id (BIGINT PK), username (VARCHAR), email (VARCHAR), password_hash (VARCHAR), created_at (TIMESTAMP)
                        UNIQUE(email), UNIQUE(username)
                      

                      

                        videos
                        id (BIGINT PK), user_id (BIGINT FK), title (VARCHAR), description (TEXT), video_url (VARCHAR), thumbnail_url (VARCHAR), visibility (VARCHAR), created_at (TIMESTAMP)
                        FK(user_id → users.id), INDEX(user_id, created_at)
                      

                      

                        comments
                        id (BIGINT PK), video_id (BIGINT FK), user_id (BIGINT FK), content (TEXT), created_at (TIMESTAMP)
                        FK(video_id → videos.id), FK(user_id → users.id)
                      

                      

                        video_likes
                        id (BIGINT PK), video_id (BIGINT FK), user_id (BIGINT FK), liked_at (TIMESTAMP)
                        UNIQUE KEY uq_video_user (video_id, user_id)
                      

                      

                        subscriptions
                        id (BIGINT PK), subscriber_id (BIGINT FK), channel_id (BIGINT FK), subscribed_at (TIMESTAMP)
                        UNIQUE KEY uq_sub_channel (subscriber_id, channel_id)
                      

                      

                        video_views
                        id (BIGINT PK), video_id (BIGINT FK), user_id (BIGINT FK nullable), viewed_at (TIMESTAMP)
                        INDEX(video_id, viewed_at)
                      

                    
                  

                


                
7. SOLID Principles Applied in MyTube

                

                  

                    
                      

                        SOLID Principle
                        Architectural Implementation in MyTube
                      

                    
                    
                      

                        Single Responsibility (SRP)
                        VideoService manages business metadata; StorageService handles binary bytes; VideoController handles HTTP mapping.
                      

                      

                        Open/Closed (OCP)
                        Add a new S3VideoStorage or CloudflareR2Storage without modifying existing video service code.
                      

                      

                        Liskov Substitution (LSP)
                        Any VideoStorage implementation can be swapped transparently without breaking the upload workflow.
                      

                      

                        Interface Segregation (ISP)
                        Segregate media upload from streaming URLs: MediaUploadService and MediaStreamingService instead of one fat interface.
                      

                      

                        Dependency Inversion (DIP)
                        VideoService depends on the abstract interface VideoStorage, injected via Constructor Injection.
                      

                    
                  

                


                

                  
StorageDIPExample.java

                  
// 1. Storage Abstraction (DIP)
public interface VideoStorage {
    String uploadVideo(byte[] bytes, String fileName);
    void deleteVideo(String storageKey);
}

// 2. Concrete Local Provider
@Component
public class LocalVideoStorage implements VideoStorage {
    @Override
    public String uploadVideo(byte[] bytes, String fileName) {
        // Save to /var/mytube/videos/...
        return "http://localhost:8080/media/" + fileName;
    }

    @Override
    public void deleteVideo(String storageKey) {
        // Delete from local disk
    }
}

// 3. Service utilizing Constructor Injection (SRP + DIP)
@Service
public class VideoServiceImpl {

    private final VideoStorage videoStorage;

    public VideoServiceImpl(VideoStorage videoStorage) {
        this.videoStorage = videoStorage;
    }
}

2. The Video JPA Entity

                

                  
Video.java

                  
package com.mytube.video;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

@Entity
@Table(name = "videos")
public class Video {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @NotBlank(message = "Video title must not be blank")
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String title;

    @Column(columnDefinition = "TEXT")
    private String description;

    @NotBlank(message = "Video URL must not be blank")
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String videoUrl;

    @Column(nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;

    // Required by JPA specification
    protected Video() {
    }

    public Video(String title, String description, String videoUrl) {
        this.title = title;
        this.description = description;
        this.videoUrl = videoUrl;
        this.createdAt = LocalDateTime.now();
    }

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getTitle() {
        return title;
    }

    public String getDescription() {
        return description;
    }

    public String getVideoUrl() {
        return videoUrl;
    }

    public LocalDateTime getCreatedAt() {
        return createdAt;
    }

    public void update(String title, String description, String videoUrl) {
        this.title = title;
        this.description = description;
        this.videoUrl = videoUrl;
    }
}

5. Transactional Video Service (Constructor Injection)

                

                  
VideoService.java

                  
package com.mytube.video;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import java.util.List;

@Service
@Transactional
public class VideoService {

    private final VideoRepository videoRepository;

    // Constructor Injection
    public VideoService(VideoRepository videoRepository) {
        this.videoRepository = videoRepository;
    }

    public Video createVideo(String title, String description, String videoUrl) {
        Video video = new Video(title, description, videoUrl);
        return videoRepository.save(video);
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<Video> getAllVideos() {
        return videoRepository.findAll();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public Video getVideoById(Long id) {
        return videoRepository.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new VideoNotFoundException(id));
    }

    public void deleteVideo(Long id) {
        Video video = getVideoById(id);
        videoRepository.delete(video);
    }
}

                


                
6. REST Controller with Modern Java Record DTO

                

                  
VideoController.java

                  
package com.mytube.video;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/videos")
public class VideoController {

    private final VideoService videoService;

    public VideoController(VideoService videoService) {
        this.videoService = videoService;
    }

    // Immutable Request DTO via Java 21 Record
    public record CreateVideoRequest(
            @NotBlank(message = "Title is required") String title,
            String description,
            @NotBlank(message = "Video URL is required") String videoUrl
    ) {}

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public Video createVideo(@Valid @RequestBody CreateVideoRequest request) {
        return videoService.createVideo(
                request.title(),
                request.description(),
                request.videoUrl()
        );
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<Video> getAllVideos() {
        return videoService.getAllVideos();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Video getVideoById(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return videoService.getVideoById(id);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void deleteVideo(@PathVariable Long id) {
        videoService.deleteVideo(id);
    }
}

package com.mytube.video;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

                  Chapter 6: Classes, Fields & State Engineering
                  
Fields in Java: Instance State, Static Shared Memory, Default Values & Encapsulation
