                        Enables polymorphic capability without forcing a shared lineage.
                      

                      

                        Allow a class to provide multiple distinct capabilities
                        Interface
                        A class can implement multiple interfaces (implements Flyable, Swimmable).
                      

                      

                        Provide swappable / pluggable implementations
                        Interface
                        Complete decoupling of client caller from supplier.
                      

                      

                        Share common instance fields & mutable state
                        Abstract Class
                        Interfaces cannot maintain instance fields.
                      

                      

                        Share constructor logic & initialization order
                        Abstract Class
                        Subclasses invoke parent constructor via super(...).
                      

                      

                        Model a strict "is-a" parent-child relationship
                        Abstract Class
                        Ensures cohesive semantic hierarchy (e.g. Eagle is-a Bird).
                      

                      

                        Combine shared state and pluggable contract
                        Both (Hybrid)
                        Abstract class extends base state while implementing capability interface.
                      

                    
                  

                


                

                  
BirdHybridExample.java

                  
interface Flyable {
    void fly();
}

abstract class Bird {
    protected String name;

    // Shared constructor logic
    Bird(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    // Shared concrete behavior
    void eat() {
        System.out.println(name + " is eating seeds");
    }
}

// Eagle is-a Bird (state & identity) and can-do Flyable (capability)
class Eagle extends Bird implements Flyable {

    Eagle(String name) {
        super(name);
    }

    @Override
    public void fly() {
        System.out.println(name + " soars high in the sky");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Eagle eagle = new Eagle("Bald Eagle");
        eagle.eat();
        eagle.fly();
    }
}

                


                

                  
Console Output

                  
Bald Eagle is eating seeds
Bald Eagle soars high in the sky

                


                
4. When Should You AVOID Creating an Interface?

                

                  Over-abstraction leads to the dreaded "Interface Soup" anti-pattern, where code navigation is bloated by meaningless 1-to-1 interfaces:
                

                
    
                  
  • Only One Trivial Implementation: If a class is a simple private helper or internal orchestrator with no alternative implementations and no dynamic mocking requirements, creating an interface adds pure boilerplate.
    • 
                  
  • Premature Abstraction: Defining interfaces before requirements stabilize forces developers to update both the interface and the class for every minor signature change.
    • 
                  
  • Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) & Value Objects: Plain data holders should be concrete classes or Java records, never interfaces.
    • 
                


                

                  ⚠️ Rule of Clean Architecture: Create an abstraction when it solves an actual design variation, testing isolation, or third-party contract boundary — not merely to satisfy dogmatic conventions.
                


                
5. High-Frequency Interview Questions

                

                  
Q1. Why do we use interfaces in Java?

                  
To define architectural contracts, support multiple implementations, achieve loose coupling, enable polymorphism, and support multiple inheritance of type.

                


                

                  
Q2. Can a Java class implement multiple interfaces?

                  
Yes. Java allows a class to implement any number of interfaces simultaneously (e.g. class SmartPhone implements Camera, MusicPlayer, GpsLocator), overcoming the single-inheritance restriction of classes.

                


                

                  
Q3. Can an interface have a constructor in Java?

                  
No. Interfaces have no instance state (fields) to initialize and cannot be instantiated with new, so they cannot possess constructors.

                


                

                  
Q4. Can an interface contain method implementations?

                  
Yes. Modern Java allows interfaces to have concrete bodies via default methods (Java 8), static utility methods (Java 8), and private helper routines (Java 9).

                


                

                  
Q5. Does every Spring Boot service require an interface?

                  
No. While commonly practiced for layered decoupling and proxy generation, having an interface for a single, trivial CRUD service is optional. Modern Spring supports class-based CGLIB proxies. Use interfaces when you foresee multiple strategies, remote RPC boundaries, or clean domain isolation.

                


                

                  
Q6. How does an interface support runtime polymorphism?

                  
An interface reference variable can hold a reference to any object that implements that interface. Method dispatch is determined dynamically at runtime based on the actual concrete instance assigned to the reference.

                


                
6. Quick Revision Summary

                

                  
    
                    
  • Interface = Contract / Capability: Defines what needs to be done, leaving how to concrete implementors.
    • 
                    
  • Loose Coupling: High-level classes depend on abstractions (interfaces) rather than volatile concrete classes.
    • 
                    
  • Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules do not import low-level modules; both depend on abstractions.
    • 
                    
  • Multiple Implementations: Easily swap storage (Local vs S3), payments (UPI vs Card), or notifications (Email vs SMS).
    • 
                    
  • Frictionless Testing: Replace external dependencies with fast in-memory mock or fake test doubles.
    • 
                    
  • Abstract Class vs Interface: Choose abstract classes for shared state, constructors, and "is-a" identity; choose interfaces for capabilities and pluggable contracts.
    • 
                    
  • Avoid Overengineering: Don't introduce interfaces blindly — introduce them when they solve real design problems!
    •
